condensed.angle: A. Sequential dependencies in repeated play (win-stay/lose-shift, cycles, opponent switching, exploitability)

verified.statement: In Wang et al.'s experiment at the standard payoff (a=2: win 2, tie 1, loss 0, i.e., zero-sum-equivalent), conditional on a player's own previous outcome with hand X, the next throw was: after a WIN - repeat X 0.528, the hand X beats (X-) 0.247, the hand that beats X (X+) 0.226; after a TIE - repeat X 0.432, X+ 0.334, X- 0.234; after a LOSS - X- 0.365, repeat X 0.360, X+ 0.276. Concretely: after winning with Rock -> Rock 0.528; after a Rock-Rock tie -> Rock 0.432, Paper 0.334, Scissors 0.234; after losing with Rock to Paper -> Scissors (beats the winning Paper) 0.365, Rock 0.360, Paper (copying the winner) 0.276. So in this sample the loser did NOT tend to copy the hand that beat them; copying was the least likely response. (Wang, Xu & Zhou 2014, Sci Rep 4:5830, Fig. 3G; 72 Zhejiang students in 12 six-person groups, 300 rounds, random re-matching; values pooled over hands and averaged over groups.)
verified.evidence: Re-digitized independently from the arXiv vector source ExpWLTall.eps (https://arxiv.org/e-print/1404.5199; gnuplot, panel baseline y=2030, '0.2' tick at y=2297, so 1.0 = 1335 units). a=2 panel (2nd column, black bars) stroke heights: W- 330, W0 704, W+ 301; T- 312, T0 576, T+ 446; L- 487, L0 480, L+ 368 -> 0.247/0.527/0.225; 0.234/0.431/0.334; 0.365/0.360/0.276. Error bars: W0 spans 2680-2787 (mid 0.527, +/-0.040); W- 2327-2392 (0.247 +/-0.024); L- 2495-2538 (0.364 +/-0.016). A separate figure in Wang & Xu arXiv:1407.1170 (lose.pdf/tie.pdf/win.pdf, 1.0 = 3520.83 units) gives a=2 lose 0.365/0.357/0.278, tie 0.233/0.436/0.332, win 0.248/0.527/0.225 (-,0,+). Published version (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5376050/), Fig. 3 caption: '(F-J) Empirically determined CR parameters, with the mean (vertical bin) and the SEM (error bar) of each CR parameter obtained by considering all the populations of the same a value.' Text: 'if a player wins over her opponent in one play, her probability (W0) of repeating the same action in the next play is considerably higher than her probabilities (W- and W+)'; 'for payoff parameter a >= 2, if a player loses ... she is more likely to shift action clockwise (probability L-)'; clockwise = '(R -> S, S -> P, P -> R)'. Methods: 360 students, 60 groups of N=6, 300 rounds, a in {1.1, 2, 4, 9, 100}, random pairwise matching each round, 40-s limit; reward y = r*x + 5 with r = 0.45/(1+a) so the expected TOTAL is 50 RMB including the 5 RMB show-up fee. Derived edges recomputed: X+ after opponent win = 0.528-0.247 = +0.281; X+ after tie = 0.432-0.234 = +0.198; X after opponent loss = 0.365-0.276 = +0.089.
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed (Sci Rep 2014); lab, cash-incentivised, human opponents; 72 subjects / 12 groups at a=2; 300 rounds with up to 40 s per decision; values only in a figure (exactly recoverable from vector source); not independently replicated outside the Zhejiang group.
verified.design: Lab, Zhejiang University (China). 360 students in 60 groups of 6 (72 students / 12 groups at a=2); 300 rounds; each round random pairwise re-matching within the group (P(same opponent next round)=1/(N-1)=1/5 per S2); feedback = own and opponent's hand and payoff; paid real cash proportional to points (exchange rate set so Nash play earns 50 RMB, plus 5 RMB show-up); human opponents; 40-s decision limit.
verified.effect: vs 1/3: win-stay +19.5 pp; tie-stay +9.9 pp; tie->X+ +0.1 pp, tie->X- -9.9 pp; after loss X- +3.2 pp, repeat +2.7 pp, copy-the-winner (X+) -5.7 pp. SEMs across 12 groups 0.015-0.040.
verified.implication: Against a population behaving like this (derived, my arithmetic: edge = P(they play the hand I beat) - P(they play the hand that beats mine)): if the opponent just WON with X, throw X+ (e.g., they won with Paper -> you throw Scissors): +0.281 per throw; after a TIE on X, throw X+ (Rock-Rock tie -> Paper): +0.198; if the opponent just LOST with X, throw X itself (they lost with Rock -> you throw Rock, which beats their likely Scissors and ties a repeat): +0.089.
verified.caveats: Values are digitized from a figure, not printed in the paper. They are means over groups. Random re-matching means the 'previous outcome' was usually against a different opponent. Single Chinese student sample with long decision windows. Other datasets differ markedly (see A2, B1-B5, C1). Edges are upper bounds that assume a non-adapting, population-average opponent.

verified.statement: In Wang et al.'s Zhejiang data (S1 Fig. 3F-J), the post-loss downgrade (lost with Rock -> Scissors, L-) was 0.325 (a=1.1), 0.365 (a=2), 0.379 (a=4), 0.414 (a=9), 0.397 (a=100), and win-stay was 0.568, 0.528, 0.504, 0.448, 0.453 (both trends non-monotonic at a=100); only at a=1.1 was the post-loss upgrade (Rock -> Paper) the most common response (0.364). Wang & Xu (arXiv:1407.1170; 7 levels incl. a=1 and a=infinity, 72 subjects each, overlapping S1's data) report L- rising with a (Spearman rho = 0.355) and an overall repeat rate of 0.440 at a=2 (0.708 at a=1, 0.531 at 1.1, 0.411 at 4, 0.370 at 9, 0.386 at 100, 0.376 at infinity). A knockout with tie-replay corresponds to a=2. The direction of a stakes effect on win-stay is NOT robust across labs: Forder & Dyson (2016) found that raising the win value (+2/0/-1, equivalent to a = 3) increased win-stay from 35.9% to 48.4%.
verified.evidence: ExpWLTall.eps bar heights /1335 (arXiv:1404.5199): a=1.1 L-/L0/L+ 434/414/486 -> 0.325/0.310/0.364, W0 758 -> 0.568; a=4 506/453/374 -> 0.379/0.339/0.280, W0 672 -> 0.503; a=9 552/404/377 -> 0.413/0.303/0.282, W0 598 -> 0.448; a=100 529/457/348 -> 0.396/0.342/0.261, W0 604 -> 0.452. Wang & Xu LaTeX (https://arxiv.org/abs/1407.1170), Table 'The three types of transit', a=2: T_RSP 0.282 (s.e. 0.011), stay 0.440 (0.020), T_RPS 0.279 (0.013); 'when people lose, they tend to increase L- behavior with the winning payoff a (Spearman's rho=0.355, Prob > |t|=0.000)'; left-shift (-) = 'turn to the dominated strategy beaten by the current strategy'. Their lose.pdf at a=infinity: 0.429/0.324/0.247. Forder & Dyson 2016 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5034336/) Discussion: 'as the variable value of a (incentive) increased, so too did the frequency of lose-downgrade responses ... but the frequency of win-stay responses actually decreased. Here, there appears to be contrast with the data from our win-heavy condition (where win = +2 and loss = -1 and so incentive was also high) in which the frequency of win-stay responses actually increased relative to baseline condition'.
verified.reliability: S1 peer-reviewed; S3 unpublished preprint sharing 5 of 7 treatments with S1; between-group, 12 groups per level; figure-derived values.
verified.design: Same as A1 (S1: 59 analysed groups of 6, 300 rounds, a in {1.1, 2, 4, 9, 100}); S3 adds a=1 and a=infinity (84 groups x 6, 72 subjects per level). Cash incentives, random re-matching, human opponents.
verified.effect: Loss->X- ranges from -0.8 pp (a=1.1) to +8.1 pp (a=9) above 1/3. Win-stay ranges from +12.0 to +23.5 pp. Overall stay at a=2 is +10.7 pp.
verified.implication: In a knockout bout, a tie is effectively worth half-way between a win and a loss, which corresponds to a=2. Larger stakes for winning (larger a) predict more downgrading after a loss and less win-stay.
verified.caveats: Figure-derived. A different 'a' changes the game itself, not only the motivation. S3 is an unpublished preprint, and its treatments overlap S1's data.

verified.statement: Both widely read 2014 media summaries of Wang et al. reversed the paper's post-loss direction. NPR (S. Neuman, 2 May 2014) wrote that 'if the player lost with rock, he or she was likely to try paper in the next round'; MIT Technology Review (30 Apr 2014) wrote that losers 'switch to the next action in a clockwise direction (where R -> P -> S is clockwise)', whereas the paper defines clockwise as R->S, S->P, P->R. In the paper's a=2 data, Rock->Paper after a loss (L+ 0.276) was the least likely response and Rock->Scissors (L- 0.365) the most likely, so the media-derived tip 'opponent lost with Rock, throw Scissors to beat their Paper' has a derived edge of 0.276 - 0.360 = -0.084 per throw against that population (the same move is positive in repeat-averse Western samples for a different reason: losers rarely repeat).
verified.evidence: NPR original (https://www.npr.org/sections/thetwo-way/2014/05/02/308953770/rock-scissors-paper-strategy-could-be-more-than-mere-childs-play): 'if the player lost, he or she tended to choose an easily predicted next option that fell in sequence of the order of the game's name: rock, then paper, then scissors. For example, if the player lost with rock, he or she was likely to try paper in the next round'. MIT Technology Review (https://www.technologyreview.com/2014/04/30/13423/how-to-win-at-rock-paper-scissors/): 'players who win tend to stick with the same action while those who lose switch to the next action in a clockwise direction (where R -> P -> S is clockwise).' Paper (arXiv v1 LaTeX and PMC5376050): counter-clockwise '(i.e., R -> P, P -> S, S -> R ...)' or clockwise '(R -> S, S -> P, P -> R)'. arXiv:1404.5199 has only v1 (21 Apr 2014), which uses the same definition; pooling across the five a levels would not reverse the result either (mean L- 0.376 vs L+ 0.293 from the digitized bars).
verified.reliability: Two news outlets (secondary) compared with the peer-reviewed primary source and its LaTeX/figure source.
verified.design: Media articles (2014) describing S1; compared against S1 data (see A1).
verified.effect: Media claim implies a loss->upgrade effect above 1/3. The data show loss->upgrade at -5.7 pp below 1/3 at a=2. Only at a=1.1 did upgrades lead (0.364).
verified.implication: Do not use the popular 'losers move Rock->Paper->Scissors' rule as stated. In Western lab and dyad samples, the same Scissors response happens to be positive for a different reason: losers rarely repeat there (see C2).
verified.caveats: The media may have pooled conditions or relied on the arXiv preprint wording. The a=1.1 treatment does show a weak loss-upgrade.

verified.statement: Wang et al. (2014): marginal frequencies R 0.36 +/- 0.08, P 0.33 +/- 0.07, S 0.32 +/- 0.06 (354 players; a=2 subset 0.36/0.32/0.32). Population-level counter-clockwise cycling (slightly Rock-rich -> Paper-rich -> Scissors-rich) was weak: 0.027 +/- 0.008 cycles per round at a=2 (about one cycle per 37 rounds; about 0.03, 'one cycle in about 35 rounds', across conditions per Zhou 2016), measured in 6-person random-matching groups. Xu, Zhou & Wang (2013) reported 0.029 +/- 0.009 for 12 standard-RPS groups, but those 12 sessions (Zhejiang, December 2010, 72 subjects, 0.15 RMB per point) appear to be the same a=2 sessions later included in Wang et al. (experiment run December 2010-March 2014; 12 a=2 groups, r = 0.45/3 = 0.15 RMB per point), so this is a re-analysis with a different counting method, not an independent replication.
verified.evidence: PMC5376050: 'Averaged among the 354 players of these 59 populations, the probabilities that a player adopts action R, P, S at one game round are, respectively, 0.36 +/- 0.08, 0.33 +/- 0.07 and 0.32 +/- 0.06'; 'mean frequency to be 0.031 +/- 0.006 (a = 1.1, mean +/- SEM), 0.027 +/- 0.008 (a = 2), 0.031 +/- 0.008 (a = 4), 0.022 +/- 0.008 (a = 9) and 0.018 +/- 0.007 (a = 100)'. arXiv Table S1: a=2, m=72, R 0.36, P 0.32, S 0.32. Methods: 'The experiment was performed at Zhejiang University in the period of December 2010 to March 2014'; r = 0.45/(1+a). Zhou 2016 review (arXiv:1903.05991): 'The mean cycling frequency is nu approx +0.03 (one counter-clockwise cycle in about 35 game rounds)'. Xu, Zhou & Wang 2013 (arXiv:1301.3238 LaTeX): 'These 12 experimental sessions were conducted during December 2010 in the experimental social science laboratory of Zhejiang University. The 72 experimental subjects ...'; 'one experimental point equals 0.15 Yuan RMB'; abstract: 'The mean cycling frequency was measured to be 0.029 +/- 0.009 period per experimental round.'
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed (Sci Rep; Physica A); 12 groups of 6 at a=2; same laboratory and likely same sessions.
verified.design: As A1 (S1). S4: 12 populations of N=6, standard RPS, random pairwise matching (abstract only).
verified.effect: Rock +2.7 pp above 1/3. The cycle is a slow drift (0.027 cycles/round), and the social-state deviation per round is small.
verified.implication: Population cycles are too slow and weak to time throws in a short team match. They also arise from players' own conditional responses, so exploit the conditional responses directly.
verified.caveats: Cycling was measured in 6-person random-matching groups, not in 1-vs-1 head-to-head play.

verified.statement: Wang et al. (2014) report NO payoff advantage for a player who exploits others' conditional responses. Their payoff analysis covers only the case where ALL players adopt the same conditional-response strategy. That advantage scales with (a-2), so it is zero for standard zero-sum RPS (a=2).
verified.evidence: PMC5376050: 'By uniformly sampling 2.4 x 10^9 instances of Gamma from the three-dimensional probability simplex, we find that for a > 2, gcr has high chance of being lower than g0 ..., with the mean value of (gcr - g0) being -0.0085(a - 2)'; best sampled sets give gcr = g0 + 0.035(a-2), 0.034(a-2), 0.033(a-2); 'For large a these CR strategies outperform the NE mixed strategy in payoff by about 10%'; abstract: 'if all players adopt the same optimized conditional response strategy, their accumulated payoff will be much higher than the reference value of the NE mixed strategy'. arXiv SI: empirical mean payoff minus g0 = 0.009 +/- 0.004 (a=1.1), 0.000 +/- 0.006 (a=2), 0.004 +/- 0.012 (a=4), 0.01 +/- 0.02 (a=9), 0.05 +/- 0.37 (a=100). No single-deviator or exploiter payoff is computed anywhere in the paper or SI. The arXiv v1 abstract said the strategy 'may offer higher payoffs to individual players', which the published abstract reworded to the all-players case.
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed; analytic/numerical Markov model calibrated on the experiment; reading unambiguous.
verified.design: Analytic and numerical Markov-chain model calibrated on the S1 experiment.
verified.effect: Collective gain up to +0.035(a-2) per round, which is 0 at a=2. No individual exploitation edge is reported.
verified.implication: The 'higher payoff' claims in press coverage of this paper are irrelevant to a zero-sum knockout tournament. Exploitation edges must come from other studies or derivations (C2, D1-D3).
verified.caveats: None regarding the reading. The lead's expectation of a reported exploitation edge was not met.

verified.statement: Dyson et al. (2016), Canadian students vs a balanced-random computer. After a LOSS with X: X- (downgrade, e.g., lost with Rock -> Scissors) 0.405, X+ (e.g., -> Paper) 0.372, repeat 0.223. After a DRAW: X+ (Rock-Rock draw -> Paper) 0.401, X- 0.324, repeat 0.275. After a WIN: repeat 0.357, X- 0.336, X+ 0.307 (no significant differences). Rock was played 35.60% of the time (n.s.). Switch directions persisted: after upgrading, players upgraded again 0.435; after downgrading, they downgraded again 0.424.
verified.evidence: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4740902/ Results: outcome x strategy 'F(4, 120) = 6.71, MSE = 0.061, p < 0.001, eta_p^2 = 0.183'; 'No significant differences in trial n + 1 strategy were observed following a win although numerically the data were in favour of staying. In contrast, a loss more likely prompted item switching than staying (numerically in favour of item downgrading) and following a draw, participants were inclined to switch and specifically upgrade their item relative to staying'; second-order 'F(4, 120) = 13.12 ... participants who upgraded were more likely to continue upgrading'; 'Rock (80.10 trials; 35.60%)', F(2,60) = 1.64, p = 0.203. Method: 31 undergraduates (26 female), Ryerson, course credit; 225 trials (3 x 75); 'In each block, the computer played Rock, Paper and Scissors 25 times in a random order'. My recomputation from srep20479-s2.xls (Europe PMC supplementary files; 31 rows; outcome-level value = unweighted mean of the three item cells per participant, then mean over participants): loss stay 0.223 (SEM 0.026), up 0.372 (0.018), down 0.405 (0.028); draw 0.275/0.401/0.324; win 0.357/0.307/0.336; up->up 0.435 (0.022), down->down 0.424 (0.027), stay->stay 0.305; item marginals 0.356/0.322/0.322 and outcome marginals W 0.343, D 0.326, L 0.332 reproduce the paper's text exactly. Derived edges reproduced: +0.149 (X- after opponent loss), +0.126 (X- after draw), +0.029 best after opponent win.
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed; N=31; computer opponent; no performance pay; single lab; conditional values computed from authors' per-participant spreadsheet.
verified.design: Lab, Ryerson University (Canada). N=31 undergraduates (26 female), course credit, no performance pay. 225 trials (3 x 75) vs a computer playing each hand 25 times per block in random order (unexploitable).
verified.effect: Loss: downgrade +7.2 pp, upgrade +3.9 pp, repeat -11.0 pp vs 1/3. Draw: upgrade +6.8 pp, repeat -5.8 pp. Win: repeat +2.4 pp (n.s.). Second-order continuation about +9-10 pp.
verified.implication: Against such players (derived): after the opponent loses with X, throw X- (e.g., they lost with Rock -> you throw Scissors; beats their Paper, loses only to a Rock repeat): +0.149. After a draw on X, throw X- (Rock-Rock -> Scissors): +0.126. After the opponent wins, edges are tiny (best +0.029).
verified.caveats: Small N. Computer opponent, no money. The direction contrasts within lose and win cells were not individually significant (only the interaction was). Conditional numbers are my computation from the authors' spreadsheet.

verified.statement: Forder & Dyson (2016; 36 Sussex undergraduates, 450 trials vs a random computer, course credit or GBP 20 independent of performance): after a WIN stay 42.45%, upgrade 29.32%, downgrade 28.23%; after a LOSS upgrade 39.13%, downgrade 39.41%, stay 21.46%; after a DRAW upgrade 37.32%, downgrade 33.40%, stay 29.28% (n.s.). In the block where wins were worth +2 (vs +1, loss -1, draw 0) win-stay rose from 35.92% to 48.44% (Tukey p < .05) while lose-shift was unchanged; responses after wins were slower (708 ms) than after losses (555 ms) or draws (505 ms; 29 participants). Derived: opponent won with X -> X+ +0.142; opponent lost with X -> X- +0.177; repeating your own winning hand -0.179. The stakes effect on win-stay is not established across labs: Wang & Xu's between-group manipulation found win-stay DEcreasing as the value of a win rose.
verified.evidence: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5034336/: outcome x strategy 'F(4, 140) = 18.17, MSE = 0.051, p < 0.001, eta_p^2 = 0.342'; 'following a win (42.45%, 29.32% and 28.23%, respectively)' [stay, upgrade, downgrade]; 'following a loss (39.13%, 39.41% and 21.46%, respectively)' [upgrade, downgrade, stay]; draw '(37.32%, 33.40% and 29.28%, respectively) were not statistically significant'; 'the proportion of stay responses following win trials was significantly larger during win-heavy conditions relative to the baseline condition (48.44% versus 35.92%, respectively; Tukey's HSD, p < 0.05)'; RT 'responses following wins were slower than responses following losses or draws (708, 555 and 505 ms, respectively' (data from 29 participants after exclusions); Method: 36 undergraduates (30 female), 'course credit or GBP 20 ... Compensation was independent of task performance'; 3 blocks of 150, 'the computer played Rock, Paper and Scissors 50 times in a random order'; baseline +1/-1/0, win-heavy +2/-1/0, lose-heavy +1/-2/0. Discussion explicitly contrasts with Wang & Xu (win-stay decreased with incentive a).
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed; N=36; within-subject; computer opponent; points not converted to money; EEG lab.
verified.design: Lab, University of Sussex (UK), EEG. N=36 undergraduates (30 female); course credit or GBP 20 independent of performance. 450 trials (3 blocks of 150: baseline +1/-1/0, win-heavy +2/-1/0, lose-heavy +1/-2/0) vs a computer playing each hand 50 times per block in random order.
verified.effect: Win-stay +9.1 pp overall (+15.1 pp in the win-heavy block). Lose-shift = 78.5% (+11.9 pp vs 66.7%). Loss directions about equal (downgrade +6.1 pp, upgrade +5.8 pp).
verified.implication: Derived: after the opponent WINS with X, throw X+ (they won with Paper -> Scissors): +0.142. After they LOSE with X, throw X- (lost with Rock -> Scissors): +0.177. Do not repeat your own winning hand: -0.179. Higher stakes for a win increase opponents' win-stay.
verified.caveats: Computer opponent; points not converted to money. The UK sample is similar to B1, with the same lab procedure.

verified.statement: Across six Dyson-lab samples (Dyson 2021 Exps 1-3, n=36 each, Alberta; Srihaput et al. 2020 Exps 1-2, n=40 each, Sussex/Alberta; Forder & Dyson 2016, n=36, Sussex), all against computer opponents with no or token performance pay, lose-shift was consistently above the 66.7% chance level (73.9%-82.3% per sample, i.e., the losing hand was repeated only 17.7%-26.1% of the time), while win-stay varied from 30.2% to 44.2% (chance 33.3%) and was often not significant. In Srihaput et al. the lose-shift excess (+12.65 pp) exceeded the win-stay excess (+7.78 pp; t(79) = 1.817, p = .037 one-tailed).
verified.evidence: Dyson 2021 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7859242/): Exp 1 win-stay 36.67% (t[35] = 1.10, p = 0.280), lose-shift 77.23% (t[35] = 4.75, p < 0.001), draw-shift 70.65% (n.s.); Exp 2 win-stay 30.15% (t[35] = -1.15), lose-shift 80.18% (t[35] = 9.11), draw-shift 73.70%; Exp 3 win-stay 43.88% (t[35] = 3.16, p = 0.003), lose-shift 73.86% (t[35] = 2.55, p = 0.015), draw-shift 66.09% (n.s.); 'All participants completed the studies for course credit'. Srihaput et al. 2020 (games-11-00025.pdf): Exp 1 win-stay 41.88% (repeat) vs 34.17% (change), lose-shift 81.83% vs 82.78%; Exp 2 win-stay 46.17% vs 42.24%, lose-shift 76.04% vs 76.63%; combined win-stay 44.02% vs 38.21%, lose-shift 78.93% vs 79.70%; 'the average lose-shift deviation from 66.6% was significantly larger than the average win-stay deviation from 33.3% (+12.65% versus +7.78%; t[79] = 1.817, p = 0.037, one-tailed)'. Forder & Dyson 2016: win-stay 42.45%, lose-shift 78.54%.
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed; one lab family and procedure; computer opponents; n = 36-40 per sample; course credit or small/raffled rewards.
verified.design: S9: University of Alberta, 3 x 36 participants, course credit, 270 trials each vs computer (Exp. 1 balanced random; Exp. 2 counters the participant's item frequencies every 6 trials; Exp. 3 51.11% item bias). S8: 80 participants (Sussex and Alberta), 288 trials vs 8 computer avatars playing balanced random sequences. S7: see B2.
verified.effect: Lose-stay is 7-14 pp below 1/3 (i.e., lose-shift +7 to +14 pp above 66.7%). Win-stay ranges from -3.2 to +10.6 pp around 1/3.
verified.implication: Against Western-style players, the most dependable prediction is that a player who just lost will NOT repeat that hand (about 75-80% switch). So throwing the hand that beats the loser's last hand (= repeating your own winning hand) is a poor bet.
verified.caveats: All from one lab and its procedure (fast computer trials, gloved-hand pictures, no performance pay). Opponents were computers. Zhejiang human-vs-human data (A1) show the opposite balance: win-stay strong (0.528) and lose-stay 0.360, near chance.

verified.statement: When the opponent changes between consecutive throws, win-stay weakens but lose-shift persists. Win-stay fell from 44.02% (same opponent again) to 38.21% (new opponent), while lose-shift stayed at 79.70% vs 78.93%. The number of individuals with a significant win-stay bias dropped from 38 to 31 of 80; for lose-shift bias it was 44 vs 47.
verified.evidence: Srihaput, Craplewe & Dyson 2020, Games 11:25 (https://mdpi-res.com/d_attachment/games/games-11-00025/article_deploy/games-11-00025.pdf): 'Win-stay behavior was significantly reduced for opponent change trials relative to opponent repeat trials (44.02% versus 38.21%; F[2,78] = 6.951, MSE = 0.019, p = 0.010, eta_p^2 = 0.082)'; 'lose-shift behavior was equivalent across opponent change and repeat trials (78.93% versus 79.70%; F[1,78] = 0.292 ... p = 0.591)'; Exp 1: 41.88% vs 34.17% (t[34] = 2.322, p = 0.026); Exp 2: 46.17% vs 42.24% (t[34] = 1.350, p = 0.185); binomial tests: 38 vs 31 individuals (win-stay), 44 vs 47 (lose-shift). Design: 80 participants (40 Sussex, GBP 25 voucher raffled; 40 Alberta, course credit), 288 trials in 144 trial pairs (72 repeat, 72 change), 8 avatars all playing balanced sequences (Exp 1 also had two Rock-biased avatars); 'There was never an indication that participants would be competing against other humans.'
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed; N=80; computer avatars with random policies; minimal incentives; single study.
verified.design: Two lab experiments: Exp. 1 Sussex (n=40; one GBP 25 voucher raffled), Exp. 2 Alberta (n=40; course credit). 288 trials organised into 144 trial pairs: 72 'repeat' pairs (same avatar on trial n+1) and 72 'change' pairs (different avatar). All 8 computer avatars played balanced random sequences (Exp. 1 also had 2 Rock-biased avatars). Participants were not told whether opponents were human.
verified.effect: Win-stay vs 33.3%: +10.7 pp (repeat) vs +4.9 pp (change). Lose-shift vs 66.7%: +13.0 pp vs +12.3 pp.
verified.implication: For relay or 'winner stays on' team formats, a champion facing a new challenger still win-stays above chance (38%), and losers still shift about 79% even against new opponents. Derived only under the assumption that the 62% of shifts split evenly: a challenger throwing the hand that beats the champion's last winning hand gains about +0.07 per throw. The direction of shifts was not reported.
verified.caveats: Single study, computer opponents, no performance pay, low incentives. 'Opponent change' here means a different avatar with an identical random policy. Shift direction not reported.

verified.statement: Outcome-conditioned biases are not universal. Sundvall & Dyson (2022; two Sussex experiments, n=40 each; Exp 1 course credit or GBP 10, Exp 2 GBP 10 plus 10p per point in high-value blocks) found no significant group-level differences between stay, upgrade and downgrade after any outcome against unexploitable computer opponents; individual binomial tests classified 16-32 of 40 participants per outcome cell as 'no bias' (e.g., Exp 1 low value: 21/21/29 after win/lose/draw), and among biased players a win-SHIFT bias was more common than a win-stay bias (e.g., Exp 1: 13 vs 6 and 16 vs 5). Zhang, Moisan & Gonzalez (2021; 90 MTurk workers in 45 human-human dyads, 100 trials, non-standard payoffs with Nash 1/4 R, 1/2 P, 1/4 S) found statistically detectable outcome-dependence in only 36 of 90 players (individual chi-square tests); exploratory clusters suggested win-stay/lose-change and win-change/lose-stay types. Failing to detect dependence in 100 trials does not show its absence, so the share of truly outcome-independent opponents is unknown (60% is an upper bound, not an estimate).
verified.evidence: Sundvall & Dyson 2022 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8809577/), abstract: 'Against unexploitable opponents, participants achieved an approximation of random behavior, contrary to previous research commonly finding reinforcement biases.' Exp 1: 'Against unexploitable opponents, there were no significant differences between the three different strategies at trial n+1 as a function of outcome at trial n (Tukey's HSD, p > .05 for all comparisons'; Exp 2: 'When playing against the unexploitable opponent, there were no significant differences ... replicating Experiment 1'. Table 3 (no bias counts): Exp 1 low 21/21/29, high 19/29/24; Exp 2 low 21/19/19, high 16/22/32; stay vs shift bias after wins: Exp 1 low 6 vs 13, high 5 vs 16; Exp 2 low 9 vs 10, high 9 vs 15. Exp 2 pay: 'flat GBP 10 reward ... and an average GBP 2 extra for performance'. Zhang et al. 2021 (games-12-00052.pdf): 'at the individual level, 36 out of 90 participants violated the independence hypothesis ... For the other 54 participants, we found that their actions are not related to the outcomes'; payoff table: tie 2, loss 1 or 0, win 3 or 4 (Rock beating Scissors = 4); 'pairs played the RPS for 100 trials'; participants 'discovered' the payoff matrix through feedback.
verified.reliability: S10 peer-reviewed, two experiments of 40, computer opponents, within-lab non-replication; S12 peer-reviewed, MTurk, 100 trials, unusual payoff matrix, low power at the individual level.
verified.design: S10: Sussex (UK), Exp. 1 n=40 and Exp. 2 n=40, course credit or GBP 10; computer opponents (unexploitable random, or exploitable). S12 Exp. 1: 90 Amazon MTurk workers in 45 human-human dyads, 100 trials, small bonus (2 points = 1 cent), NON-standard payoff matrix (Nash = 1/4 R, 1/2 P, 1/4 S).
verified.effect: S10: group-level conditional rates not different from 1/3. S12: 40% (36/90) of players were outcome-dependent.
verified.implication: Any WSLS-based read of an individual opponent is probabilistic: perhaps 60% of opponents show no outcome dependence at all. Expect realised edges well below the population-average upper bounds in C2.
verified.caveats: S12's unusual payoffs (Rock beats Scissors pays 4) may change behaviour. S10 used the same lab family as B1-B4, so the non-replication is within-lab.

verified.statement: In stable human-vs-human play (same opponent for hundreds of rounds), win-stay disappears and players under-repeat after every outcome, while lose-shift remains. US dyads (Brockbank & Vul raw data; 116 players, 300 rounds): after WIN repeat 0.322, X+ 0.358, X- 0.320; after TIE 0.294 / 0.352 / 0.354; after LOSS 0.237 / 0.377 / 0.386. Australian dyads (Moerel et al. OpenNeuro raw data; 62 players, 480 games): after WIN 0.262 / 0.365 / 0.372; TIE 0.281 / 0.337 / 0.382; LOSS 0.285 / 0.340 / 0.374 (all hand-pooled). Overall repeat rates 0.282 and 0.275 (chance 0.333). Hand-specific example corrected: after winning specifically with Rock, Australian players threw Rock 28%, Paper 37% and Scissors 35% (n = 3,221 transitions). Derived: throwing X- relative to the opponent's last hand was the best single response after every opponent outcome in both samples (+0.035/+0.058/+0.140 US; +0.103/+0.056/+0.055 AU after the opponent's win/tie/loss); 'beat their last hand' averaged about -0.07 (US) and -0.10 (AU).
verified.evidence: My re-analysis of https://raw.githubusercontent.com/erik-brockbank/rps/master/analysis/rps_v1_data.csv: 62 games, 58 complete (2 players x 300 rounds), 116 players, 34,745 valid moves; per-player means (SEM): win stay 0.322 (0.016), up 0.358 (0.012), down 0.320 (0.013); tie 0.294 (0.012), 0.352 (0.008), 0.354 (0.010); loss 0.237 (0.012), 0.377 (0.010), 0.386 (0.010); marginals R 0.319, P 0.336, S 0.346. OpenNeuro ds006761 (31 sub-*_task-RPS_events.tsv, 480 games each, outcome coding checked with 0 mismatches): 62 players, 29,511 moves; win 0.262 (0.014)/0.365 (0.013)/0.372 (0.016); tie 0.281/0.337/0.382; loss 0.285/0.340/0.374; marginals R 0.353, P 0.325, S 0.321; hand-specific after win with Rock: R 0.280, P 0.371, S 0.349. Direct counterfactual on raw sequences: 'X- vs opponent's last hand' +0.079 (US), +0.073 (AU); 'beat opponent's last hand' -0.073 (US), -0.103 (AU). Papers: Brockbank & Vul 2020 (https://www.cognitivesciencesociety.org/cogsci20/papers/0178/0178.pdf): '128 college students who received course credit ... of 62 dyads, four were removed ... leaving 58 dyads with complete data'; 10 s per move; '3 points for a win, 0 points for a tie, and -1 points for a loss'; 'chi2 (5) = 133.27, p < 0.001'. Moerel et al. 2025 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12628313/): '62 participants (31 pairs)', mean age 27.85, '$60 AUD', separate rooms, 480 games; 'Many participants were biased towards changing their response, regardless of the outcome of the previous game'; 'most Bayes Factors showed evidence for no difference between these groups'.
verified.reliability: Two peer-reviewed studies with public raw data; stable human dyads (US online, course credit; Australian lab, flat pay, EEG); 116 and 62 players; long sessions; conditional tables are my computations, not printed statistics.
verified.design: S14: UCSD (USA), 128 students (58 complete dyads), course credit, 300 rounds vs the same human opponent, points +3/0/-1, online. S20: Western Sydney University (Australia), 62 adults (31 pairs, mean age 27.85), flat AUD 60 payment, 480 games vs the same human in separate rooms, 2-s response window, EEG recorded.
verified.effect: Win-stay -1.0 pp (US) and -7.1 pp (AU) vs 1/3. Lose-stay -9.6 pp (US) and -4.8 pp (AU). Overall repeat about -5 to -6 pp. After a loss, downgrade exceeds upgrade by 0.9 pp (US) and 3.4 pp (AU).
verified.implication: Derived: in these samples the best response to every opponent outcome was X- relative to the opponent's last hand. Their last hand was Rock -> throw Scissors (beats their likely Paper, loses only to a Rock repeat). Edges were +0.035 / +0.058 / +0.140 (US) and +0.103 / +0.056 / +0.055 (AU) after the opponent's win / tie / loss. Beating the opponent's last hand (Cournot best response) was negative in both: about -0.069 and -0.100 on average.
verified.caveats: Conditional tables are my analyses of public data, not statistics printed in the papers; the parses were validated against reported N and marginals. Long sessions with fixed opponents allow mutual adaptation, so early-round behaviour in short bouts may differ. S20's media-popularised advice ('forget the previous round') rests on EEG decoding, and the paper notes that 'most Bayes Factors showed evidence for no difference between these groups'.

verified.statement: Cross-study synthesis (derived): using each dataset's conditional table, only two outcome-specific rules hold across most datasets. (i) After YOU WIN, do not repeat your winning hand: that edge was negative in 5 of 6 datasets (-0.005 to -0.182; +0.070 only vs the Zhejiang humans-vs-AI data). Throwing the hand the loser just lost with (won with Paper over Rock -> throw Rock) was between -0.015 and +0.089 in all six. (ii) After YOU LOSE, throw the hand that beats the winner's hand (lost with Rock to Paper -> Scissors): +0.003 to +0.281 in 5 of 6, but -0.110 in the Australian dyads. After a TIE no rule is robust: 'beat the tied hand' (Rock-Rock -> Paper) was +0.198 / +0.091 in the Zhejiang data but -0.041 to -0.101 in Western data. Single 'beat their last hand' rules flip sign between Zhejiang (+0.13 to +0.16) and Western (-0.03 to -0.10) samples.
verified.evidence: I independently re-derived all six input tables (A1 from the EPS; B1 from the Dyson 2016 spreadsheet; B2 from the Forder & Dyson text; Wang L. 2020 from both supplementary .xlsx files - 52 players x 300 rounds, per-player means after W/T/L: stay 0.469/0.394/0.375, up 0.284/0.303/0.320, down 0.248/0.303/0.305; US and AU from raw data, see C1) and recomputed the edges with edge(X+) = stay - down, edge(X) = down - up, edge(X-) = up - stay: opponent lost, repeat winner -0.005/-0.182/-0.179/+0.070/-0.149/-0.089; loser's hand +0.089/+0.033/+0.003/-0.015/+0.009/+0.034; opponent won, beat winner +0.281/+0.021/+0.142/+0.221/+0.002/-0.110; tie X+ +0.198/-0.049/-0.041/+0.091/-0.060/-0.101; tie X- -0.098/+0.126/+0.080/-0.091/+0.058/+0.056; always X- -0.161/+0.075/+0.042/-0.110/+0.078/+0.071; always X+ +0.158/-0.070/-0.026/+0.127/-0.069/-0.100. Direct counterfactuals on raw sequences agree (US always X- +0.079, AU +0.073, Zhejiang-vs-AI -0.107; beat-last-hand -0.073, -0.103, +0.126). Three further Western tables (Dyson 2021 Table 2) agree with rule (i): repeat-winner -0.153/-0.222/-0.134, loser's hand +0.006/+0.039/+0.053.
verified.reliability: Secondary derivation from six datasets of mixed quality (two Zhejiang lab datasets with cash; two computer-opponent labs without pay; two stable human-dyad datasets); assumes non-adapting, population-average opponents.
verified.design: Secondary computation over six datasets: Chinese lab with cash and random re-matching (S1); UK and Canadian labs vs computer without pay (S6, S7); Chinese lab vs adaptive AI with cash (S19); US and Australian stable human dyads (S14, S20).
verified.effect: Per-throw expected (win - loss) of up to +0.28 in the most favourable cell. Robust rules are worth roughly 0 to +0.09 per throw.
verified.implication: Practical recommendations, each probabilistic: (1) after winning, switch away from the winning hand, with the loser's last hand as a safe default; (2) after losing, lean towards the hand that beats the winner's hand, except against opponents who habitually avoid repeats; (3) after ties, there is no evidence-based edge, so randomise. Whether your opponents resemble the 'repeat-prone' Zhejiang samples or the 'repeat-averse' Western samples is the key unknown.
verified.caveats: These are my derivations, not published results. They assume a non-adapting opponent with population-average behaviour. Individual heterogeneity (B5) and opponent adaptation (D3) shrink real edges. Datasets differ in incentives, opponent type (computer/AI/human), time pressure and culture.

verified.statement: The pattern 'win-stay, lose-downgrade, draw-upgrade' is behaviourally identical to always throwing the hand that beats the OPPONENT's previous hand (other-upgrade, Cournot best response) (Dyson 2019, Games 10:32, Table 1); Dyson et al. (2016) summarised their data as 'if the computer played Scissors on trial n the participant would be more likely to play Rock on trial n + 1, irrespective of the item selection and outcome at trial n'. The counter to such a player is to throw the hand that YOUR OWN previous hand beats (you threw Rock -> they expect to beat it with Paper -> you throw Scissors). It is NOT the hand that loses to the opponent's previous hand, which coincides only after ties and has zero expected edge against a pure Cournot player. In real samples this correct counter is worth little: +0.022 (US dyads), -0.007 (Australian dyads), +0.029 (Zhejiang students vs AI) per throw from raw data, and +0.06 to +0.09 in the Dyson 2016, Forder & Dyson 2016 and Wang et al. a=2 tables.
verified.evidence: Dyson 2019 (https://mdpi-res.com/d_attachment/games/games-10-00032/article_deploy/games-10-00032.pdf), section 3: 'a player winning as a result of paper should be more likely to repeat the paper response on the next trial (win-stay), which is equivalent to upgrading the opponent's previous play of rock also to paper (other-upgrade). All other eight possible outcomes follow the same pattern: The heuristic set out by the standard version of the win-stay/lose-shift self-outcome strategy yields the same trial n + 1 behavior as does simply utilizing an other-upgrade heuristic'; Table 1 lists WIN-REPEAT, LOSE-DOWNGRADE, DRAW-UPGRADE. Dyson et al. 2016 (PMC4740902) Discussion quote verified. Logic: if they play (my last)+, my best reply is ((my last)+)+ = (my last)-. Relative to the opponent's last hand X this is X+ after their win, X after their loss and X- after a tie. Against a pure Cournot player, 'always X- relative to their last hand' wins after ties, loses after their wins and ties after their losses, giving 0 net. Raw-data counterfactuals (my scripts on S25 v1, S26, S19): self-downgrade +0.022 (SEM 0.012) US, -0.007 (0.014) AU, +0.029 (0.018) Zhejiang vs AI; table-derived (unweighted over outcomes) +0.091 (Wang a=2), +0.060 (Dyson 2016), +0.075 (Forder & Dyson).
verified.reliability: Review (peer-reviewed, Games) for the equivalence; small computer-opponent study (N=31) for the Scissors -> Rock summary; counterfactual edges from public raw data (my computation).
verified.design: Review and logical equivalence (S11); interpretation of the S6 data (31 participants vs computer).
verified.effect: Not applicable (mapping). In S6, the outcome x strategy interaction had eta_p^2 = 0.183.
verified.implication: Against players who follow this pattern, throw the hand that LOSES to the opponent's previous hand (opponent just threw Rock -> you throw Scissors, which beats their expected Paper). This is the 'always X-' rule in C2: positive in all four Western datasets (+0.042 to +0.078) but strongly negative in the two Zhejiang datasets (-0.161, -0.110), where opponents repeat more.
verified.caveats: Equivalence describes behaviour, not players' intentions. Whether players actually use the pattern varies by sample (B5, C1, C2).

verified.statement: In 2.64 million online best-of-3 matches, players reacted to the opponent's displayed throw history, which makes them exploitable. When the opponent's historical first-throw Rock share was 42-100%, players opened with Paper 46.58% of the time (vs 27.07% when it was 0-25%). A best response to this predicted behaviour would win 41.66%, draw 30.97% and lose 27.37% of first throws (+14.29 pp). Always playing 'k2' (the counter to the opponent's expected counter to your own history) would win 42.68% and lose 27.74%. Experienced players actually netted only +1.49 pp.
verified.evidence: Batzilis et al. 2019, Games 10:18 (https://mdpi-res.com/d_attachment/games/games-10-00018/article_deploy/games-10-00018.pdf): 340,213 users; 'Our dataset contains 2,636,417 matches, all the matches played between 23 May 2007 ... and 14 August 2007'; 'best-two-out-of-three matches for prestige points known as creds'; a 'scouting sheet' showed the opponent's first-throw and all-throw distributions and last five matches; 'For all the empirical analysis we focus on the first throw in each match'. Table 2: 0%-25% -> Paper 27.07, Rock 35.84, Scissors 37.09 (N = 1,006,726); 42%-100% -> 46.58, 30.35, 23.06 (N = 1,056,162). Table 5: Full Sample 33.8/32.4/33.8/0; Experienced 34.66/32.17/33.17/1.49; Best Response to Predicted Play 41.66/30.97/27.37/14.29 (coefficients estimated on half the data and used to predict the other half). 'If a player always played k2 he would win 42.68% (and lose 27.74%)'; k1 35.09% vs 32.61%. Table 3: Opp's Scissors Lag 0.0139 on P(Rock); appendix Opp's Rock Lag 0.0112, Opp's Paper Lag 0.0123. Footnote 14: 'We also find serial correlation both across throws within a match and across matches'.
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed; very large field dataset (Facebook app, 2007); prestige points, not money; first throws only; no demographics.
verified.design: Field and online data: Facebook app 'Roshambull' (2007), 340,213 users, human vs human matched by the app, no money (prestige points). A 'scouting sheet' showed the opponent's first-throw and all-throw distributions and their last 5 matches. Analyses restricted to first throws; 7,758 'experienced' players with at least 100 matches.
verified.effect: Best response: +14.29 pp (W-L) per first throw. k2: +14.94 pp. k1: +2.48 pp (35.09% vs 32.61%). Response to the opponent's last displayed throw: +1.1 to +1.4 pp.
verified.implication: In team formats where opponents can watch your earlier bouts, expect them to throw the counter to your apparently favourite hand. The counter to that counter (k2) is the profitable move. Avoid revealing a skewed hand distribution. The opponent's very last throw shifts others' choices by only about 1 pp.
verified.caveats: First throws of matches only; within-match win-stay/lose-shift was not analysed (footnote 14 only notes 'serial correlation'). The exploitation edges are computed out-of-sample by the authors, not realised by any player. The 2007 Facebook population played for prestige, not money.

verified.statement: A multi-model Markov 'AI' (fixed-memory predictors of order 1-5 or 1-10, switching to whichever predicted best in the last 5 or 10 rounds) beat 50 of 52 Chinese students over 300 money-incentivised rounds. Its mean net score was +37.39 (SD 33.12) and +35.64 (SD 21.21) per 300 rounds. Recomputed from the raw data, it won 41.55% and lost 29.21% of rounds (+12.3 pp per round). Memory lengths of 2-6 predicted humans best.
verified.evidence: Wang L et al. 2020 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7431549/): 'We experimented with 52 different people, each playing 300 rounds continuously against one specific multi-AI model ... could win against more than 95% of human opponents'; Table 5 MEAN 35.64 (Multi-10AI) and 37.39 (Multi-5AI), STDEVA 21.21 and 33.12; 'overall AI 2-6 perform better than AI 1 or higher-order Markov chains of longer memory length'; 'All experiments are conducted with money incentive'; win 2, draw 1, loss 0 points, r = 0.15 RMB per point + 5 RMB; 40-s limit; July-September 2019, Zhejiang University; players were asked 'Do you know that at each game round you will play with an AI opponent?'. My recomputation from MOESM1/MOESM2 .xlsx (human move vs 'Multi AI played' column): 52 x 300 rounds; AI net mean 37.39 (SD 33.12, n=41) and 35.64 (SD 21.21, n=11); overall AI win 0.4155, loss 0.2921; AI ahead for 50/52; human marginals R 0.354, P 0.320, S 0.326.
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed; 52 students; lab; cash; adaptive AI opponent; long sessions; raw data public and reproduced exactly.
verified.design: Lab, Zhejiang University (China), July-Sept 2019. 52 students, 300 rounds each vs the multi-AI (41 vs a 5-model version, 11 vs a 10-model version). Payoff win 2 / tie 1 / loss 0 (a=2), paid 0.15 RMB per point plus 5 RMB show-up; 40-s limit.
verified.effect: +12.3 pp per round (win - loss), i.e., 41.6% wins vs 29.2% losses against a 33.3% baseline.
verified.implication: Humans carry short-memory sequential regularities that a simple frequency-of-recent-sequences model can exploit at about +12 pp per throw over long play. A human tracker would need to remember the opponent's last 2-6 throws and their outcomes.
verified.caveats: 300-round sessions give the AI time to learn. Human opponents may have behaved differently against a computer. Which specific human patterns were exploited is not reported.

verified.statement: When a bot actively exploited humans' outcome-conditioned transitions (the win-stay/lose-shift family) over 300 rounds, humans neutralised it: the bot's mean net was +0.5 per 300 rounds (t(21) = 0.07, p = 0.95). Bots exploiting the most complex dependencies won consistently: +36.9 (previous two moves), +32.3 (previous outcome x previous transition) and +27.8 (own and opponent's previous move) per 300 rounds, about +9 to +12 pp per round. Bots exploiting the simplest transition base rates were counter-exploited (own-transition base rate -17.3, t(20) = -2.30; opponent-transition/Cournot base rate -48.1, t(25) = -6.09 per 300 rounds). Among intermediate 9-cell bots, 'transition given opponent's prior choice' was also counter-exploited (-26.8; t(27) = -3.11), while 'transition given player's prior choice' (-13.2; t(23) = -1.63, p = .12) did not differ from zero.
verified.evidence: Brockbank & Vul 2021, CogSci 43 (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/1rc5v2nn, PDF read): 194 undergraduates, course credit, 2 excluded; 300 rounds vs one of eight adaptive bots; '3 points ... -1 point ... 0 points'; 10 s per move. 'Transition baserate: t(20) = -2.30, p = 0.03; Opponent transition baserate: t(25) = -6.09, p < 0.01'; 'Choice given player's prior choice & opponent's prior choice: t(24) = 2.44, p = 0.02; Choice given player's prior two choices: t(19) = 4.36, p < 0.001; Transition given prior transition & prior outcome: t(25) = 5.68, p < 0.0001'; 'Transition given player's prior choice: t(23) = -1.63, p = 0.12; Transition given prior outcome: t(21) = 0.07, p = 0.95 ... Transition given opponent's prior choice: t(27) = -3.11, p < 0.01'; 'only 4 out of 20 and 4 out of 26 participants ... had win count differentials greater than or equal to zero'. My recomputation from rps_v3_data.csv (196 complete 300-round games; bot wins minus human wins): opponent_courn_transitions -48.1 (n=27), bot_prev_move -26.8 (n=29), opponent_transitions -17.3 (n=22), opponent_prev_move -13.2 (n=24, t = -1.63), opponent_outcome_transitions +0.5 (n=22, t = 0.07), opponent_bot_prev_move +27.8 (n=26), opponent_outcome_prev_transition_dual +32.3 (n=26, t = 5.68), opponent_prev_two_moves +36.9 (n=20, t = 4.35).
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed conference paper (also Experiment 2 of Brockbank & Vul 2024, Cogn Psychol); online, course credit; 20-29 participants per bot; public raw data reproduced.
verified.design: Online lab, UCSD (USA). 194 undergraduates (course credit; 2 excluded), each played 300 rounds vs one of 8 adaptive bots that always threw the counter to the participant's most likely next move under one dependency. Points +3 win / -1 loss / 0 tie; 10-s limit per round.
verified.effect: Complex-dependency bots: +9.3 to +12.3 pp per round. Outcome-conditioned (WSLS) exploitation: +0.2 pp (null). Simple-transition bots: -4.4 to -16 pp (humans won).
verified.implication: An opponent exploiting your win-stay/lose-shift over a long match is detectable and counterable. In short bouts there is no time to adapt, so randomising after losses matters most. Conversely, exploiting a human requires tracking two-step dependencies, beyond what most players do.
verified.caveats: 300-round sessions vs bots; adaptation speed over the first few throws (the relevant horizon for a tournament bout) was not analysed. Exact per-bot means are my recomputation from the public data; the paper shows them only in a figure.

verified.statement: Humans exploit simple 'after X, play Y' transition patterns far better than outcome-conditioned ones. Against bots following 90%-deterministic patterns for 300 rounds (Brockbank & Vul 2024, Exp 1; N=218), humans won 57.9-66.5% vs simple transition bots, but only 41.3% and 39.7% vs win/loss-conditioned bots (e.g., 'stay after win, upgrade after loss, downgrade after tie'), still netting about +13 to +17 pp (losses 24.8% and 26.7%). They won 34.1% (chance) vs a bot combining outcome and previous transition. Against 80%-deterministic WSLU/WDLS bots (100 trials, non-standard payoffs), MTurk players netted +4.72 and +19.10 wins and 'had difficulty in using an upgrade/downgrade direction'. Implication corrected: C2's rules are not an opaque outcome-conditioned plan. 'After a win throw the loser's hand, after a loss throw what beats the winner's hand' is the simple self-transition 'throw the hand your last hand beats', and humans beat a 90% bot of exactly that type in 62.2% of rounds (losing 17.6%).
verified.evidence: Cross et al. 2025 (arXiv:2508.06503 LaTeX): 'Each participant (N=218) played 300 rounds against one of seven bot opponents'; 'The bot opponents chose moves according to different sequential dependencies with 90% probability'; 'Against bots using simple transition rules, participants achieved strong performance, with win rates ranging from 57.9-66.5%'; 'win rates of 41.3% and 39.7% for the two outcome-dependent strategies'; 'participants failed to perform above chance against the most complex bot ... (34.1%, p = .30)'; outcome bots defined as 'Stay transitions after wins, positive transitions after losses, negative after ties' and 'Positive transitions after wins, negative after losses, stay after ties'. My recomputation from the public raw data of that experiment (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/erik-brockbank/rps/master/analysis/rps_v2_data.csv.zip; 220 complete games): human win/loss vs prev_move_positive 66.5/16.6%, opponent_prev_move_nil 65.0/17.7%, prev_move_negative 62.2/17.6%, opponent_prev_move_positive 58.5/12.7%, win_nil_lose_positive 41.3/24.8%, win_positive_lose_negative 39.7/26.7%, outcome_transition_dual_dependency 34.1/32.0%. Brockbank & Vul 2024 abstract (Semantic Scholar record, DOI 10.1016/j.cogpsych.2024.101654) quote verified. Zhang et al. 2021 Exp 2: 'WSLU (M = 4.72, t(98) = 4.01, p < 0.001, d = 0.81) and WDLS (M = 19.10, t(96) = 7.89, p < 0.001, d = 1.60)'; procedure 'the same as in Experiment 1' (100 trials, payoff 4/3/2/1/0 matrix); algorithms choose the rule action 'with a probability of 0.8'.
verified.reliability: S17 peer-reviewed (closed access; raw data public); S18 preprint; S12 peer-reviewed, MTurk, 100 trials, non-standard payoffs; bots far more predictable than humans.
verified.design: S17/S18: N=218 adults, 300 rounds each vs one of 7 bots (90%-deterministic patterns), points +3/0/-1. S12 Exp. 2: 196 MTurk workers (bonus 2 points = 1 cent), 100 trials vs bots with 0.8-probability WSLU or WDLS rules.
verified.effect: Win rate vs 1/3: +24.6 to +33.2 pp (simple transitions); +6.4 and +8.0 pp (outcome-conditioned); +0.8 pp n.s. (outcome x transition). S12: +4.7 and +19.1 pp win differential.
verified.implication: If you deliberately follow an outcome-conditioned plan (e.g., the C2 rules), human opponents are unlikely to read it within a short match. Avoid fixed 'after X I play Y' habits, which humans pick up quickly.
verified.caveats: S18 is a preprint reporting data from a closed-access paper (S17) that I could not read. 90%-deterministic bots are far more predictable than humans. Long sessions.

verified.statement: Cook et al. (2012; 45 UCL adults in 15 triads, 14 analysed; GBP 5 plus GBP 2.50 per match won; nine 20-round matches per triad, live hand gestures with umpire) found 36.3% draws when one player was blindfolded and the other sighted vs 33.3% when both were blindfolded (one-sample t13 = 2.49, p < .025 one-tailed; paired t13 = 1.72, p = .05 one-tailed); blindfolded players' Rock and Scissors (not Paper) predicted imitation by the sighted player. A replication with more than twice the sample (Aczel, Bago & Foldes 2012; 114 Hungarian adults, 34 triads analysed) found no effect: 36.54% draws blind-sighted vs 37.77% blind-blind (t33 = -1.02, p = .32). Face-to-face imitation is therefore not a reliable effect.
verified.evidence: Cook et al. full text is open (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3248720/): 'Forty-five healthy adults (23 females)'; 'small honorarium for participating (GBP 5) ... additional GBP 2.50 win bonus'; 'Triads were required to play nine matches of RPS, each comprising 20 individual rounds'; Table 4 draws 36.3 (s.d. 4.6) vs 33.3 (5.0); 'paired-samples t-test revealed that the frequency of draws was significantly higher in the blind-sighted than in the blind-blind condition (t13 = 1.72; p = 0.05 (one-tailed))'; logistic regressions: Scissors beta 0.266 (p = .006), Rock 0.245 (p = .034), Paper 0.086 (p = .298); gestures overall R 32.4%, P 33.3%, S 34.4%. Video sub-study (4 pairs): blind player first in 44.7% of rounds, by more than 200 ms in 17.2%. Aczel et al. 2012, Proc R Soc B 279(1741):3231-3233 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3385727/): 'One hundred and fourteen participants'; 'A paired-sample t-test comparing two conditions indicated no significant difference between the mean proportion of draws, t33 = -1.02, p = 0.32 (two-tailed). In fact, the mean proportion was numerically higher in the blind-blind condition (M = 37.77 ...) than in the blind-sighted condition (M = 36.54 ...)'; Scissors most frequent (36.76% and 36.64%). Nat Geo (S22) wrote 'the sighted players made their move more than 200 milliseconds after their opponent on around half of the games', which misreports the 44.7% / 17.2% figures.
verified.reliability: Original: peer-reviewed, 14 triads, marginal one-tailed statistics. Replication: peer-reviewed comment, 34 triads, null result. Media: secondary, partly inaccurate.
verified.design: Lab, UCL (UK). 45 participants, real money, in-person play with one or both players blindfolded. Exact rounds and statistics not read: abstract plus media only.
verified.effect: Draw rate +3.0 pp above 1/3 when one player could see.
verified.implication: In live team bouts, throwing even slightly late raises the chance of copying the opponent (a draw). Commit to your hand before seeing theirs. A slow-throwing opponent may mirror your Rock or Scissors.
verified.caveats: Numbers come from a media report; the full paper was not accessible. A failure-to-replicate commentary (Aczel, Bago & Foldes 2012, Proc R Soc B 279:3231-3233) exists but was not read. This is about simultaneous imitation, not sequential dependence.

verifier_added.statement: C2's two 'robust' rules are one fixed cycle. After you WIN, throw the loser's last hand; after you LOSE, throw the hand that beats the winner's hand. In both cases this is 'throw the hand your own last hand beats' (your last was Rock -> Scissors; Scissors -> Paper; Paper -> Rock), which is also the exact counter to the win-stay/lose-downgrade/draw-upgrade (Cournot) pattern. Its realised edge is small: +0.022 (US dyads), -0.007 (Australian dyads) and +0.029 (Zhejiang students vs AI) per throw in raw data, and +0.03 to +0.09 in six lab tables. Because it is a simple self-transition, it is the kind of pattern humans exploit best: against a 90%-deterministic bot of this type, humans won 62.2% and lost 17.6% of 300 rounds.
verifier_added.evidence: My counterfactual scripts on raw sequences (opponent's actual next move scored against the rule's move): self-downgrade +0.022 (SEM 0.012, n=116) US, -0.007 (0.014, n=62) AU, +0.029 (0.018, n=52) Zhejiang vs AI. Table-derived averages over W/T/L: Wang a=2 +0.091, Dyson 2016 +0.060, Forder & Dyson +0.075, Dyson 2021 Exps 1-3 +0.050/+0.028/+0.066. Raw data of Brockbank & Vul 2024 Exp 1 (rps_v2_data.csv): vs 'prev_move_negative' bot (plays the hand its last hand beats, 90%) humans won 62.2% and lost 17.6% (n=31 complete games); vs 'opponent_prev_move_positive' (beats the human's last hand) 58.5% and 12.7%. Cross et al. 2025 report 57.9-66.5% wins against these transition bots.
verifier_added.study_design: Secondary computation on public raw data: 58 US dyads (300 rounds), 31 Australian dyads (480 games), 52 Zhejiang students vs adaptive AI (300 rounds); 220 complete games of humans vs fixed 90%-pattern bots (Brockbank & Vul 2024, Exp 1, course-credit undergraduates, +3/0/-1 points).
verifier_added.effect_size: About -0.01 to +0.03 per throw against human-dyad populations (vs 0 for random play); +0.03 to +0.09 against lab tables; a fixed rule followed 90% of the time loses about 44.6 pp per round to an adapting human over 300 rounds.
verifier_added.strategic_implication: Treat 'play what your last hand beats' at most as a mild lean mixed with randomness. Never use it as a fixed rule in repeated bouts against the same opponent or when the next opponent can watch you. In a relay where your previous bouts are visible, rotating Rock -> Scissors -> Paper is the easiest pattern for an observant opponent to read.
verifier_added.caveats: Derived, not published. Counterfactual edges assume opponents do not react to your rule. A 90%-deterministic bot is far more predictable than a human using the rule occasionally, and the 62% figure comes from 300-round sessions.

verifier_added.statement: Outcome-conditioned tendencies are much weaker in the first rounds of a session than in the 300-480-round averages used throughout the sweep. In rounds 1-20, stay rates after W/T/L were 0.375/0.329/0.336 for Zhejiang students vs AI (vs 0.469/0.394/0.402 in rounds 51-300), 0.279/0.331/0.296 in US dyads (vs 0.324/0.286/0.223), and 0.261/0.285/0.275 in Australian dyads (vs 0.261/0.282/0.280). The strong Zhejiang win-stay and the US lose-stay deficit therefore build up later in long sessions.
verifier_added.study_design: Secondary analysis of public raw data: 116 US players (stable dyads, course credit), 62 Australian players (stable dyads, flat AUD 60), 52 Zhejiang students vs adaptive AI (cash).
verifier_added.effect_size: Early-round deviations from 1/3 are mostly within about 2 SE (SE about 0.018-0.027 per cell). The largest are US and AU win-stay at -5 and -7 pp. Late-session Zhejiang win-stay is +14 pp.
verifier_added.strategic_implication: In a short knockout bout (1-5 throws), opponents' first transitions are close to random. Do not expect the large edges in A1/C2 (e.g., +0.28). The most stable early regularity is mild repeat-avoidance after wins in Western dyads.
verifier_added.caveats: Small early-round cells, counts pooled over players, and only three datasets. The Zhejiang data are against an adaptive AI, which may itself shape later behaviour.

verifier_added.statement: The face-to-face imitation effect (extra draws when one player can see the other) failed to replicate. Aczel, Bago & Foldes (2012; 114 Hungarian adults, 34 triads analysed) found 36.54% draws blind-sighted vs 37.77% blind-blind (t33 = -1.02, p = .32). In that live-hand sample Scissors, not Rock, was the most frequent gesture (36.76% and 36.64%), and in Cook et al.'s own UK live play the gestures were Rock 32.4%, Paper 33.3%, Scissors 34.4%.
verifier_added.evidence: Aczel et al. 2012 (PMC3385727), Results: 'scissors gesture was the most frequently used in the blind-sighted (M = 36.76%, s.d. = 5.05), as well as in the blind-blind condition (M = 36.64%, s.d. = 3.99)'; 'no significant difference between the mean proportion of draws, t33 = -1.02, p = 0.32 (two-tailed)'. Cook et al. 2012 (PMC3248720): 'the rock gesture was executed on 32.4 per cent of rounds, the paper gesture on 33.3 per cent of rounds and the scissors gesture on 34.4 per cent of rounds'; original paired test t13 = 1.72, p = 0.05 one-tailed.
verifier_added.study_design: Aczel et al.: 114 adults in triads, 3 blocks x 3 matches x 20 live rounds, umpire, chocolate bar plus 300 HUF per block won. Cook et al.: 45 adults, 14 triads analysed, nine 20-round matches, GBP 5 plus GBP 2.50 per match won.
verifier_added.effect_size: Replication difference -1.2 pp (n.s.) vs the original +3.0 pp (one-tailed p = .05).
verifier_added.strategic_implication: Do not count on opponents unconsciously copying your Rock or Scissors in live play. Do not assume the Rock excess from screen-based studies carries over to live hand play; both live samples show Scissors slightly over-played.
verifier_added.caveats: Hungarian and UK university samples; triad-level analysis; the gesture frequencies concern Angle B but come from the same live-play studies.

verifier_added.statement: Whether a higher value for winning raises or lowers opponents' win-stay is unresolved, so stakes should not be used to predict win-stay. Wang & Xu (2014) found win-stay falls as the win/tie payoff ratio a rises (Spearman rho = -0.29; W0 0.528 at a=2 vs 0.504 at a=4). Forder & Dyson (2016) found that raising the win value to +2 (loss -1, draw 0; equivalent to a = 3) raised win-stay from 35.92% to 48.44% (Tukey p < .05), with lose-shift unchanged.
verifier_added.evidence: S3 LaTeX: 'As the winning payoff a goes up, one of the best response behavior decline, i.e., win-stay (Spearman's rho = -0.2917, Prob > |t| = 0.0000, obs=504)'. S1 digitized W0 by a: 0.568/0.528/0.504/0.448/0.453. S7 Results: '48.44% versus 35.92%, respectively; Tukey's HSD, p < 0.05'; Discussion explicitly contrasts the two findings.
verifier_added.study_design: S1/S3: between-group, 6-person random-matching groups, 300 rounds, human opponents, cash (Zhejiang). S7: within-subject point-value blocks, 36 Sussex students vs random computer, points not paid out.
verifier_added.effect_size: S3 rho = -0.29 across 7 levels; S1 a=2 -> 4: -2.4 pp (n.s.). S7: +12.5 pp.
verifier_added.strategic_implication: Team pressure or bonus structures in a tournament give no reliable basis for predicting more (or less) win-stay from opponents.
verifier_added.caveats: Different manipulations (relative tie value vs win magnitude), populations, opponents and incentive schemes.

verifier_added.statement: Dyson (2021) Table 2 gives outcome x direction tables for three further Alberta samples (n=36 each, vs computer), which the sweep did not use. Averaged over credit conditions: after a loss stay 0.233/0.198/0.261, up 0.381/0.381/0.343, down 0.387/0.421/0.396 (Exps 1/2/3); after a win stay 0.372/0.301/0.439; after a draw stay 0.297/0.263/0.339, up 0.366/0.357/0.351, down 0.338/0.380/0.309. Derived edges: repeating your winning hand -0.153/-0.222/-0.134; throwing the loser's last hand +0.006/+0.039/+0.053; after the opponent loses with X, throwing X- +0.147/+0.183/+0.082.
verifier_added.evidence: S9 (PMC7859242) Table 2 'Proportion of strategy at trial n + 1 (stay, upgrade [shift], downgrade [shift]) relative to outcome at trial n (win, lose, draw) as a function of credit (no, variable, fixed)'. Example, Exp 1 no credit: Stay 0.376/0.234/0.294, Upgrade 0.329/0.385/0.380, Downgrade 0.295/0.382/0.327 (W/L/D). I averaged the three credit columns per experiment and applied edge(X+) = stay - down, edge(X) = down - up, edge(X-) = up - stay.
verifier_added.study_design: Three experiments x 36 University of Alberta students, course credit, 270 trials (3 x 90) vs computer: Exp 1 balanced random; Exp 2 counter-exploiting the participant's item frequencies every 6 trials; Exp 3 item-biased (51.11%).
verifier_added.effect_size: Lose-stay 7-14 pp below 1/3. Repeat-winner edge -0.13 to -0.22 per throw; loser's-hand edge +0.01 to +0.05.
verifier_added.strategic_implication: This independently supports C2 rule (i): after you win, do not repeat the winning hand, and use the loser's last hand as a low-risk default. Against repeat-averse opponents who just lost with X, X- (e.g., they lost with Rock -> you throw Scissors) is the strongest single reply.
verifier_added.caveats: Same lab family as B1-B4; computer opponents (two non-random); no performance pay; Table 2 win-stay averages differ slightly from the text values (e.g., 0.372 vs 36.67% in Exp 1).

verifier_added.statement: Japanese face-to-face janken data (Prof. Yoshizawa Mitsuo, Obirin University; 725 students, 11,567 throws) reportedly showed Rock 35.0%, Paper 33.3%, Scissors 31.7%, and the same hand twice in a row in only 22.8% of 10,833 consecutive pairs (chance 33.3%). This is a repeat-averse East Asian sample, unlike the repeat-prone Zhejiang computer-lab samples.
verifier_added.evidence: Lifehacker Japan, citing Nikkei Plus One of 20 June 2009: '学生725人が2回続けてジャンケンした10833回のうち、同じ手を出す（あいこ）回数は2465回（22.8％）にとどまった'; 'グーで4054枚（35.0％）、次はパーで3849回（33.3％）、最も少ないのはチョキで、3664回（31.7％）'. ITmedia blog (16 Dec 2007), citing THE NIKKEI MAGAZINE: '2回続けてじゃんけんをすると同じ手が続くのは22.8%'.
verifier_added.study_design: Reported in Japanese newspapers; 725 university students; presumably live hand play; collection about 1999; no peer-reviewed publication or methods located.
verifier_added.effect_size: Repeat rate 22.8% vs 33.3% (-10.5 pp); Rock +1.7 pp.
verifier_added.strategic_implication: For East Asian live play, assuming repeat-aversion (opponents rarely throw the same hand twice) is at least as plausible as the Zhejiang 'repeat-prone' pattern. The Zhejiang pattern also grows only late in long computer sessions (MF2).
verifier_added.caveats: Secondary newspaper reports only; methods, conditioning on outcome and independence of observations unknown; Japanese rather than Korean sample.

verifier_added.statement: After a tie on X, throwing X- (the hand the tied hand beats: Rock-Rock -> Scissors, Scissors-Scissors -> Paper, Paper-Paper -> Rock) had a positive derived edge in all seven Western samples: +0.126 (Dyson 2016), +0.080 (Forder & Dyson), +0.069/+0.094/+0.012 (Dyson 2021 Exps 1-3), +0.058 (US dyads), +0.056 (AU dyads). It is also the post-tie rule popularised from Yoshizawa's Japanese data. It was negative in both Zhejiang samples (-0.098, -0.091), and in rounds 1-20 it was close to 0 (US -0.003, AU +0.027, Zhejiang vs AI +0.036).
verifier_added.evidence: Edge(X-) after a tie = P(up) - P(stay) from each tie distribution: Dyson 2016 0.401-0.275; Forder 0.3732-0.2928; Dyson 2021 0.366-0.297, 0.357-0.263, 0.351-0.339; US 0.352-0.294; AU 0.337-0.281; Wang a=2 0.334-0.432; Wang L. 0.303-0.394. Early-round values from my round-window analysis (MF2). Lifehacker/Nikkei: 'あいこになったら、今の相手が出している手に負ける手を出せば勝つ、またはあいこで勝ち残れる'.
verifier_added.study_design: Table-derived from nine datasets (computer-opponent labs; stable human dyads; Zhejiang human and AI-opponent labs) plus a popular Japanese report.
verifier_added.effect_size: +0.01 to +0.13 per post-tie throw in repeat-averse samples; -0.09 to -0.10 in Zhejiang samples; about 0 to +0.04 early in a session.
verifier_added.strategic_implication: Ties are replayed immediately in knockouts. Against opponents who avoid repeating, lean slightly toward the hand the tied hand beats, but mix it, because the edge is small early and reverses against repeat-prone players.
verifier_added.caveats: Derived; assumes non-adapting population-average opponents; population type of Korean opponents unknown.

dead_ends: Lead 1 (Wang, Xu & Zhou 2014): metadata confirmed (Sci Rep 4:5830; 360 students; 300 rounds; random pairwise re-matching in groups of 6; cash incentive). However, (a) the conditional-response values are not printed in the text, tables or SI text; they exist only as Fig. 3F-J bars. I recovered them from the arXiv vector EPS and cross-checked them against S3 and the published figure. (b) The paper does NOT compute a payoff advantage for a player who exploits others' tendencies. It only computes payoffs if all players adopt the same optimised CR strategy (+0.035(a-2), which is zero at a=2).

Lead 2: Bi & Zhou (2014) PLoS ONE 9(10):e111278 exists but is purely theoretical (cooperation-trap strategies between rational players, non-zero-sum a>2) with no human data. Zhou's review is Contemporary Physics 57(2):151-163 (published online 26 Mar 2015). For Xu, Zhou & Wang (2013) Physica A 392:4997-5005 only the arXiv abstract (1301.3238) was read.

Lead 3 (Dyson et al. 2016): confirmed (31 participants, 225 trials vs computer). The outcome-conditional percentages are not stated numerically in the text (Fig. 1c only); I derived them from the supplementary .xls. Response times are not reported in this paper; outcome-specific RTs come from Forder & Dyson (2016) and Dyson (2021).

Lead 5 (Srihaput et al. 2020): confirmed, but the paper reports only binary win-stay/lose-shift rates, with no upgrade/downgrade direction. mdpi.com returned HTTP 403 to both curl and WebFetch; the PDF was obtained from mdpi-res.com.

Lead 6: Brockbank & Vul (2021, Games 12(3):70) is a framework and re-analysis paper with no new experiment; its data are the CogSci 2020 dyads. Brockbank & Vul (2024, Cognitive Psychology 151:101654) is closed access; only the abstract was read, and its numbers were taken from the Cross et al. (2025) preprint.

Lead 8 (Batzilis et al. 2019): all analyses concern the first throw of each match. No within-match win-stay/lose-shift or outcome-conditioned rates are reported; footnote 14 only says 'We also find serial correlation both across throws within a match and across matches'. The source is 2,636,417 matches, not 'a million' throws.
Lead 9 (Wang L. et al. 2020): confirmed (Sci Rep 10:13873). The paper does not say which human patterns were exploited beyond 'AI 2-6 perform better than AI 1 or higher-order' models.

West & Lebiere (2001), Cognitive Systems Research 1(4):221-239: existence confirmed via bibliographic records, but full text not accessible. Only second-hand descriptions (in Zhang et al. 2021 and Brockbank & Vul 2021) were seen, so it was not used.

Eyler, Shalla, Doumaux & McDevitt (2009), College Mathematics Journal 40(2):125-128: full text not accessible (the NASA PUMAS link returned HTML). A search-engine summary claiming a repeat probability 'well above one-third' could not be verified, so it was not used.
Lee, McGreevy & Barraclough (2005), Cogn Brain Res 25:416-430: abstract only (monkeys' choices were biased by the computer's previous choice). Not used, since the subjects were not human.

Cook et al. (2012): the PMC copy is not open access (abstract only). Numbers (36.3% vs 33.3% draws, 45 participants) are from a National Geographic report. The Aczel, Bago & Foldes (2012) failure-to-replicate reply was located (PMC3385727), but full text could not be retrieved.

No peer-reviewed behavioural study of TEAM or relay-format RPS was found. A Korean-language search returned only combinatorics papers on koreascience.or.kr (number of games in team RPS), not behavioural data.

Media accuracy check: NPR (2 May 2014) states 'if the player lost with rock, he or she was likely to try paper', which contradicts Wang et al.'s data (L+ = Rock->Paper was the least likely post-loss response at a=2). The MIT Technology Review piece (30 Apr 2014) says 'clockwise' without a hand mapping.

Moerel et al. (2025): the text reports switch rates only graphically (Fig. 1e) and gives no exact conditional percentages; I computed them from OpenNeuro ds006761. The popular claim that 'players influenced by previous rounds lose more' rests on EEG decoding with mostly null between-group Bayes factors.
open_questions: Which population pattern applies to Korean adults in an in-person team contest? The evidence splits into a 'repeat-prone' pattern (Zhejiang samples: overall stay 0.41-0.44, win-stay 0.47-0.53, lose-stay 0.36-0.38) and a 'repeat-averse' pattern (UK/Canada/US/Australia: overall stay about 0.28-0.31, lose-stay 0.20-0.29). The best counter-move after a tie, and the value of 'beat their last hand', flip sign between these groups. No Korean data were found.

How do conditional tendencies behave over the first 1-5 throws of a short knockout bout, as opposed to 100-480-round lab sessions? Nearly all estimates pool hundreds of rounds, and players adapt over long sessions (D3).

Ties: in knockouts a tie is replayed immediately. Post-tie behaviour is the least consistent finding across studies (upgrade-dominant in Dyson-lab and Zhejiang data, downgrade-dominant in the Australian dyads).

Relay or 'winner stays on' formats: does a champion facing successive new challengers win-stay more or less than the 38% observed with computer avatars (Srihaput et al.)? Do challengers who watched earlier bouts best-respond to the champion's last or most-frequent hand (Batzilis-style k1 behaviour)?
Do monetary or social stakes (team pressure) amplify the loss-driven predictability (faster, more reflexive post-loss choices) reported by the Dyson lab?
Does the imitation effect in face-to-face play (Cook et al. 2012) survive simultaneous 'rock-paper-scissors-shoot' timing, and does it hold up given the Aczel et al. (2012) reply?

condensed.angle: B. Base rates: first-throw and overall hand frequencies, after-tie behavior, repetition avoidance, cultural/demographic data (incl. Korea/Japan/China)

verified.statement: Largest field dataset (Roshambull Facebook app, 2007). First throws of a match: Paper 34.82%, Rock 33.99%, Scissors 31.20% (5,012,128 observations). Experienced players (≥100 matches) opened with Paper 34.56%, Scissors 32.84%, Rock 32.60%, so Rock was their least common opener. Across all throws, the average of opponents' histories was Rock 35.45%, Paper 34.01%, Scissors 30.54%: Rock is commoner over a whole match than on the first throw. For 82% of experienced players the first-throw distribution was not significantly different from 1/3 each (uniform play rejected for 18%). (Batzilis et al. 2019, Games 10:18, Table 1)
verified.evidence: Batzilis et al. 2019, Table 1 'Summary Statistics of First Throws' (p.6 of 34), full / restricted sample: Throw Rock 33.99 / 32.60; Throw Paper 34.82 / 34.56; Throw Scissors 31.20 / 32.84. Opp's Historical %Rock is 34.27 for first throws and 35.45 for all throws; %Paper 35.14 and 34.01; %Scissors 30.59 and 30.54. Total observations 5,012,128 / 1,472,319. Table note: 'The Restricted Sample uses data only from 7758 players who play at least 100 matches.' Sec. 2: 'we present evidence that 82% of experienced players have first throw distributions that do not differ from 1/3, 1/3, 1/3'. Sec. 3: 'we reject uniform random play for 18% of experienced players'. Fn 10: 'there is no demographic information'. Fn 14: 'We also find serial correlation both across throws within a match and across matches' (no numbers). Sec. 1: 2,636,417 best-of-3 matches, 23 May to 14 Aug 2007. URL: https://knowledge.uchicago.edu/records/jfcf3-13r07/files/games-10-00018-v2.pdf
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed (Games, MDPI). Very large N (334,661 players; 5.0M first throws). Online field data from 2007 with non-monetary stakes ('creds'). Players saw the opponent's history before each match. No demographics. Opponents were humans.
verified.design: Online field data from Facebook app Roshambull: 334,661 players with at least one clean match, 2,636,417 best-of-3 matches, 23 May to 14 Aug 2007. Human vs human (challenged or auto-matched Facebook users). Incentive was non-monetary prestige points ('creds') plus a leaderboard. Before each match players saw the opponent's history. Country and demographics not recorded.
verified.effect: Versus 33.33%, first throws (full sample): Rock +0.66 pp, Paper +1.49 pp, Scissors −2.13 pp. Experienced first throws: Rock −0.73, Paper +1.23, Scissors −0.49. All-throws proxy: Rock +2.12, Paper +0.68, Scissors −2.79. My calculation of net value per throw (win% − loss%) against the full-sample first-throw distribution: Paper +2.8 pp, Scissors +0.8, Rock −3.6. Against experienced openers: Scissors +2.0, Paper −0.2, Rock −1.7.
verified.implication: For a first throw against a typical opponent, Paper is marginally best (+2.8 pp) and Rock worst. Against experienced players, Rock is the weakest opener (−1.7 pp) and Scissors the best (+2.0 pp). All edges are only 2–4 pp.
verified.caveats: Showing the opponent's history changed behaviour (players responded to it). Online play for prestige only, in 2007, with unknown demographics. The 'all throws' values average opponents' histories weighted by matches played; they are not pooled frequencies. No within-match repeat or after-tie statistics are reported; footnote 14 mentions serial correlation without numbers.

verified.statement: As reported in secondary sources, Eyler et al. (2009) found that 119 people playing 50 games against a computer opened with Rock 55.5% (66), Paper 32.8% (39), Scissors 11.8% (14). Players tended to REPEAT: after throwing Paper, P(Paper again) = 0.421. A program that predicted from the opponent's previous two throws won 42.1%, lost 27.7% and tied 30.2% over 241 participants × 100 games. The widely quoted 'Rock 35.4%, Paper 35.0%, Scissors 29.6%' does not appear in any account of this paper that I found. (Peterson 2009 blog; Lock5 Ex. 2.15)
verified.evidence: Peterson, Mathematical Tourist, 12 Mar 2009 (http://mathtourist.blogspot.com/2009/03/rock-paper-scissors-for-winners.html). Quotes: 'collected data from 119 people who played 50 games of rock-paper-scissors against a computer using this optimal strategy. Their subjects had a strong preference for rock: 55.5% started with rock, 32.8% with paper, and 11.8% with scissors.' 'Players seem to have a distinct preference for repeating plays.' 'a player who chose paper on one trial had a .421 probability of repeating this play on the next trial'. 'In one test that involved 241 participants each playing 100 games against the computer, the computer won 42.1%, lost 27.7%, and tied 30.2%'. Lock5 Table 2.6 via vaia.com: Rock 66, Paper 39, Scissors 14, Total 119, with part (d): 'in repeated plays, a player is more likely to repeat the option just picked than to switch to a different option.' Zhang et al. 2021 Introduction (econstor PDF): 'Eyler et al. [4] noted that players tended to repeat choices consecutively (e.g., rock-rock-rock) or to cycle in a sequence'.
verified.reliability: Secondary reports only: a science writer quoting the authors, a textbook exercise, and one sentence from a peer-reviewed review.
