The original is a short classroom capsule with 119 first throws against a computer. Recruitment and incentives are unknown. Low to moderate reliability.
verified.design: From secondary sources: 119 people × 50 games against a computer playing an exploitative strategy. A second test had 241 participants × 100 games against an adaptive program that used the opponent's last two choices. Authors were at Elizabethtown College, USA, and the web game was on McDevitt's page. Recruitment, population and incentives are not stated.
verified.effect: First throw: Rock +22.1 pp (55.5 vs 33.3), Paper −0.6 pp, Scissors −21.6 pp. Repeat after Paper: +8.8 pp. The exploiting program netted +14.4 pp per throw (42.1 − 27.7). My calculation of opener value against this distribution: Paper +43.7 pp, Rock −21.0, Scissors −22.7.
verified.implication: Against opponents like these subjects (novices), open with Paper. After an opponent's Paper, expect another Paper and throw Scissors (beat their last throw). This repeat tendency conflicts with C06 and C07, so it depends on the population.
verified.caveats: I could not read the primary text. The figures come from a contemporaneous science writer quoting the authors and from a textbook exercise. Only 119 first throws. The opponent was a computer. Repeat probability is reported only after Paper, and the number of transitions is unknown.

verified.statement: The triplet 'Rock 35.4%, Paper 35.0%, Scissors 29.6%' is attributed in popular articles to the World RPS Society, not to any study. The archived WRPS strategy page (2009) contains only 'scissors ... 29.6% ... in competition play', with no sample size or method, and no '35.4'. WRPS's own 'Roshambull' figures (36% Rock, 30% Paper, 34% Scissors from '10 million throws in over 1.6 million games') contradict the peer-reviewed analysis of the same app (C01).
verified.evidence: WRPS 'How to beat anyone' (Wayback raw capture https://web.archive.org/web/20091118200539id_/http://www.worldrps.com:80/index.php/%20http:/www.worldrps.com/propaganda/index.php?option=com_content&task=view&id=256&Itemid=37), tip 7: 'Statistically, in competition play, it has been observed that scissors is thrown the least often. Specifically, it gets delivered 29.6% of the time, so it slightly under-indexes against the expected average of 33.33% by 3.73%.' The strings '35.4' and '35%' are absent. WRPS 'Definitive Guide' (https://web.archive.org/web/20100427110805id_/http://www.worldrps.com:80/component/content/article/17/439-is-there-strategy-in-rock-paper-scissors-the-definitive-guide): 'Facebook's Roshambull application ... has logged a staggering 10 million throws in over 1.6 million games from real players and their stats come out as 36% Rock, 30% Paper and 34% Scissors.' Linux Journal, Dave Taylor, 18 Jul 2017 (https://www.linuxjournal.com/content/scissors-paper-or-rock): 'according to the World Rock, Paper, Scissors Society, rock is chosen 35.4%, paper 35% of the time and scissors only 29.6% of the time.' Batzilis Table 1, all throws: R 35.45 / P 34.01 / S 30.54.
verified.reliability: Organisation web pages with no data or method, and a popular magazine, set against a peer-reviewed field study. Reliable as a statement about the absence of support on the two archived pages I examined.
verified.design: Organisation web pages that disclose no data, sample size, population or method, compared against peer-reviewed field data on the same app (S01).
verified.effect: WRPS Scissors 29.6% would be −3.7 pp versus 1/3 (unverifiable). WRPS's Roshambull Paper figure of 30% versus Batzilis first-throw Paper 34.82% is a discrepancy of 4.8 pp; Scissors 34% versus 31.20% is 2.8 pp.
verified.implication: Treat the 35.4/35.0/29.6 numbers as anecdote. The message behind them (Scissors is least common, so Paper is safe) is still consistent with several real datasets (C01, C04, C05).
verified.caveats: I could not check every version of every WRPS page, so the triplet may exist somewhere I did not see. The Roshambull discrepancy could come from a different data extract, but WRPS gives no method.

verified.statement: In incentivised Zhejiang University lab experiments (China), Rock was chosen slightly more than 1/3 and Paper and Scissors slightly less. Xu et al. 2013 (72 students, 21,600 throws): R 7,702 (35.66%), P 6,937 (32.12%), S 6,961 (32.23%). Wang et al. 2014 (354 players): mean individual frequencies R 0.36±0.08, P 0.33±0.07, S 0.32±0.06, with R at 0.35–0.37 in every payoff treatment. Wang L. et al. 2020 (against an AI, 300 rounds): mean R 106.6, P 96.3, S 97.1 (35.5/32.1/32.4%). Wang 2014's authors note that the Rock excess 'might be linked to' Rock being the left-most choice on screen.
verified.evidence: Xu, Zhou & Wang 2013 (arXiv 1301.3238v3, Sec. 3): 'the total number of times the strategy R, P and S being used is, respectively, 7702, 6937 and 6961 ... x = 0.357 ± 0.005, y = 0.321 ± 0.004'. Design: 12 groups of N=6, December 2010, 0.15 RMB per point, 5 RMB show-up fee, about 50 RMB average. Wang, Xu & Zhou 2014 (PMC5376050), Results: 'Averaged among the 354 players of these 59 populations ... 0.36 ± 0.08, 0.33 ± 0.07 and 0.32 ± 0.06'. Methods: 360 students, 217 F : 143 M, Dec 2010 to Mar 2014; 'lists the three candidate actions “Rock”, “Scissors”, “Paper” horizontally from left to right'. SI Table S1 (arXiv 1404.5199): R mean 0.37 (a=1.1), 0.36 (2), 0.35 (4), 0.35 (9), 0.35 (100); range 0.11–0.68. S2: 'might be linked to the fact that “Rock” is the left-most candidate choice'. Wang L et al. 2020 (PMC7431549), Table 4: MEAN 106.6098 / 96.29268 / 97.09756 (×41 = 4,371/3,948/3,981 exactly); July–September 2019; decision window again lists 'Rock', 'Scissors', 'Paper' from left to right.
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed (Physica A, Sci Rep) plus SI, all from one lab. Cash incentives. N = 72–354. Screen play with random re-matching in groups of 6, or play against an AI. The datasets overlap and are not independent.
verified.design: Lab experiments with Zhejiang University undergraduate and graduate students, China. Xu 2013: 12 groups of 6 with random pairwise re-matching each round, 300 rounds, payoff win 2 / tie 1 / loss 0, cash 0.15 RMB per point + 5 RMB show-up (about 50 RMB average), December 2010. Wang 2014: 360 students (217 F, 143 M) in 60 groups of 6, random re-matching, 300 rounds, win payoff a in {1.1, 2, 4, 9, 100}, cash in proportion to points; 354 analysed; December 2010 to March 2014. Its a=2 groups probably include Xu's data, so the two are not independent. Wang L 2020: 52 students against a Markov-chain AI, 300 rounds, a=2 cash payoff, July–September 2019; Table 4 means correspond to 41 players (my inference).
verified.effect: Versus 33.33%: Rock +2.2 to +2.7 pp, Paper −0.3 to −1.2 pp, Scissors −1.0 to −1.3 pp. Net value of always throwing Paper is P(Rock) − P(Scissors), about +3.2 to +3.4 pp per throw (Xu: 35.66 − 32.23 = 3.43; Wang L: 35.54 − 32.37 = 3.17).
verified.implication: Against a population that plays like these Chinese students, defaulting to Paper yields about +3 net wins per 100 throws. Scissors is the weakest default (about −3.4 pp).
verified.caveats: Rock was the left-most button, and the authors themselves suspect a position effect. Groups of 6 with random re-matching and 300-round sessions differ from a 1-on-1 elimination format. Individuals varied widely (Table S1 Rock range 0.11–0.68). All datasets come from the same lab.

verified.statement: Japan, Yoshizawa's real-hand janken data: 725 people threw 11,567 hands, グー (Rock) 4,054 = 35.05%, パー (Paper) 3,849 = 33.28%, チョキ (Scissors) 3,664 = 31.68%. The author reports that equal 1/3 shares are rejected at the 5% level for 'more Rock' and 'fewer Scissors'. (Yoshizawa, Toyo Keizai Online 2019; 2006 book)
verified.evidence: Toyo Keizai 2019-08-07, p.1 (https://toyokeizai.net/articles/-/295436?page=1; body visible with a mobile user agent): '1990年代後半に、当時勤めていた大学でのゼミナール生とさまざまな統計データを収集した ... じゃんけんに関してはゼミ生10人にノートを渡し、多くの人たちのじゃんけんデータを記録した。調査対象はのべ725人になり、それぞれ20回以下までじゃんけんを行ってもらった。なお、当該ゼミ生は調査のじゃんけんに加わっていない。' p.2: '725人から集めたのべ11567回のじゃんけんデータ ... グーが4054回、チョキが3664回、パーが3849回 ... 棄却され（有意水準5％の正規検定とする）「人間はグーが多い」、「人間はチョキが少ない」'. NDL record 1000179084, citing 『じゃんけんの算数』 (日本評論社, 2006) p.7: 'のべ11567回のじゃんけんのうち、グーは4054回、チョキは3664回、パーは3849回'.
verified.reliability: Not peer-reviewed. The researcher's own popular article and a children's book. Large N, but sampling and recording are undocumented and throws are clustered within people. Real-hand play in Japan, late 1990s, no incentives.
verified.design: Field observation in Japan, late 1990s. Ten seminar students recorded other people's real-hand janken: 725 people, up to 20 throws each, 11,567 throws in total. Opponents were other people. No incentives were reported. Published in a 2006 children's maths book, in Nikkei (2007 and 2009, per S16) and on Toyo Keizai Online (2019). Not peer reviewed.
verified.effect: Versus 33.33%: Rock +1.72 pp, Paper −0.06 pp, Scissors −1.66 pp. My naive one-sample z-scores, which ignore clustering by person: Rock +3.9, Scissors −3.8. Net value per throw: Paper +3.4 pp, Rock −1.6, Scissors −1.8.
verified.implication: In Japanese real-hand play, Paper is the best default (+3.4 pp) and Scissors the worst. This is the same small Rock-high / Scissors-low pattern as the Chinese lab data and the only East Asian dataset from live hand play.
verified.caveats: Not peer reviewed. How people were sampled and how throws were recorded is undocumented. Throws are clustered within 725 people, so significance is overstated. Later retellings say '725 students'; the article says 'のべ725人'. The data are about 25 years old. A small replication found no win advantage for Paper (C13).

verified.statement: In the same Japanese data, only 2,465 of 10,833 consecutive throw pairs (22.75%) repeated the same hand, against 33.3% under random play. Yoshizawa derived, but did not measure, the rule that after a tie on X you should throw the hand that loses to X (e.g., after a Rock–Rock tie, throw Scissors). Popular retellings misreport the 22.8% as the repeat rate specifically after a tie. (Yoshizawa, Toyo Keizai 2019; PRESIDENT Online 2024)
verified.evidence: Toyo Keizai p.2: '2回続けたじゃんけんは延べ1万833回であったが、そのうち同じ手を続けて出した回数は2465回であった' (worked example counts all consecutive pairs) and '「2人でじゃんけんをしてあいこになったら、次に自分はその手に負ける手を出すと有利」という結論が得られる ... (有意水準1％の正規検定とする)'. PRESIDENT Online 2024-03-06 p.2 (https://president.jp/articles/-/79230?page=2): 'あいこになったとき、次も同じ手を出す確率は22.8％ということがわかりました。'. Miyagawa 2011, 国民経済雑誌 204(4):53 (Kobe PDF), abstract: '例えばグーを出してあいこになると，次はグーの確率を下げるのである'.
verified.reliability: Same data as C05, not peer-reviewed. Miyagawa is a theory paper in a university economics journal.
verified.design: Same Japanese field data as C05: 10,833 consecutive pairs drawn from 725 people, covering all outcomes, not only ties.
verified.effect: Repeat −10.6 pp (22.75% vs 33.33%); naive z ≈ −23, ignoring clustering. As an illustration only (my assumption): if non-repeats split evenly at about 38.6% each, throwing the hand that loses to X after a tie on X nets about +15.9 pp (win against their switch to the hand that beats X, lose only if they repeat).
verified.implication: Against repeat-avoiders, after a tie on X: Rock tie → throw Scissors; Paper tie → throw Rock; Scissors tie → throw Paper. This throw beats the opponent's 'upgrade', ties their 'downgrade', and loses only if they repeat.
verified.caveats: 22.75% pools pairs after wins, losses and ties; after-tie behaviour was not reported separately. Clustering is ignored. Not peer reviewed. The rule rests on an assumption that switches split evenly; C07 supports it but C08 contradicts it.

verified.statement: Western lab data, behaviour after a DRAW on X. Dyson et al. 2016 (Canada; my aggregation of the supplementary per-participant data) found, weighted by hand: repeat X 28.7%, switch to the hand that beats X 39.6%, switch to the hand that X beats 31.7%. By tied hand: after a Rock tie, Rock 32.1 / Paper 37.2 / Scissors 30.7%; after a Paper tie, Paper 24.8 / Scissors 40.8 / Rock 34.3%; after a Scissors tie, Scissors 25.5 / Rock 42.3 / Paper 32.1%. The paper reports a significant shift to the beating hand relative to staying. Forder & Dyson 2016 (UK) found 37.32% / 33.40% / 29.28% for beating hand / hand X beats / repeat, differences not significant.
verified.evidence: I re-aggregated srep20479-s2.xls myself (Nature ESM: https://static-content.springer.com/esm/art%3A10.1038%2Fsrep20479/MediaObjects/41598_2016_BFsrep20479_MOESM2_ESM.xls; 31 participants, columns Item n × Outcome n × STAY/UP/DOWN). Weighting each draw cell by the participant's item share gives STAY 28.7 / UP 39.6 / DOWN 31.7; unweighted 27.5/40.1/32.4. Per tied hand: Rock 32.1/37.2/30.7, Paper 24.8/40.8/34.3, Scissors 25.5/42.3/32.1. All match the sweep exactly. Dyson 2016 Results (PMC4740902): 'following a draw, participants were inclined to switch and specifically upgrade their item relative to staying' (Tukey HSD p<0.05). Methods: 31 undergraduates (26 F), mean age 20.23, Ryerson University, course credit; 225 trials; the computer played each item 25 times per block in random order. Forder & Dyson 2016 (PMC5034336): 'upgrading was numerically more popular than both the other form of switch- downgrading- and staying during draw trials, although the differences between these forms of strategy (37.32%, 33.40% and 29.28%, respectively) were not statistically significant'. Methods: 36 undergraduates (30 F), course credit or £20 not tied to performance, 450 trials.
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed (Sci Rep). Small N (31, 36). Opponent was a random computer, with no performance pay. My independent re-aggregation of the open spreadsheet matches the sweep exactly.
verified.design: Lab, opponent a computer that played each hand equally often in random order. Dyson: 31 undergraduates (26 F, mean age 20.2) at Ryerson University, Canada; 225 trials; course credit, no performance pay. Forder & Dyson: 36 undergraduates (30 F) at the University of Sussex, UK; 450 trials in three point-value blocks; course credit or £20 not tied to performance.
verified.effect: Versus 33.33% (Dyson): repeat −4.6 pp, beating hand +6.3 pp, hand X beats −1.6 pp. Forder: −4.1, +4.0, +0.1 pp. My best-response calculation: throwing the hand X beats nets +10.9 pp (Dyson) or +8.0 pp (Forder); repeating X nets −7.9 pp; throwing the hand that beats X nets −3.0 pp (Dyson). By tied hand (Dyson): Rock tie → Scissors +5.1 pp; Paper tie → Rock +16.0 pp; Scissors tie → Paper +16.8 pp.
verified.implication: Against Western-lab-like opponents, after a tie: Rock tie → throw Scissors, Paper tie → throw Rock, Scissors tie → throw Paper. This matches Yoshizawa's rule (C06) and the WRPS 'Step Ahead' tip (C15).
verified.caveats: Small samples, and the opponent was a computer (ties occur at random and nothing is at stake socially). Forder's after-draw differences were not significant. Per-hand cells are small. The weights in my aggregation are approximate.

verified.statement: Chinese lab data (Zhejiang; 6-player groups randomly re-matched every round; a tie pays 1 point, a win pays a) show more repeating after a tie than Western data, but the pattern depends on the tie payoff. Repeat is the clear majority response only when ties are rewarded. Wang et al. 2014 Fig. 3F–J, digitised as repeat T0 / switch to the hand that beats the tied hand T+ / switch to the hand the tied hand beats T−: a=1.1 0.60/0.25/0.14; a=2 0.43/0.33/0.23; a=4 0.39/0.38/0.23; a=9 0.36/0.35/0.29; a=100 0.36/0.37/0.27. So repeat leads only at a=1.1 and a=2; at a=4–100 repeat and upgrade are tied. Wang & Xu 2014 Fig. 7 (504 students) adds a=1 (repeat 0.80) and a=∞, where ties pay nothing: repeat 0.34, upgrade 0.38, downgrade 0.28. Downgrade is the least common post-tie move in every treatment. Best response to the tied hand X: at a=2, throwing the hand that beats X nets about +0.20; at a=∞, it nets +0.055 against +0.039 for the hand X beats. Two fixed-opponent human-vs-human datasets show the opposite of the a=2 pattern (see MF01). The rule 'after a Rock–Rock tie throw Paper' should not be used in a real match.
verified.evidence: Definitions (Wang 2014, PMC5376050): '+' = 'counter-clockwise (i.e., R → P, P → S, S → R)'; '−' = 'clockwise (R → S, S → P, P → R)'. My pixel digitisation of Fig. 3F–J (Nature image 41598_2014_Article_BFsrep05830_Fig3_HTML.jpg), given as T−/T0/T+ with each triple summing to 1.00 ± 0.002: a=1.1 0.143/0.604/0.253; a=2 0.232/0.432/0.334; a=4 0.230/0.388/0.382; a=9 0.291/0.358/0.349; a=100 0.269/0.364/0.368. Wang & Xu 2014 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1407.1170) p.8, Fig. 7 'Tie Condition ... the first stick is T−, the second is T0, and the third is T+', digitised at 400 dpi: a=1 0.060/0.800/0.138; 1.1 0.136/0.623/0.237; 2 0.232/0.434/0.331; 4 0.228/0.392/0.377; 9 0.292/0.357/0.349; 100 0.270/0.361/0.367; ∞ 0.283/0.338/0.377. Fig. 1 payoff matrices: a=1 pays a tie as much as a win; a=∞ is '0 0 1 / 1 0 0 / 0 1 0', where a tie pays 0. Text: 'when people tie, they tend to decrease T0 behavior with the winning payoff a (Spearman's rho=-0.531 ...), while increase T− (Spearman's rho=0.507 ...) and T+ (Spearman's rho=0.432 ...)'.
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed Sci Rep paper plus an arXiv preprint from one lab. N = 354 and 504, incentivised, 300 rounds. Random re-matching means the post-tie opponent is usually someone else. Values are digitised from bar charts (about ±0.005).
verified.design: Same Zhejiang lab protocol as C04: groups of 6 with random pairwise re-matching each round (the opponent after a tie is usually a different person), 300 rounds, decision window up to 40 s, cash incentives. Wang 2014: 354 players. Wang & Xu 2014: 504 players, 72 per treatment.
verified.effect: At a=2, versus 33.3%: repeat about +10 pp, T+ about 0, T− about −10 pp. My best-response calculation at a=2: throwing the hand that beats X nets about +0.20 (wins against a repeat 0.43, loses against T− 0.23); throwing the hand X beats nets about −0.10. At a=4, 9 and 100, throwing the hand that beats X still nets about +0.07 to +0.16.
verified.implication: Against opponents behaving like these Chinese students, after a Rock–Rock tie throw Paper, not Scissors. This directly contradicts C06 and C07, so the right after-tie move depends on the opponent; observe their actual after-tie habit before relying on either rule.
verified.caveats: Values come from a bar chart, not a table. Random re-matching differs from playing the same opponent until a winner is decided. In the a=1.1 treatment a tie pays almost as much as a win, which encourages coordination. Long, repetitive sessions.

verified.statement: Overall repetition (same hand as the player's own previous throw, any outcome) varies sharply across populations. It is above 1/3 in Chinese lab data (Wang & Xu stay rate: 0.440 at a=2, 0.411 at a=4, 0.370 at a=9, 0.386 at a=100, 0.376 at a=∞, 0.531 at a=1.1; 'stay' was the most used transition in every treatment) and in Eyler's US sample playing a computer (P(Paper→Paper) = 0.421). It is below 1/3 in Japanese field data (22.75%) and in Canadian lab data (about 29.6% by my estimate; 20 of 31 participants under 1/3; individual range 3.5–70.1%). Australian human-vs-human players also tended to change hands regardless of the previous outcome.
verified.evidence: Wang & Xu 2014 Table 2, stay column (Obs=72): a=1 0.708; 1.1 0.531; 2 0.440; 4 0.411; 9 0.370; 100 0.386; ∞ 0.376. Text: 'In all of the treatments, the most frequently used strategy is “stay” strategy'. Peterson 2009: '.421 probability of repeating'. Toyo Keizai p.2: 2,465 of 10,833. Dyson spreadsheet, my re-aggregation weighting cells by item × outcome shares: mean 29.6%, 20 of 31 below 1/3, range 3.5–70.1%. Moerel 2025 (PMC12628313): 'Many participants were biased towards changing their response, regardless of the outcome of the previous game.' My computation from Moerel's raw data (OpenNeuro ds006761, 28,978 transitions): repeat 27.5%, 50 of 62 players below 1/3. Brockbank & Vul raw data: 28.2%, 88 of 124 below 1/3.
verified.reliability: Mixed designs: a peer-reviewed lab study and preprints, a popular article and a blog. My checks of raw human-pair data support below-chance repetition when the opponent is fixed.
verified.design: Mixed designs. China: incentivised lab, 6-person groups with re-matching (n=72 per treatment). USA: computer opponent (n not stated for transitions). Japan: field, real hands, 725 people. Canada: lab against a random computer, n=31. Australia: human–human pairs, n=62, flat pay.
verified.effect: Versus 33.33%: China at a=2 +10.7 pp, at a=∞ +4.3 pp; US repeat after Paper +8.8 pp; Japan −10.6 pp; Canada about −3.7 pp.
verified.implication: There is no universal 'people avoid repeats' law. In a team event, watch each opponent's first few throws. Against a repeater, throw the hand that beats their last throw. Against an avoider, throw the hand their last throw beats (it wins against their upgrade and ties their downgrade).
verified.caveats: Designs differ (re-matching vs fixed opponent, computer vs human, screen vs real hands). The Dyson figure is my approximation. Moerel's values appear only in a figure.

verified.statement: Evidence on 'three in a row' is thin. In Dyson 2016's data, after a participant had repeated a hand once (X, X), a third X followed 30.5% of the time, versus 33.3% at random, and a repeat did not predict another repeat. Cycling did persist: after an upgrade (e.g., Rock→Paper) the next move was another upgrade (Paper→Scissors) 43.5% of the time, and after a downgrade (e.g., Rock→Scissors) another downgrade (Scissors→Paper) 42.4%. The WRPS 'Double Run' rule (after X, X you can 'safely eliminate' X) and the Sazae-san observation are anecdotal. (Dyson et al. 2016 supplementary data)
verified.evidence: Dyson spreadsheet second-order columns, mean of 31 participants, re-aggregated by me. After STAY: STAY 30.5 / UP 34.6 / DOWN 34.9. After UP: UP 43.5 (STAY 27.9, DOWN 28.7). After DOWN: DOWN 42.4 (STAY 28.4, UP 29.2). Dyson 2016 Results: 'staying with item selection between trial n and n + 1 failed to impact on the strategy adopted between trial n + 1 and n + 2. However, participants who upgraded were more likely to continue upgrading and participants who downgraded were more likely to continue downgrading' [F(4,120)=13.12, p<0.001]. WRPS 2009 tip 3: 'When this happens you can safely eliminate that throw'. ねとらぼ 2018: '3週連続で同じ手は出ていない'.
verified.reliability: One small peer-reviewed lab study against a computer. Replicated in my analysis of two larger human-pair datasets.
verified.design: Dyson: 31 Canadian undergraduates against a random computer, 225 trials. WRPS: no data. Sazae-san: a TV production sequence.
verified.effect: Third identical throw: −2.8 pp versus 33.3%. Continued upgrade +10.2 pp; continued downgrade +9.1 pp.
verified.implication: After an opponent throws X, X, X is only slightly less likely (about 30%), so do not treat it as eliminated. After a cyclic step, expect the next step: after Rock→Paper, expect Scissors and throw Rock; after Rock→Scissors, expect Paper and throw Scissors.
verified.caveats: One small lab study against a computer. Second-order proportions are means of per-participant proportions, extracted by me. Chinese high-repeat data would likely show more triples. No large dataset reports three-in-a-row rates directly.

verified.statement: In face-to-face, real-hand play in Europe the Rock bias did not appear. Cook et al. 2012 (UK) found Rock 32.4%, Paper 33.3%, Scissors 34.4%, with no significant difference. Aczel et al. 2012 (Hungary) found Scissors the MOST frequent gesture: 36.76% when one player was blindfolded and 36.64% when both were (equal proportions rejected, p=0.001 and p<0.001). A 2021 review (Brockbank & Vul 2021) concludes that the Rock bias is 'not always significant', that some studies show a preference for Paper or Scissors, and that many show none.
verified.evidence: Cook 2012 (PMC3248720): 'the rock gesture was executed on 32.4 per cent of rounds, the paper gesture on 33.3 per cent of rounds and the scissors gesture on 34.4 per cent of rounds ... (F2,26 = 1.24; p > 0.30) and blind–blind conditions (F2,26 = 0.117; p > 0.80)'. Cook design: 45 adults (23 F), mean age 24.9; 14 triads analysed; £5 plus a £2.50 bonus per 60-round match; 'presenting a clenched fist ... Following a count of three made by the umpire'. Aczel 2012 (PMC3385727): 'F1.92,63.49 = 7.47, p = 0.001 ... F1.92,63.44 = 14.16, p < 0.001 ... scissors gesture was the most frequently used in the blind–sighted, (M = 36.76%, s.d. = 5.05), as well as in the blind–blind condition (M = 36.64%, s.d. = 3.99)'. Aczel design: 114 Hungarians (61 F), mean age 22.46; four triads discarded, leaving 34; chocolate bar plus 300 HUF per block winner; 3 blocks × 3 matches of 20 rounds. Brockbank & Vul 2021, p.4: 'slight overall bias towards “rock”, though this is not always significant ... modest preference for “paper” or “scissors” ... in many cases people show no distinguishable preference at all'.
verified.reliability: Two peer-reviewed real-hand studies with few independent units (14 and 34 triads) and small incentives, plus a peer-reviewed review.
verified.design: Cook: 45 adults (23 F, mean age 24.9) at UCL, London; physical play in triads, 14 triads analysed; an umpire announced the gestures; one or both players blindfolded; £5 fee plus £2.50 to the winner of each 60-round match. Aczel: 114 Hungarian adults (61 F, mean age 22.5); physical play in triads with blindfold conditions, 3 × 3 matches of 20 rounds; a chocolate bar plus 300 HUF to each block winner; 34 triads analysed.
verified.effect: Cook versus 33.33%: Rock −0.9, Paper −0.0, Scissors +1.1 pp. Aczel: Scissors +3.4 / +3.3 pp.
verified.implication: For live real-hand team matches, do not assume opponents over-throw Rock. In the Hungarian sample Rock (which beats Scissors) would have been the best default. Marginal biases are small and depend on the population.
verified.caveats: Blindfold manipulations and spoken announcements may change choices. Players pumped closed fists before each throw. Few independent triads. Neither study is East Asian.

verified.statement: With the on-screen order of options randomised in every block, which removes screen-position effects, an Australian human-vs-human study still found Rock was the most-played hand for 51.61% of participants, Paper for 33.87% and Scissors for only 14.52%. Participants also tended to change hands from one game to the next regardless of the outcome. (Moerel et al. 2025, SCAN)
verified.evidence: Moerel 2025 (PMC12628313), Fig. 1 caption: '51.61% of participants had Rock as their most played response, followed by Paper (33.87%), and Scissors (14.52%)'. Results: 'there was a bias towards Rock'. Methods: 'The order of the Rock, Paper, and Scissors images was chosen at random for each participant and each block'. Design: 62 participants (38 F/22 M/2 non-binary), mean age 27.85, AUD 60 flat, 480 games in 12 blocks of 40, Decision 2 s + Response 2 s. My recount from the raw data (OpenNeuro ds006761) reproduces 32/21/9 players with Rock/Paper/Scissors as their most-played hand. Overall shares: Rock 35.34%, Paper 32.54%, Scissors 32.12% (29,511 valid throws).
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed (SCAN 2025). N=62 in 31 fixed human pairs, flat pay, EEG lab. Public raw data are consistent with the paper.
verified.design: Lab with EEG hyperscanning at Western Sydney University, Australia: 62 adults in 31 human–human pairs (38 F, 22 M, 2 non-binary; mean age 27.9). 480 games each with a 2-s response window. Flat payment of AUD 60, not tied to performance.
verified.effect: Share of players whose most-played hand was Rock: +18.3 pp above the 33.3% expected if most-played hands were evenly spread. Scissors: −18.8 pp.
verified.implication: The small Rock-over / Scissors-under tendency survives without interface artefacts in Western adults, which supports Paper as a weak default. Repeat avoidance appears in fixed-pair human play.
verified.caveats: Small sample. Reports only each player's most-played hand, not overall frequencies. No performance incentive. Fast responses in an EEG setting.

verified.statement: A small Japanese classroom replication (Ogawa 2013) found no evidence for Yoshizawa's rules. First, the hand thrown on the first bout did not affect mean wins (F(2,116)=0.049, n.s.), so opening with Paper did not win more. Second, after a tie, throwing 'the hand that loses to the tied hand' did not win more; 'not-losing' hands won significantly more (F(1,58)=44.534, p<.001).
verified.evidence: Ogawa 2013, 人間文化研究 31:27–38 (https://kyotogakuen.repo.nii.ac.jp/record/141/files/KJ00009489619.pdf). Experiment I: '大学生68名(男性43名，女性25名，平均年齢18.7歳) ... 二人ずつリーグ戦でジャンケンを行い，双方の出した手と勝敗を実験参加者自身が記録した ... (F(2, 116)＝.049, ns)'. Experiment II: 'あいこに負ける手か否かに有意な効果が得られ(F(1, 58)＝44.534, p＜.001) ... 負ける手よりも負けない手を出した方が有意に勝てる'. Ogawa also restates Yoshizawa's data as 'グー：35.0%，パー：33.3%，チョキ：31.7%' from '725人の学生'.
verified.reliability: Non-peer-reviewed university bulletin. Small classroom sample, self-recorded, count-based analyses. Weak evidence.
verified.design: Classroom study in Japan (Kyoto Gakuen University): 68 students (43 M, 25 F; mean age 18.7) in three classes of 20-odd, round-robin pairwise janken, self-recorded. No incentives. Experiment III used 65 students with announced throws.
verified.effect: No first-throw effect, F(2,116)=0.049. The after-tie comparison favours the 'not-losing' category, F(1,58)=44.5, but this compares win counts, not rates (see caveats).
verified.implication: Yoshizawa's 'Paper first' and 'after a tie throw the losing hand' rules are fragile in a direct, if weak, Japanese test, so treat them as small or uncertain edges.
verified.caveats: Non-peer-reviewed university bulletin. Small and self-recorded. The after-tie analysis compares win counts for one hand against two hands combined (the 'not-losing' category holds both the repeat and the beating hand), which favours that category by construction. It therefore does not cleanly refute the rule. No hand frequencies were reported.

verified.statement: Stated preferences in a 2023 Japanese online survey (n=1,000) differ from observed play. Asked what they throw first in a one-shot game, respondents said Scissors 42.0% (420), Rock 37.4% (374), Paper 20.6% (206). Men most often said Rock (42.43%; Scissors 32.34%, Paper 25.22%; n=337). Women most often said Scissors (46.91%; Rock 34.84%, Paper 18.25%; n=663). After a tie, stated next throws were close to equal thirds (34.2 / 33.2 / 32.6%). (Toint survey 2023)
verified.reliability: Commercial online self-report from a non-probability panel. These are stated intentions, not observed throws.
verified.design: Commercial internet survey of self-reported intentions (not observed throws). Japan, ages 20s–70s, 337 men and 663 women, 24–26 July 2023. No incentives.
verified.effect: Stated first throw versus 33.33%: Scissors +8.7 pp, Rock +4.1 pp, Paper −12.7 pp. Men's Rock +9.1 pp; women's Scissors +13.6 pp.
verified.implication: If these stated habits held in real play (unverified), the best opener against Japanese women would be Rock (+28.7 pp = 46.91 − 18.25) and against men Paper (+10.1 pp). This conflicts with observed Japanese data (C05), so it is weak evidence at most.
verified.caveats: Self-report from a non-probability online panel. Stated and actual choices are known to differ. The order of the after-tie columns is my inference.

verified.statement: The World RPS Society's best-known claims rest on no published data. Claims checked: 'Rock is for Rookies' (males lead with Rock), 'Scissors on First' against experienced players, 'Double Run' (eliminate a hand thrown twice), 'Step Ahead Thinking' (after a stalemate, the opponent often throws the hand that beats their last one, so throw the hand that loses to their last throw) and 'scissors 29.6%'. None reports a sample, method or population. (WRPS web pages, 2009–2010 Wayback captures)
verified.evidence: WRPS 2009 capture (raw id_ URL as in C03). Tip 1: 'males have a tendency to lead with Rock on their opening throw ... generally won't work in tournament play'. Tip 2: 'play scissors as your opening move against a more experienced player'. Tip 3: 'you can safely eliminate that throw'. Tip 5: 'Try playing the throw that would have lost to your opponents last throw? ... Inexperienced (or flustered) players will often subconsciously deliver the throw that beat their last one ... This is a good tactic in a stalemate situation or when your opponent lost their last game.' Tip 7: the 29.6% figure. Author: Graham Walker. No sample, data source or method anywhere on the page.
verified.reliability: Organisation strategy articles with no data.
verified.design: Organisation strategy articles (Graham Walker, co-author of the 'Official Rock Paper Scissors Strategy Guide'). No data.
verified.effect: Not quantifiable; the only number given (Scissors 29.6%) is unsourced.
verified.implication: Treat these as hypotheses. 'Step Ahead' after a tie matches Western lab data (C07) and Yoshizawa (C06) but is contradicted by Chinese lab data (C08). 'Males lead with Rock' has only self-report support (C14). 'Rock is a rookie opener' is loosely consistent with experienced Facebook players opening with Rock least often (C01).
verified.caveats: The high confidence refers only to the absence of supporting data in the sources examined; it does not mean the claims are false.

verified.statement: Anecdotal Japanese case: Sazae-san's televised janken hands (1,347 bouts, 1991-11-10 to 2018-08-05) were near-uniform overall (グー 436 = 32.4%, チョキ 467 = 34.7%, パー 444 = 33.0%). They still showed sequence regularities: in recent years no hand appeared three weeks in a row, and the hand absent longest tended to appear next. A fan group predicting from recent hands reached 50.2% prediction accuracy (chance 33.3%) and a record of 570 wins, 240 losses, 324 draws; the reported 70.3% win rate excludes draws.
verified.evidence: ねとらぼ 2018-08-14 (https://nlab.itmedia.co.jp/cont/articles/3281688/): '1991年11月10日放送回から、2018年8月5日放送回までの手を全て集計'; '過去22年半の勝負で、570勝240敗324分・予想的中率50.2％・勝率70.3％'; '1347回中、グーは436回、チョキは467回、パーは444回'; '近年の放送では「パー、チョキと続いた次の週は圧倒的にグーが出やすい」「3週連続で同じ手は出ていない」「最も長期間出ていない手は出やすい」'.
verified.reliability: A news report of a fan group's analysis. The sequence is produced by TV staff, not a competing human, and it is not peer-reviewed.
verified.design: A sequence generated by TV production staff, recorded weekly by fans. Not a human competitor under incentive.
verified.effect: Marginal shares within ±1.4 pp of 1/3. Prediction accuracy +16.9 pp over chance. Wins over all bouts including draws: 570/1,134 = 50.3%; 70.3% is 570/(570+240).
verified.implication: An opponent can be near-uniform overall yet exploitable through sequence, especially by avoiding repeats and 'catching up' the least-used hand. Watch for a hand that has been absent for a while.
verified.caveats: Not a competitive human player. Fan analysis that is not peer reviewed. Prone to selective reporting.

verified.statement: Anecdotal age difference from a Japanese junior-high free-research project (76 people, 4,600 rapid-fire throws). Kindergarteners threw Scissors most and Rock least overall. Junior-high pupils and the overall sample threw Rock most and Paper least. First throws were most often Scissors among both junior-high pupils and kindergarteners (order Scissors > Paper > Rock), while adults' first throws were exactly 1/3 each. (Uchida 2017)
verified.evidence: 内田さくら 2017, 自由研究 第42集 (https://f.osaka-kyoiku.ac.jp/tennoji-j/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2020/09/42-06.pdf): '計76人 年長 33人 小学生 ４人 中学生 34人 大人 ５人'; 'じゃんけん総数 4600回'; '１回目に出した手の多い順では中学生ではチョキ，パー，グーであり、年長児もチョキ，パー，グーであった。大人はぴったり1/3'; '全体と中学生はグーが１番多く，次にチョキ、そしてパーが１番少なかった ... 年長児は，チョキが１番多く，次にパー，そしてグーが１番少なかった'.
verified.reliability: A junior-high student project. Tiny subgroups (5 adults), rapid-fire format, values in pie charts. Not research-grade.
verified.design: Student project in Japan (Osaka): 76 people, of whom 33 kindergarteners, 4 elementary, 34 junior-high and 5 adults. One minute (30 s for kindergarteners) of rapid repeated janken, video-coded. No incentives.
verified.effect: Percentages are given only in pie charts, so exact values are not reliably extractable.
verified.implication: Children and teenagers may not share the adult Rock-high pattern, and first throws may differ from later throws. This is too weak to act on, but it argues against assuming that opponents open with Rock.
verified.caveats: Not research-grade: tiny subgroups, rapid-fire format, and pie-chart values that are hard to read.

verified.statement: In observed-play datasets with a Rock excess, always throwing Paper is worth about +3 to +5 net wins per 100 throws: Batzilis all throws +4.9 pp, first throws +2.8, Yoshizawa +3.4, Xu +3.4, Wang L +3.2, Dyson 2016 +3.4, Forder +2.8, and Moerel raw data +3.2 (95% CI 1.4–5.2). In other populations it is zero or negative: Batzilis experienced openers −0.2, Cook UK −2.0, Brockbank & Vul US dyads −2.7 (CI −4.8 to −0.7), Sazae-san −2.3, Japanese stated openers −4.6, and Hungarian live play had a Scissors excess. After-tie edges are larger but depend on the setting. In every fixed-opponent dataset (Dyson 2016 Canada, Forder 2016 UK, Moerel 2025 Australia, Brockbank & Vul 2020 USA), throwing the hand the tied hand beats nets +5 to +11 pp, and throwing the hand that beats the tied hand nets −3 to −10 pp. The reverse holds only in Chinese random-rematch labs where ties earn points (a=2: about +20 pp for the hand that beats the tied hand). When ties are worth nothing (a=∞), both switches are mildly positive (+4 to +6 pp). Yoshizawa's Japanese field data measure overall repeats (22.75%), not after-tie behaviour.
verified.evidence: Arithmetic re-checked; every listed difference is correct: 35.45−30.54=4.91; 33.99−31.20=2.79; 35.05−31.68=3.37; 35.66−32.23=3.43; 35.54−32.37=3.17; 35.60−32.16=3.44; 35.16−32.35=2.81; 32.60−32.84=−0.24; 32.4−34.4=−2.0; 32.37−34.67=−2.30; 37.4−42.0=−4.6. New raw-data computations (pair-cluster bootstrap, 2,000 resamples): Moerel P(R)−P(S) +3.2 [1.4, 5.2]; Brockbank −2.7 [−4.8, −0.7]. After ties, Moerel nets +5.4 [1.2, 9.7] for the hand the tied hand beats and −9.8 [−14.0, −5.3] for the hand that beats it; Brockbank +5.8 [2.4, 9.1] and −6.3 [−10.6, −1.7]. Wang & Xu Fig. 7 at a=∞ (T−/T0/T+ 0.283/0.338/0.377) gives +5.5 pp for the hand that beats the tied hand and +3.9 pp for the hand it beats.
verified.reliability: Derived synthesis across heterogeneous designs. Arithmetic is correct. The main correction comes from adding two large public raw datasets of human-vs-human play with fixed opponents.
verified.design: Derived. Combines the designs listed in C01, C04, C05, C07, C08, C11, C14 and C16.
verified.effect: Paper default: +2.8 to +4.9 pp per throw in Rock-biased datasets; −0.2 to −4.6 pp in others. After-tie conditional edges: about +8 to +20 pp, but with opposite optimal moves across populations.
verified.implication: A blind 'always Paper' rule gives at best a few percent. Larger edges need population-specific, outcome-conditioned reads: after-tie behaviour, repeat versus avoid, and continued cycling. These must be checked against the actual opponent, because published populations disagree on their direction.
verified.caveats: Values are computed from heterogeneous designs (screen vs real hands, computer vs human opponents, incentives) and are not independent across Zhejiang datasets. Edges are relative to marginal frequencies and ignore the opponent's own adaptation.

verifier_added.statement: In fixed-opponent human-vs-human play, the opponent repeats the tied hand least often after a tie. After a tie on X, throwing the hand X beats (Rock tie→Scissors, Paper tie→Rock, Scissors tie→Paper) therefore wins on balance, and throwing the hand that beats X (Rock tie→Paper, Paper tie→Scissors, Scissors tie→Rock) loses. Moerel 2025 raw data (Australia, 31 fixed pairs, 9,661 ties): repeat 28.3%, switch to the hand that beats X 33.7%, switch to the hand X beats 38.0%. Net for throwing the hand X beats: +5.4 pp (95% CI 1.2 to 9.7); for throwing the hand that beats X: −9.8 pp (−14.0 to −5.3). Brockbank & Vul 2020 raw data (USA, 58 fixed dyads, 11,656 ties): 29.1/35.2/35.6%, with nets of +5.8 pp (2.4 to 9.1) and −6.3 pp (−10.6 to −1.7). By tied hand, 'throw the hand X beats' was positive in all 9 hand × dataset cells across Moerel, Brockbank and Dyson 2016 (+1.0 to +16.8 pp). 'Throw the hand that beats X' was negative in 8 of 9.
verifier_added.evidence: My computation from OpenNeuro ds006761 sub-*_task-RPS_events.tsv (player1_resp/player2_resp, 31 pairs × 480 games) and github.com/erik-brockbank/rps-games-analysis data/rps_v1_data.csv. Scripts: fcB_scripts/moerel_analysis.py, brockbank_analysis.py, boot_afterdraw.py, rule_eval2.py in the session scratchpad. Opponent's next throw R/P/S %, by tied hand. Moerel: Rock tie 30.4/31.4/38.2, Paper tie 40.1/27.8/32.2, Scissors tie 38.0/35.8/26.2. Brockbank: Rock tie 30.7/34.7/34.6, Paper tie 35.4/26.1/38.5, Scissors tie 32.5/36.7/30.8. Dyson 2016 per-hand cells as in C07. Per player: after-tie repeat was below 1/3 for 40/62 (Moerel) and 73/116 (Brockbank) players. The 'hand X beats' rule had a positive net against 38/62 and 72/116 individual players.
verifier_added.study_design: Moerel: 62 adults at Western Sydney University in 31 fixed human-human pairs; 480 computerised games with a 2-s decision and 2-s response window; option order randomised per block; flat AUD 60; EEG. Brockbank & Vul: 128 US college students (course credit), 58 complete stable online dyads, 300 rounds, 10-s limit, points win +3 / tie 0 / loss −1.
verifier_added.effect_size: For throwing the hand X beats: +5.4 and +5.8 pp per post-tie throw, both CIs excluding 0. For throwing the hand that beats X: −9.8 and −6.3 pp. Per-hand range for the first rule: +1.0 to +16.8 pp.
verifier_added.strategic_implication: After a tie with the same opponent: Rock–Rock → Scissors, Paper–Paper → Rock, Scissors–Scissors → Paper. Never answer a tie with the hand that beats the tied hand. This supports Yoshizawa's rule and the WRPS 'Step Ahead' tip for fixed-opponent play, and argues against carrying the Chinese a=2 pattern (C08) into a real match. The expected edge is about +5 pp, and about 4 in 10 individual opponents behave otherwise, so update once an opponent's own after-tie habit is visible.
verifier_added.caveats: This is my own secondary analysis, not reported by the authors. Play was computerised (buttons or cards), not face-to-face hands. Samples are Western university or community adults in long sessions. No Korean data. Opponents in these data were not facing an exploiter, so an adaptive opponent could counter a rule used every time.

verifier_added.statement: The Chinese 'repeat after a tie' pattern depends on the payoff. In Wang & Xu 2014 Fig. 7 (504 Zhejiang students, 72 per treatment; my digitisation), the share repeating the tied hand fell steadily as the tie's value shrank: 0.80 when a tie paid as much as a win (a=1), then 0.62 (a=1.1), 0.43 (a=2), 0.39 (a=4), 0.36 (a=9), 0.36 (a=100), and 0.34 when ties paid nothing (a=∞). At a=∞ the most common response was to switch to the hand that beats the tied hand (0.38). Switching to the hand the tied hand beats was the least common move in every treatment. Consistently, Dyson 2022 (Canada, against a random computer) found draw-stay of about 30–31% when draws scored 0 or +1 (Exp. 1, n=40). In Exp. 2 (n=36), draw-stay was 36% at +1 vs 26% at −1 (draw-shift 63.98% vs 73.73%, Tukey p<.05).
verifier_added.evidence: Wang & Xu 2014, arXiv:1407.1170 p.8, Fig. 7 'Tie Condition. For each of the group of three, the first stick is T−, the second is T0, and the third is T+'. Digitised at 400 dpi as T−/T0/T+ (each triple sums to 0.996–0.998): a=1 0.060/0.800/0.138; 1.1 0.136/0.623/0.237; 2 0.232/0.434/0.331; 4 0.228/0.392/0.377; 9 0.292/0.357/0.349; 100 0.270/0.361/0.367; ∞ 0.283/0.338/0.377. Fig. 1 matrix for a=∞: '0 0 1 / 1 0 0 / 0 1 0'. Dyson 2022 PLoS ONE e0270475 (PMC9255737), Table 1 Draw-Shift: D+1 .690, D0 .695, D−1 .736. Exp. 2: 'draw-shift behaviour was significantly larger when draws were assigned the value of -1 relative to +1 (73.73% and 63.98%, respectively; Tukey's HSD, p < .05)'.
verifier_added.study_design: Wang & Xu: incentivised lab at Zhejiang University; 6-player groups re-matched at random every round; 300 rounds; seven payoff treatments (win=a, tie=1, loss=0; a=∞ means ties pay 0). Dyson 2022: University of Alberta undergraduates (course credit); 3 blocks of 120 trials against a computer that played each item 40 times per block; draw value manipulated.
verifier_added.effect_size: T0 falls 46 pp from a=1 to a=∞ (Spearman rho −0.531, n=504). At a=∞, best responses to the tied hand X are: the hand that beats X +5.5 pp, the hand X beats +3.9 pp, repeat X −9.4 pp. At a=2: +20.2, −9.8 and −10.2 pp.
verifier_added.strategic_implication: The C08 rule ('after a tie, throw the hand that beats the tied hand') rests on lab conditions where a tie earns points and opponents are re-shuffled. In a real elimination match a tie earns nothing and the opponent stays the same, so expect the opponent to switch after a tie. Do not adopt the C08 rule as a default.
verifier_added.caveats: Bar-chart digitisation. Random re-matching means the post-tie opponent is usually a different person. a=∞ makes a tie as bad as a loss, harsher than a neutral replay. The Dyson samples are small and played a computer.

verifier_added.statement: The Rock excess is not universal, even in large human-vs-human datasets. Brockbank & Vul 2020 (USA, 58 stable online dyads, 34,557 throws in complete games; my computation): Rock 31.9% (95% CI 30.7–33.0), Paper 33.6%, Scissors 34.6% (33.6–35.6). Always throwing Paper would have lost 2.7 pp per throw (CI −4.8 to −0.7). Moerel 2025 (Australia, 31 fixed pairs, 29,511 throws, option order randomised per block): Rock 35.3% (34.4–36.4), Paper 32.5%, Scissors 32.1%, so always-Paper gained +3.2 pp (1.4–5.2). Dyson 2022 (Canada, against a computer): Rock 34.8–37.0% across conditions.
verifier_added.evidence: My pair-cluster bootstrap (2,000 resamples) on rps_v1_data.csv (complete games) and the OpenNeuro ds006761 events files. All-games Brockbank marginals: rock 11,457, paper 12,068, scissors 12,444 (31.85/33.55/34.60%). Dyson 2022 Table 1, Rock .370 / .356 / .348; Paper .323 / .327 / .335; Scissors .307 / .316 / .318.
verifier_added.study_design: As in MF01 for Brockbank and Moerel. Dyson 2022: 40 undergraduates against a computer, course credit.
verifier_added.effect_size: Expected value of a Paper default ranges from −2.7 pp (US dyads) to +3.2 pp (Australian pairs); both CIs exclude 0.
verifier_added.strategic_implication: A blanket 'Paper is safe' default is worth at most about 3 pp and can be negative. Moerel's randomised-position data show the Rock excess is not just a screen artefact, but the US dyads show the opposite. Rely on observed opponent tendencies rather than a population prior.
verifier_added.caveats: Online or computerised play. The on-screen card order in Brockbank is not reported. Neither dataset is East Asian.

verifier_added.statement: Opening-throw distributions are unstable across samples, so no opener is reliably favoured. In the first round of the Brockbank & Vul dyads (n=120), openers were Paper 44.2%, Rock 33.3%, Scissors 22.5% (χ² p=0.015). In the first game of the Moerel pairs (n=49 valid), they were Scissors 46.9%, Rock 28.6%, Paper 24.5% (p=0.12). Compare Eyler (n=119): Rock 55.5%. Batzilis (5.0M match openers): Paper 34.8 / Rock 34.0 / Scissors 31.2. Japanese self-report (n=1,000): Scissors 42.0 / Rock 37.4 / Paper 20.6. Japanese children's first throws (Uchida): Scissors > Paper > Rock.
verifier_added.evidence: My counts. Brockbank round_index=1: paper 53, rock 40, scissors 27. Moerel trial_num=1: scissors 23, rock 14, paper 12, with 13 no-responses. χ² against equal thirds, df=2. Other values are from the cited sources (verified above).
verifier_added.study_design: First trial of long computerised human-pair sessions (US online, Australian lab), compared with other designs.
verifier_added.effect_size: Expected value of opening with Paper: −18.3 pp (Moerel), +10.8 (Brockbank), +43.7 (Eyler), +2.8 (Batzilis), −4.6 (Japanese stated).
verifier_added.strategic_implication: Treat the first throw as close to random. Any 'opener rule' is specific to one population. A first-throw edge needs scouting of the actual opponent pool.
verifier_added.caveats: Small n for first trials. The first trial of a computerised session may not reflect a one-shot live opener.

verifier_added.statement: Persistence of cycling replicates in human-vs-human data. After an upgrade (e.g., Rock→Paper), the next move was another upgrade 43.1% of the time in Moerel (n=10,049) and 46.6% in Brockbank (n=12,455). After a downgrade (e.g., Rock→Scissors), another downgrade followed 44.8% and 45.2% of the time. Dyson 2016 reported 43.5% and 42.4%. A third identical throw after two followed 28.5% (Moerel, n=7,970) and 34.0% (Brockbank, n=10,060) of the time, so the repeated hand is not eliminated.
verifier_added.evidence: My computation (fcB_scripts/second_order.py). Moerel: after STAY → STAY 28.5 / UP 33.7 / DOWN 37.8; after UP → STAY 27.1 / UP 43.1 / DOWN 29.9; after DOWN → STAY 27.3 / UP 27.9 / DOWN 44.8. Brockbank: after STAY → 34.0 / 32.4 / 33.6; after UP → 25.9 / 46.6 / 27.5; after DOWN → 26.1 / 28.7 / 45.2.
verifier_added.study_design: As in MF01, with sequences pooled within players.
verifier_added.effect_size: Continued cycling runs +10 to +13 pp above 33.3%. A third identical throw runs −4.8 to +0.7 pp relative to 33.3%.
verifier_added.strategic_implication: After an opponent goes Rock→Paper, expect Scissors and throw Rock. After Rock→Scissors, expect Paper and throw Scissors. After X, X, do not treat X as eliminated (28–34%), contrary to WRPS 'Double Run'.
verifier_added.caveats: Pooled across players, so part of the effect reflects stable individual preferences for one step direction. Computerised play.

verifier_added.statement: Below-chance repetition is the norm against a fixed human opponent, after every outcome, including wins. In Moerel's raw data, overall repeat was 27.5% (50 of 62 players below 1/3): 26.1% after a win, 28.1% after a loss, 28.3% after a tie. In Brockbank's, it was 28.2% (88 of 124 below 1/3): 32.1% after a win, 23.5% after a loss, 29.1% after a tie. A simple rule ('throw the hand the opponent's last throw beats') netted +7.3 pp (Moerel, n=28,978) and +7.9 pp (Brockbank, n=34,557). The opposite rule ('throw the hand that beats their last throw') netted −10.2 and −7.3 pp. By contrast, the Chinese random-rematch lab shows repeating above chance (stay 0.376–0.531 for a ≥ 1.1). There the opposite rule wins: +15.8 pp at a=2, from Wang & Xu Table 2.
verifier_added.evidence: My direct rule evaluation (fcB_scripts/rule_eval2.py) on the two raw datasets. Wang & Xu 2014 Table 2 at a=2: TRSP 0.282, stay 0.440, TRPS 0.279. Forder & Dyson 2016, after win: stay 42.45%, upgrade 29.32%, downgrade 28.23% (win-stay is present in that computer-opponent lab).
verifier_added.study_design: As in MF01. Wang & Xu: 6-player groups with random re-matching. Forder: UK students against a computer.
verifier_added.effect_size: Exploiting repeat-avoidance in fixed human pairs: +7.3 to +7.9 pp per throw. In random-rematch Chinese data the sign reverses (about ±16 pp at a=2).
verifier_added.strategic_implication: In a bout against one opponent, the hand they just threw is their least likely next throw, even after they win. Favour the hand their last throw beats, and verify with the opponent's first few transitions. The Chinese win-stay / tie-stay data come from re-shuffled opponents and should not be the default for a fixed bout.
verifier_added.caveats: Computerised Western samples. The rule's edge would shrink against an opponent who notices it. Results from re-shuffled designs differ sharply, which suggests the opponent structure matters (Brockbank & Vul 2020 make the same point).

verifier_added.statement: Japanese stated after-tie habits show strong repeat-avoidance with a downgrade preference. In the Toint 2023 survey (n=1,000), the cross-tab of stated first throw × stated throw after a tie gives repeat 19.3%, upgrade 36.9% and downgrade 43.8%. The most common sequences were Rock→Scissors (180) and Scissors→Paper (187); Paper→Paper was the rarest (37). Uchida's video-coded rapid-fire play likewise reports that Rock was followed most often by Scissors, Scissors by Paper, and Paper by Rock (the グー・チョキ・パー order), after wins, losses and ties alike.
verifier_added.evidence: Toint (https://media.toint.co.jp/entry/janken). Men: グー→グー 40, グー→チョキ 62, グー→パー 41, チョキ→グー 41, チョキ→チョキ 30, チョキ→パー 38, パー→グー 29, パー→チョキ 31, パー→パー 25. Women: 52, 118, 61, 128, 34, 149, 42, 67, 12. Text: '女性で最も多いパターンは、チョキからのパーで22.47％'. Uchida 2017, p.34: '１回目にグーを出した後はチョキ，チョキを出した後はパー，パーを出した後はグーを出す割合が多かった。勝った後，負けた後、あいこの後のどの場合も全体を通してグー，チョキ，パーの順に出されていることが多かった。'
verifier_added.study_design: Toint: commercial online self-report survey, Japan, July 2023, 337 men and 663 women. Uchida: student project, 76 people, 4,600 rapid-fire throws coded from video.
verifier_added.effect_size: Against the stated after-tie distribution: throwing the hand the tied hand beats +17.6 pp, repeating the tied hand +6.9 pp, throwing the hand that beats it −24.5 pp.
verifier_added.strategic_implication: East Asian (Japanese) evidence agrees with the fixed-pair data in MF01: after a tie, expect a switch, often to the hand the tied hand beats. The hand that beats the tied hand is the worst answer.
verifier_added.caveats: Self-report and a school project. No Korean data. Whether the Korean call order (가위-바위-보 = Scissors→Rock→Paper, an 'upgrade' sequence) primes a different cycle direction is untested.

verifier_added.statement: Ties are common in live real-hand play, and the 'automatic imitation' boost to ties did not replicate. Cook 2012 (UK): draws were 36.3% when one player could see the other vs 33.3% when both were blindfolded (above chance, t13=2.49, p<.025 one-tailed). Aczel 2012 (Hungary): 36.54% (one player sighted) vs 37.77% (both blindfolded), t33=−1.02, p=.32. Ties ran at about 36–38% in Hungarian live play, above 1/3, consistent with shared hand biases.
verifier_added.evidence: Cook 2012 Table 4: blind–sighted draws 36.3% (s.d. 4.6), blind–blind 33.3% (s.d. 5.0). Aczel 2012: 'no significant difference between the mean proportion of draws, t33 = −1.02, p = 0.32 (two-tailed). In fact, the mean proportion was numerically higher in the blind–blind condition (M = 37.77, s.d. = 6.37) than in the blind–sighted condition (M = 36.54, s.d. = 4.24)'.
verifier_added.study_design: Physical play in triads with blindfold manipulations and small cash incentives. UK: 14 triads; Hungary: 34 triads.
verifier_added.effect_size: Draw rates of +3 to +4.4 pp above 33.3% in live play. The imitation effect is not reliable.
verifier_added.strategic_implication: Expect roughly one throw in three, or slightly more, to tie, so the after-tie rule (MF01) will be used often. Do not count on opponents copying a visibly early hand.
verifier_added.caveats: Small numbers of independent triads; blindfolds and spoken announcements make play unnatural; European samples.

dead_ends: Lead 1 (Eyler et al. 2009): the 'Rock 35.4%, Paper 35.0%, Scissors 29.6%' figures do not come from this paper. Secondary sources (Peterson 2009 blog; Lock5 Exercise 2.15; Zhang et al. 2021) give first throws of Rock 55.5% / Paper 32.8% / Scissors 11.8% (n=119) and a repeat PREFERENCE (P(Paper→Paper)=0.421), not repeat avoidance. The primary text was inaccessible (Taylor & Francis and Ingenta returned 403). OpenAlex and Crossref do not index it under its own title; Crossref lists only a 'Classroom Capsules' record, DOI 10.4169/193113409x469578, pp.125-130.

The 35.4/35.0/29.6 triplet: the archived WRPS pages contain only 'scissors ... 29.6% ... in competition play', with no sample size or method. '35.4' is not on the 2009 'How to beat anyone' page or the 2010 'Definitive Guide'. The triplet appears in popular articles (e.g., Linux Journal 2017, Korean news) attributed to WRPS or WRPSA without a primary source.

Lead 2 (Batzilis 2019): there are no demographics ('there is no demographic information'), no gender, age or experience-by-demographic analysis, no after-tie statistics and no within-match repeat rates. Only first-throw-of-match frequencies and summaries of opponents' histories are reported. Experience effects concern responses to opponent history, not base rates.

Lead 3 (Dyson 2016): the Rock over-selection (35.60%) was NOT significant (F(2,60)=1.64, p=0.203). After-draw percentages are not in the text, only in Fig. 1c, so I computed them from the supplementary spreadsheet.

Lead 4 (Wang 2014): conditional (after-tie) probabilities appear only in figures, with no table. No gender analysis despite 217 F / 143 M. Chinese media coverage (chinanews.com.cn 2014-05-04; Zhejiang University news) adds no new data.

Lead 5 (Yoshizawa): the numbers are confirmed (4,054 / 3,664 / 3,849 of 11,567; 2,465 of 10,833 repeats) via his own Toyo Keizai article and the NDL reference record of his 2006 book (日本評論社). The data were collected in the late 1990s at 'the university where I worked then', not stated as Obirin; WRPS calls it a '1998 Japanese study'. His article says 'のべ725人', not '725 students'. The 22.8% covers all consecutive pairs, not ties specifically; President Online 2024 misreports it as the after-tie repeat rate. I did not read the original 2006 book or the Nikkei 2007/2009 pieces.

CiNii / J-STAGE: Ogawa (2013) is a bulletin paper with no hand frequencies. Hase & Aoyama (2019, 日本科学教育学会研究会研究報告) compares janken win counts with YG personality types (no significant differences) and has no hand frequencies. Miyagawa (2011, Kobe) is theory only. No peer-reviewed Japanese behavioural dataset with first-throw or after-tie frequencies was found.
Sazae-san: only the news summary of the fan group's data was read. The doujinshi PDF and the group's site (park11.wakwak.com/~hkn/) were not read.

Korea: no Korean behavioural dataset on 가위바위보 hand frequencies, first throws or after-tie behaviour was found, despite Korean-language web, news and KCI/RISS/DBpia/ScienceON searches via web search. Korean academic hits (Cho 2010; Cho 2019, Korean Journal of Applied Statistics) are mathematical models that assume random 1/3 play for team elimination. Baek et al. 2013 (KAIST/Keimyung; 50 healthy Korean adults) exists but its full text is paywalled or login-only, and the abstract has no frequencies. Korean TV-show claims (SBS 호기심천국: shouting '보!' primes Paper) and 'people throw Paper first' appear only as unsourced Namu Wiki statements. Korean news in 2025 recycles Yoshizawa, Zhejiang, WRPSA and the Western Sydney study.

WRPS / USA RPS League claims ('rock is for rookies', male Rock openers, gambits): no supporting dataset found anywhere. WRPS's own Roshambull figures (36/30/34) conflict with the peer-reviewed analysis of that app.

Gender: blog claims citing studies in the 'Journal of Social Psychology' and 'Evolution and Human Behavior' (men Rock, women Scissors or Paper) could not be located and appear unsupported. The only gender data found are self-reports (Japanese online survey, 2023).

Large public human datasets with first-throw or after-tie statistics: none beyond Batzilis. The Kaggle 'Rock, Paper, Scissors' competition is bot-vs-bot. The datagenetics 2013 post is simulation only. Hoffman et al. 2015 (Sci Rep 5:8817) reports no marginal hand frequencies in its text. Kim, Ohara & Kurokawa (arXiv 2605.18616; 9 Japanese participants) analyses randomness complexity, not base rates.
Three-in-a-row rates: no dataset reports P(three identical throws) directly. Only Dyson's second-order transitions (my derivation) and anecdotal claims (WRPS, Sazae-san) exist.
open_questions: Does Korean live 가위바위보 show the Rock-high / Scissors-low marginals seen in Japanese real-hand data and Chinese lab data, or the null / Scissors-high marginals seen in UK and Hungarian real-hand data? No Korean observational data were found.

Which after-tie regime applies to a live Korean team match against a fixed opponent? The Western-lab and Japanese pattern is to switch, most often to the hand that beats the tied hand (so throw the hand the tied hand beats). The Chinese-lab pattern is to repeat (so throw the hand that beats the tied hand). This is the single biggest strategic uncertainty.

First throw under one-shot, high-pressure team conditions is unresolved: Eyler's novices opened Rock 55.5%, Facebook players Paper 34.8%, experienced Facebook players opened Rock least (32.6%), and Japanese self-reports favour Scissors (42%). Does social pressure or being watched by teammates shift openers?
Does the Korean call ending on '보' (or the '안 내면 진다' preamble) prime Paper on the throw? This is claimed by a TV show via Namu Wiki and untested.
Are there real gender or age differences in observed (not stated) choices? Only WRPS anecdotes and a Japanese self-report survey exist.

How much of the lab Rock excess is a screen-position artefact? Wang 2014's authors suspect the left-most button, but Moerel 2025, with randomised positions, still found a Rock-dominant majority. Does pumping fists before throwing in real-hand play push choices toward or away from Rock?

Repeat avoidance versus repetition: why do Chinese lab subjects (stay 0.37–0.44) and Eyler's US subjects repeat above 1/3 while Japanese field players (22.75%) and Canadian lab subjects (~29.6%) avoid repeats? Candidate explanations are re-matching vs a fixed opponent, incentives, session length, and computer vs human opponents.

condensed.angle: C. Foundations: equilibrium, human randomness failures, level-k, exploitation vs exploitability, algorithm contests, practical randomization

verified.statement: Uniform play (1/3 Rock, 1/3 Paper, 1/3 Scissors, independent of anything the opponent can observe) is the unique Nash/minimax strategy of RPS. It guarantees an expected net of 0 per throw against any opponent, and it also earns exactly 0 against any opponent, however predictable (Shoham & Leyton-Brown 2009, Sec. 3.4.1 and Thm 3.4.4; Batzilis et al. 2019, Prop. 1). In Billings's 1999 RoShamBo competition (45 programs plus 10 dummy bots, 1,000-turn matches), the random entry drew every match and finished 27th overall. It was entered as 'Meta-Meta-Random', i.e. Random (Optimal), and placed 32nd on Open points and 19th in Best-of-the-Best. In Lanctot et al.'s re-evaluation of 43 released bots (TMLR 2023), randbot averaged +0.234 per 1,000 throws and had the lowest within-population exploitability (1.197 per 1,000).
verified.evidence:
- **S08** (http://www.masfoundations.org/mas.pdf), Sec. 3.4.1: 'if i plays a maxmin strategy and the other agents play arbitrarily, i will still receive an expected payoff of at least his maxmin value'.
- **S08**, Thm 3.4.4 (p.75): 'In any finite, two-player, zero-sum game, in any Nash equilibrium each player receives a payoff that is equal to both his maxmin value and his minmax value.'
- **S02**, announcement (Wayback 20210420184025): 'The optimal mixed strategy is to choose an action uniformly at random (one-third probability of each). This will ensure a break-even result in the long run, regardless of how strong (or how weak!) the opponent is.'
- **S03**, standings row: '27 Meta-Meta-Random 32 19 1 UK Mark Bassett'.
- **S04**: 'In this competition, Random (Optimal) was called Meta-Meta-Random ... It finished in the middle of the pack (27th), drawing every match, as expected.'
- **S06**, Table 6: 'randbot 0.234 1.197'. Sec. 2.3: 'within-population exploitabilities range from 1.2 (randbot) to 1000'.
- **S01**, fn 2 and Prop. 1: verbatim as quoted by the sweep (Games PDF p.2, p.7).
verified.reliability:
- The minimax theorem is a textbook proof and is definitive.
- The organizer's archived 1999 reports are primary but not peer reviewed.
- Lanctot et al. was accepted at TMLR (peer reviewed).
- All the tournament evidence concerns programs, not humans.
verified.design:
- **Theory:** the minimax theorem, from a textbook and a review.
- **1999 tournament (S03):** 45 programs by 39 authors from 10 countries, plus 10 dummy bots; 1,000-turn matches; 25 independent Open tournaments.
- **2023 re-evaluation (S06):** 43 released bots; each pairing averaged over 1,000 episodes of 1,000 throws.
- No human subjects.
verified.effect:
- Expected net is 0 per throw against any opponent (win, draw and loss each 1/3 by construction).
- The random bot scored +0.00023 per throw (≈0) against the population, and its exploitability was 0.0012 per throw (≈0).
- It finished 27th of 55 in 1999.
verified.implication:
Random play is the safe floor and the only option that cannot be exploited. Use it against strong or unknown opponents, and whenever you suspect you are being read.

It cannot create an edge: it wins about 50% of matches. Any plan that aims to win must therefore deviate from it and accept some exploitability.
verified.caveats:
- The guarantee holds in expectation only; best-of-3 or best-of-5 matches are high-variance.
- It requires true independence from history (e.g., an external random device), which unaided humans do not reliably produce (C08–C13).
- The tournament evidence comes from programs, not people.

verified.statement:
**Bot evidence** (Lanctot et al., TMLR 2023; 43 released RoShamBo bots; 1,000-throw episodes; return and within-population exploitability per 1,000 throws):

| Bot | Return | Exploitability |
|---|---|---|
| greenberg (2000 winner) | +288 | 3.6 |
| Iocaine Powder (1999 winner; won all 25 Open tournaments) | +255 | 5.0 |
| phasenbott | +232 | 112 |
| halbot | +212 | 176 |
| russrocker4 | +172 | 530 |

The top programs combined exploitation with near-unexploitability.

**Poker result that does not transfer.** Johanson et al. (NIPS 2007) found best responses brittle and restricted-Nash-response frontiers 'highly concave'. That was in limit Texas Hold'em, and it does not carry over to simple frequency exploitation in RPS.

**RPS arithmetic.** Against a 36/32/32 Rock-leaning opponent:
- The sweep's leans (pure Paper, 50/25/25, 40/30/30) gain +4.0, +1.0 and +0.4 pp, with worst cases of −100, −25 and −10 pp. That is a constant 0.04 ratio, i.e. a linear trade-off, not a concave one.
- The efficient lean keeps Rock at 1/3 and moves weight from Scissors to Paper. This gives 0.08 pp of gain per pp of exploitability, up to Rock 33% / Paper 67% / Scissors 0% (+2.67 pp at a −33 pp worst case).
- Example: Rock 33% / Paper 58% / Scissors 8% gives +2.0 pp at −25 pp.

Safe-exploitation evidence specific to RPS comes from McCracken & Bowling (2004).
verified.evidence:
- **S06** Table 6 (arXiv 2303.03196v2, p.21): 'greenberg 288.153 3.648 ... iocainebot 255.003 5.006 ... phasenbott 232.245 111.708 ... halbot 212.429 176.229 ... russrocker4 172.334 529.751'.
- **S03**: 'Of the 25 independent tournaments run for the Open Competition, Iocaine Powder won ALL of them.'
- **S07** Sec. 5 (proceedings.neurips.cc 2007 Paper.pdf): 'the curves are highly concave meaning that dramatic reductions in exploitability can be achieved with only a small sacrifice in the ability to exploit the model'. Fig. 1 plots restricted Nash responses against the poker bots PsOpti4 and A80.
- **My calculation:** Billings's formula EV[x]=Pr[x+2]−Pr[x+1] (S04), with a grid search over mixes. Results:
  - 25/50/25 (R/P/S): EV +1.00 pp, exploitability 25.
  - 33.3/58.3/8.3: EV +2.00 pp, exploitability 25.
  - 33.3/66.7/0: EV +2.67 pp, exploitability 33.3.
  - Pure Paper: EV +4.00 pp, exploitability 100.
verified.reliability:
- Lanctot et al. is peer-reviewed (TMLR 2023), but covers bots only.
- Johanson et al. is a peer-reviewed NIPS paper, but about poker.
- The RPS frontier is exact arithmetic for a known opponent mix.
verified.design:
- Computer programs only.
- **S06:** 43 hand-written bots from the 1999 and 2000 RoShamBo competitions; every pairing played over 1,000 episodes of 1,000 throws. Exploitability is the best score any bot in the population achieves against the bot.
- **S03:** the 1999 competition.
- **S07:** limit Texas Hold'em programs, not RPS.
verified.effect:
Per throw, compared with the uniform-random benchmark of 0:

- greenberg: +0.288, exploitable by 0.0036.
- Iocaine Powder: +0.255, exploitable by 0.005.
- RussRocker4: +0.172, but exploitable by 0.530.
- halbot: +0.212, exploitable by 0.176.
- phasenbott: +0.232, exploitable by 0.112.
verified.implication:
Treat exploitation as a dial, not a switch: lean toward the counter of a suspected bias only partly, and keep randomness in your play.

My own worked example (my arithmetic) against a 36/32/32 Rock-leaning opponent:

| Your mix | Gain vs that opponent | Worst case if they counter you |
|---|---|---|
| Pure Paper | +4.0 pp/throw | −100 pp/throw (they always throw Scissors) |
| 50/25/25 lean to Paper | +1.0 pp | −25 pp |
| 40/30/30 lean to Paper | +0.4 pp | −10 pp |
verified.caveats:
- The evidence comes from bots and poker programs, not humans.
- Exploitability measured within the bot population understates the true worst case (S06: on average it reached 75.2% of the exploitability that trained RL agents could achieve).
- Human opponents rarely compute best responses (C16), so the real risk of being punished is below the worst case.

verified.statement:
**Iocaine Powder** (Egnor, 1999 winner) expands any predictor P into several strategies:
- **P.0** beats the prediction (P says Rock → throw Paper).
- **P.1** beats the opponent's counter to P.0 (→ Rock).
- **P.2** goes one level higher (→ Scissors).
- **P.3** equals P.0, so for a single anchor the reasoning ladder cycles with period 3.

Iocaine adds mirror variants P'.0–P'.2 (assuming the opponent applies P to you) and a random predictor. It plays whichever variant has the best running score, with a meta-meta layer choosing the scoring horizon (1 to 1,000 moves). It won all 25 Open tournaments and all six sets of 25 Best-of-the-Best tournaments.

**Batzilis et al.'s levels have a 6-level cycle, not the same 3-level one.** Their odd levels are anchored on the opponent's displayed history and their even levels on one's own history. So k(j+6)=k(j), and the authors explicitly say k(j) is not equivalent to k(j+3).
verified.evidence:
- **S05** (Wayback 20060107080414): 'P.0: naive application ... P.1: defeat second-guessing ... P.2: defeat triple-guessing ... P.3 recommends you play paper -- just like P.0!'
- **S05**: 'P'.0: second-guess the opponent ... assumes the opponent uses P themselves against you'.
- **S05**: 'picks the strategy variant with the highest score to date'.
- **S05**: 'Strategies are compared over the last 1000, 100, 10, 5, 2, and 1 moves, and a meta-meta-strategy decides which meta-strategy to use'.
- **S01** fn 26 (p.14): 'in the case of RPS the level k_{j+6} strategy is identical to the level k_j strategy for j ≥ 1 ... One might expect k_j to be equivalent to k_{j+3}, but k1, k3 and k5 strategies depend on the opponent's history ... while levels k2, k4 and k6 strategies depend on one's own history.'
- **S03**: 'In the six sets of 25 tournaments conducted for the "Best of the Best" competition, Iocaine Powder finished first every time.'
verified.reliability:
- The winner's own description of his algorithm, plus the organizer's report.
- Batzilis et al. is a peer-reviewed journal article.
- This is algorithm design, not evidence about how humans reason.
verified.design: A design description of the winning program (1,000-throw matches), plus a theoretical note in a field study. Not a human experiment.
verified.effect: Qualitative. Iocaine Powder won all 25 Open tournaments and finished first in all six sets of 25 'Best of the Best' tournaments (S03).
verified.implication:
No depth of reasoning is safe: each depth is beaten by the next one up. Choosing a depth amounts to choosing a hand relative to a focal guess, and mixing evenly over depths amounts to random play.

The practical question is how deep this particular opponent goes (usually level 0–1; see C04–C05). Play one step deeper, and change approach based on running results, as Iocaine does.
verified.caveats: This describes an algorithm, not human cognition. A person cannot keep running scores for six or more strategies without help; a teammate with a notepad could.

verified.statement:
**Data:** Roshambull (Facebook app): 2,636,417 best-of-3 matches, 23 May – 14 Aug 2007, no money, opponents' histories displayed. The level-k estimates cover 6,639 players with ≥100 clean matches and well-defined strategies, a subset of the 7,758 'experienced' players.

**Level-k shares (first throws, average across players):**
- k0 (play unaffected by any history) 73.8% of throws.
- k1 (best response to the opponent's displayed first-throw history) 18.5%.
- k2 7.7%.
- 93% of players use k0 at some point, 63% use k1, and only about 12% show significant k2.

**Model comparison:** a naive level-k model, where k1 means beating the opponent's most frequent past throw, was the likeliest of three models:
- for 48.6% of 5,405 players (the text says 50%), and for 85% of the 1,349 players with a decisive model;
- within that model, k0 still accounts for 72.2% of throws and naive k1 for 21.1%.

**Depth and payoff:** average depth is 0.339 levels, against about 1.5 in Camerer et al. Always playing k2 would have won 42.68% and lost 27.74% of throws (+14.9 pp), but it requires tracking your own history, which the app did not show.
verified.evidence:
- **S01** Table 7 (p.16): k0 0.738, k1 0.185, k2 0.077; 'N = 6639 ... players with 100 clean matches with well-defined k1 and k2 strategies'.
- **S01** Table 8: k0 93.11%, k1 62.87%, k2 11.54% (N = 6389).
- **S01** Table 10: naive model k0 0.722, k1 0.211, k2 0.067.
- **S01** Table 11: naive model likeliest for 2,629 of 5,405 players (48.6%); 1,148 (85.1%) among players with >95% probability.
- **S01** p.13: 'If a player always played k2 he would win 42.68% (and lose 27.74%) of the time.'
- **S01** pp.18–19: '0.339 levels'.
- **S01** p.19: 'This is likely a result of the Facebook application not showing players their histories'.
verified.reliability:
- Peer-reviewed (Games 2019), very large N and within-player estimation.
- Self-selected online users, no stakes, with an information display unlike live play.
verified.design:
- Online field data from the Facebook app Roshambull, 23 May – 14 Aug 2007.
- Best-of-3 matches between humans, played for prestige points ('creds'); no money.
- A scouting sheet showed each opponent's history; players did not see their own.
- Structural maximum-likelihood estimation for each player with at least 100 clean matches (N = 6,639 for Table 7).
- No demographic data; population unknown.
verified.effect:
- Compared with the 1/3 baseline for any one hand: level-1 throws are about 12 pp more likely to be the level-1-consistent hand (S01, p.13: 'a throw being k1-consistent means it is 12 percentage points more likely to be played').
- Always playing level-2 would give a net of +14.9 pp per throw (42.68 − 27.74).
verified.implication:
Most opponents, even experienced ones, mostly throw without modelling you. When they do model you, it is one step and naive ('beat their favourite').

Against this population, level-2 play is profitable: throw the hand that beats the hand that beats the opponent's estimate of your favourite. Going deeper is rarely needed.
verified.caveats:
- The setting differed from live play: opponent histories were displayed, own history was not, there was no money, and it was the 2007 Facebook population.
- Levels are defined relative to displayed history, not salience.
- Level-0 play may include genuine Nash randomizers.
- The estimates come from self-selected heavy users.
- Live face-to-face first throws (C06) may differ.

verified.statement:
**Strategic depth in lab games (none of them RPS) is shallow:**
- **Nagel (1995):** in the p=1/2 and p=2/3 sessions, almost 50% of first-period choices are near reasoning step 1 or 2; in all sessions only 6–10% are at step 3 or higher.
- **Camerer–Ho–Chong (2004):** a Poisson mean of about 1.5 steps fits many games. Across 60 game-level estimates the median is 1.55 (IQR 0.98–2.21). τ=1.5 implies about 22/34/25/13/7% at L0/L1/L2/L3/L4+. In mixed-strategy games, CH improves 'only a little' on equilibrium.
- **Crawford et al. (2013):** most weight on L1, L2 and perhaps L3. Of 88 guessing-game subjects, 43 complied exactly with one type: 20 L1, 12 L2, 3 L3, 8 Equilibrium.
- **Rubinstein–Tversky hide-and-seek:** central A was chosen by 37% of hiders and 46% of seekers, against 25% under uniform play.
- **Time pressure:** shifted play toward nonstrategic rules, especially Level-1 (Spiliopoulos et al. 2018, 29 games). In the 11–20 game it moved play closer to equilibrium (Lindner & Sutter 2013).
verified.evidence:
- **S10** p.1318 (AER 85(5)): 'In the 1/2 and 2/3 sessions, almost 50 percent of the choices are in the neighborhood interval of either iteration step 1 or 2 ... In all sessions only 6-10 percent are at step 3 and higher steps'.
- **S11** p.877: 'The interquartile range across the 60 estimates is (.98,2.21) and the median is 1.55.'
- **S11** p.881: 'Poisson-CH improves only a little on equilibrium.'
- **S12** WP (11 Apr 2012): 'most weight on L1, L2, and perhaps L3'; 'levels higher than L3 are rare'; '43 complied exactly ... (20 L1, 12 L2, 3 L3, and 8 Equilibrium)'; 'Central A ... most prevalent for hiders (37% in the aggregate) and Central A even more prevalent for seekers (46%)'.
- **S28** abstract (PubMed 30198724): 'an increase in nonstrategic decision rules (particularly Level 1)'.
- **S29** abstract (Econ Lett 120(3):542–545): 'under time pressure, behavior is, perhaps coincidentally, closer to that in equilibrium play.'
- **My recomputation** of the Poisson shares for τ=1.5: 22.3/33.5/25.1/12.6/6.6%.
verified.reliability:
- All peer-reviewed lab studies or reviews; none involves RPS.
- The Crawford et al. text is the 2012 working paper; the published version is JEL 51(1):5–62.
verified.design:
- **S10:** lab study; 3 sessions at p=1/2, 4 at p=2/3 and 3 at p=4/3; 15–18 German students per session; 4 rounds; the winner each round received 20 DM.
- **S11:** model fits to 24 beauty-contest datasets plus 60 matrix, entry and mixed games.
- **S12:** review of lab studies; the hide-and-seek data are Rubinstein–Tversky's, from six experiments.
- **S28:** 29 normal-form games, with and without time limits.
- **S29:** the 11–20 game.
- None of these is RPS.
verified.effect:
- **Nagel:** about 50% of choices at step 1 or 2; 6–10% at step 3 or higher.
- **CHC:** τ median 1.55. The implied shares (my calculation for τ = 1.5) are 22.3%, 33.5%, 25.1% and 12.6% for L0–L3, and 6.6% for L4+.
- **Hide-and-seek:** central A at +12 pp (hiders) and +21 pp (seekers) over a uniform 25%.
verified.implication:
Expect opponents at levels 0–2, most often level 1. Under tight tournament timing, expect even shallower reasoning, which makes 'one step above naive' (level-2) choices attractive.

In mixed-strategy games these models add only a little beyond random play, so keep any bet on reading levels modest.
verified.caveats:
- None of these games is RPS, and τ has not been estimated for RPS.
- The derived Poisson shares are model outputs.
- The time-pressure evidence is mixed.
- The hide-and-seek figures come via the review, not the original paper.

verified.statement:
**Roshambull first throws** (Batzilis et al. 2019, Table 1), with EV = P(hand you beat) − P(hand that beats you):
