- Full sample (N=5,012,128): Rock 33.99%, Paper 34.82%, Scissors 31.20%. EVs: Paper +2.79 pp, Scissors +0.83 pp, Rock −3.62 pp.
- Experienced players (N=1,472,319): Rock 32.60%, Paper 34.56%, Scissors 32.84%. EVs: Scissors +1.96 pp, Paper −0.24 pp, Rock −1.72 pp.

**Lab RPS, all rounds:**
- Wang–Xu–Zhou 2014: R .36 / P .33 / S .32 (354 players, human vs human).
- Dyson et al. 2016: 35.60 / 32.24 / 32.16%, not significant.
- Wang et al. 2020: 35.5 / 32.1 / 32.4% of 300 throws, against an exploiting AI.
- In these samples Paper is worth +3.2 to +4.0 pp.

**Match odds** if the edge held on every throw: best-of-3 win chances of 53.2% (Paper vs the full first-throw mix), 52.2% (Scissors vs the experienced mix) and 54.4% (Paper vs a 36/32/32 mix).
verified.evidence:
- **S01** Table 1 (p.6): 'Throw Rock (%) 33.99 ... 32.60; Throw Paper (%) 34.82 ... 34.56; Throw Scissors (%) 31.20 ... 32.84; Total observations 5,012,128 1,472,319'.
- **S32** Results (nature.com/articles/srep05830): 'Averaged among the 354 players of these 59 populations ... 0.36 ± 0.08, 0.33 ± 0.07 and 0.32 ± 0.06'.
- **S31** Results (PMC4740902): 'Rock (80.10 trials; 35.60%) ... Paper (72.55 trials; 32.24%) or Scissors (72.35 trials; 32.16%)'.
- **S33** Table 4: 'R P S MEAN (times) 106.6098 96.29268 97.09756'.
- **My recomputation** of best-of-3 (first to 2 decisive wins): 0.5321, 0.5219, 0.5441.
verified.reliability:
- The sources are peer reviewed.
- The effects are tiny compared with between-player SDs (±0.06–0.08 in Wang–Xu–Zhou).
- The populations differ, and only S01 isolates first throws (in a history-display setting).
verified.design:
- **S01:** online human-vs-human play, no money, as described in C04.
- **S32:** 360 paid Zhejiang University students; 300 rounds; random pairing within groups of 6.
- **S31:** about 31 students; 225 rounds against a uniform-random computer; course credit.
- **S33:** 52 paid Zhejiang University students; 300 rounds against an AI.
verified.effect:
Deviation from the 1/3 baseline:

- Roshambull first throws: Rock +0.66 pp, Paper +1.49 pp, Scissors −2.13 pp.
- Experienced players: Rock −0.73 pp, Paper +1.23 pp, Scissors −0.49 pp.
- Lab Rock share: +2.2 to +2.7 pp.

If the same per-throw edge held on every throw (my calculation), the chance of winning a best-of-3 match would be:

- Paper against the Roshambull first-throw mix: 53.2%.
- Scissors against the experienced mix: 52.2%.
- Paper against a 36/32/32 lab mix: 54.4%.
verified.implication:
**Opening throw:**

- Against unknown or naive players, Paper. This is the level-1 answer to a Rock-leaning level-0.
- Against players who know Rock is common and will open with Paper, Scissors (level 2).

The edges are at most about 5 pp per throw, so do not over-commit. Randomize between these when you cannot tell the opponent's type.
verified.caveats:
- The effects are small, and the Rock bias in Dyson et al. is not significant.
- The populations differ: Chinese students, Canadian/UK students, and Facebook users in 2007.
- These are mostly all-throw rates. Only S01 isolates first throws, and S01 showed opponent histories.
- Korean 가위바위보 habits are unknown.
- This advice flips once opponents know it (the level-k cycle in C03).

verified.statement:
This is an anecdote (n=1), per the original NYT report (Vogel, 29 Apr 2005).
- **Setup:** Maspro Denkoh's president asked Christie's and Sotheby's to settle by RPS which house would sell the company's collection. The collection was worth more than $20M, and its Cézanne was expected to fetch more than $12M. Each side wrote one word (rock, paper or scissors) on a form; hands were not used.
- **Christie's** followed an employee's 11-year-old twins and wrote Scissors. Their stated reasons were 'Everybody knows you always start with scissors ... Rock is way too obvious, and scissors beats paper', plus 'Everybody expects you to choose rock' as the reason to stay on scissors after a tie.
- **Sotheby's** wrote Paper and said 'this is a game of chance, so we didn't really give it that much thought. We had no strategy in mind.'
- **Result:** Christie's won.

The twins reasoned one step beyond an 'obvious Rock' focal point. However, Sotheby's Paper was by its own account not a reasoned anti-Rock (level-1) choice, so this is not level-2 beating level-1, and it says nothing about frequencies.
verified.evidence:
- **NYT original** (Wayback 20251023020503 of nytimes.com/2005/04/29/arts/design/rock-paper-payoff-childs-play-wins-auction-house-an-art-sale.html):
  - 'art collection, which is worth more than $20 million'.
  - 'They were then asked to write one word in Japanese -- rock, paper or scissors -- on the paper.'
  - '"Everybody knows you always start with scissors," she added. "Rock is way too obvious, and scissors beats paper."'
  - 'if the other side were also to choose scissors and another round was required, the correct play would be to stick to scissors -- because, as Alice explained, "Everybody expects you to choose rock."'
  - Sotheby's: '"But this is a game of chance, so we didn't really give it that much thought. We had no strategy in mind."'
  - 'Cézanne's "Large Trees Under the Jas de Bouffan" ... will sell for more than $12 million.'
- **S01** fn 8 and **S38** match parts of this account.
verified.reliability:
- Primary newspaper report.
- One event; no inferential value.
verified.design: A single throw (n=1), reported in a newspaper and repeated in a peer-reviewed footnote and in popular media. I could not access the original NYT article.
verified.effect: Not applicable (one event).
verified.implication: This is only an illustration of the idea in C06: against an opponent who reasons 'avoid the obvious Rock, so throw Paper', Scissors wins. It is not evidence about frequencies.
verified.caveats:
- The quotes differ between secondary sources.
- The value at stake differs too: $12M Cézanne in S01, $16M in S38, and a collection worth more than $20M in a search snippet.
- One event cannot establish a strategy.

verified.statement:
Unaided 'random' human sequences are reliably non-random, but the direction of the bias depends on the task:
- **Wagenaar (1972):** in a review of 15 experiments, almost all found systematic deviations, and most found negative recency (too many alternations).
- **Towse (1998):** a strong tendency to suppress immediate repetitions, decaying over intervening responses.
- **Billings's 'Flat' bot:** built on the 'common weakness' of too-even frequencies; theoretical exploitability 420 per 1,000.
- **Too few alternations in binary key-pressing:** Neuringer (1986) baseline; Guseva et al. (2023) mean run lengths 3.04–3.81 under random, free and perceptual-guessing instructions, against 2.00 for a pseudorandom generator.
- **Nickerson (2002):** the view that people cannot be random 'lack[s] the strong experimental support' claimed.
- **Komai et al. (2022):** RPS series from 500 people (50 games each vs a GA/GP algorithm) differed clearly from Mersenne Twister series in complexity and determinism.
verified.evidence:
- **S18** pp.70–71: 'First, almost all experimenters found systematic deviations from randomness ... Second, most experimenters yielded negative recency, which means too many alternations or too many runs.'
- **S18** p.66: 'The 15 experiments discussed in the present review'.
- **S21** abstract (PMID 9532724): 'a strong tendency on the part of participants to suppress response repetitions, an effect which decays over intervening responses.'
- **S04** Flat: 'more uniform than expected ... a common weakness in human generated sequences ... theoretical exploitability: 420 out of 1000'.
- **S22** p.65: 'ALTS ... started at lower than random, indicating too few alternations'.
- **S23** Sec. 7.2: 'pseudorandom sequences (M = 2.00 ...) ... (M = 3.04 ...; M = 3.39 ...; M = 3.81 ...)'.
- **S19** abstract (PMID 11990321).
- **S39** Sec. 4: 'each set ... exhibited clearly different statistical distribution'.
verified.reliability:
- Peer-reviewed reviews and experiments.
- Mostly binary tasks with no opponent; Komai is RPS against an algorithm.
verified.design:
- Mostly non-competitive random-generation tasks with no opponent.
- **S18:** review of 15 experiments.
- **S21:** 4 experiments.
- **S22:** 7 plus 4 subjects, 6,000 baseline responses each.
- **S23:** online, n=388, 1,000 binary choices each.
- **S39:** 500 people, 50 RPS games each against an algorithm, Japan.
- **S04:** a bot designed to mimic a human weakness.
verified.effect:
- Run length: humans 3.0–3.8 against 2.00 for a computer generator (binary task).
- Flat bot: exploitable for 0.42 per throw.
- Wagenaar: most of the 15 experiments found over-alternation.
verified.implication: Do not trust a feeling of being random. The common human patterns — avoiding repeats, keeping counts too even, or getting stuck on one hand — can each be exploited. Use an external device instead of intuition.
verified.caveats:
- The direction (too many vs too few switches) depends on the task and response mode.
- Most studies are binary, not three-option, and have no opponent.
- Wagenaar notes the older methods are hard to compare.

verified.statement:
**Tennis servers equalize win rates but switch serve direction too often.**
- Walker & Wooders (2001), 10 Wimbledon-level matches, 40 point games: minimax rejected in 1 of 40; serial independence rejected in 5 of 40 (2 expected; 3 for too many runs); joint KS K=1.948, p=0.001.
- In O'Neill's lab data, 15 of 50 subjects were rejected (13 for too many runs).
- Gauriot, Page & Wooders (2016 working paper; published in Quantitative Economics 2023 under a new title), about 465k Hawk-Eye serves: serial independence rejected for men and women, on first and second serves. Excess switching is stronger for women, and weaker for higher-ranked men. For men's first serves, 7.0% of point games were rejected for too many runs and 2.9% for too few.

**Penalty kicks show no detectable serial dependence.** Palacios-Huerta (2003): 'players' choices are serially independent'. Chiappori et al. (2002), 459 kicks: equal scoring rates not rejected, and the previous kick never predicts the next one. Kicks are days or weeks apart.

**Lab transfer:** professionals did not play minimax in lab games (Levitt, List & Reiley 2010).

**Not established for RPS:** binary-serve over-switching does not show that RPS players repeat less than 1/3. In Wang–Xu–Zhou (2014), RPS players repeated their last hand more often than they shifted in either direction.
verified.evidence:
- **S13** pp.1521–1533: 'even the best tennis players tend to switch from one action to another too often'; 'rejected in five of the 40 experiments ... In three cases ... too many runs'; 'K = 1.948, with a p-value of 0.001'; 'rejected for 15 subjects ... In 13 of the 15 rejections there are too many runs'.
- **S14** WP pp.4, 23 (fn 20): 'too few runs ... for 2.9% ... too many runs ... for 7.0% of the point games' (men, Hawk-Eye first serves).
- **S16** abstract (researchonline.lse.ac.uk/id/eprint/26561): '(ii) players' choices are serially independent.'
- **S15** p.1147: 'the side played on the previous penalty kick ... is never a statistically significant predictor'; fn 20: 'penalty kicks take place days or weeks apart'.
- **S17** NBER abstract.
- **S32**: 'the players are more likely to repeat their last action than to shift action either counter-clockwise ... or clockwise'.
verified.reliability:
- Peer-reviewed field studies with high stakes.
- The tennis serve is a binary choice; the RPS mapping is an inference.
verified.design:
- Field data from professional sport under high stakes: tennis serve direction (binary choice) and penalty-kick direction (three options).
- O'Neill's lab experiment: 25 pairs of students, 105 plays.
- **S17:** lab experiments with soccer, poker and bridge professionals, plus students.
verified.effect:
- **Tennis:** serial-independence rejections at 12.5% of point games against 5% expected. Hawk-Eye first serves: 7.0% of point games rejected for too many runs and 2.9% for too few.
- **O'Neill:** 30% of subjects rejected against 5% expected.
verified.implication:
Over-alternation survives expertise and high stakes. In RPS it shows up as repeating your previous hand less than 1/3 of the time, which an alert opponent can punish (C10).

Skill at randomizing in one setting does not transfer to another, so practise in the actual RPS format.
verified.caveats:
- These are binary choices (serve direction), not RPS.
- The per-point effects are small.
- I read only the abstract of Palacios-Huerta.
- Levitt, List & Reiley contradicts Palacios-Huerta & Volij (2008), whose abstract I read only in paraphrase.

verified.statement:
**The rule.** Suppose the opponent repeats their previous hand with probability r and splits the rest equally. If r < 1/3, throw the hand their previous hand beats (they threw Rock → you throw Scissors): EV = (1−3r)/2. If r > 1/3, throw the hand that beats their previous hand: EV = (3r−1)/2. This follows from Billings's EV[x] = Pr[x+2] − Pr[x+1].

**Values:**

| r | EV per throw |
|---|---|
| 0 | +0.50 |
| 0.12 | +0.32 |
| 0.20 | +0.20 |
| 0.25 | +0.125 |
| 0.30 | +0.05 |

At r=0.12 the counter wins 44%, ties 44% and loses 12% of throws, which is about 79% wins and 21% losses among decisive throws (not 66/34).

**Bot checks:**
- Billings's 'Always Switchin'' (r=0): the simple counter nets +500 per 1,000.
- 'Switch A Lot' (r=0.12): theoretical exploitability 320 per 1,000.
- Lanctot et al.: switchbot −173 return / 497 exploitability; switchalot −83 / 316.

Whether a given human over- or under-repeats must be measured. In the largest human-vs-human RPS lab study, players repeated more often than they shifted.
verified.evidence:
- **S04**: 'the simple counter-strategy would net +500 points per 1000. Even some of the strongest programs did no better than +350.'
- **S04**: 'Switch A Lot had a 12% chance of repeating the previous move' and 'theoretical exploitability: 320 out of 1000'.
- **S04**: 'EV[x] = Pr[x+2] - Pr[x+1]'.
- **S06** Table 6: 'switchalot −82.877 315.612 ... switchbot −173.178 497.182'.
- **My recomputation:** at r=0.12, win (1−r)/2=0.44, loss r=0.12, so the decisive win share is 0.44/0.56=0.786. A 66.7% share corresponds to r=0.20.
- **S32**: humans 'more likely to repeat their last action than to shift'.
verified.reliability:
- Exact arithmetic, checked against bots with known repeat rates.
- Human repeat rates in tournaments are unknown.
verified.design:
- Arithmetic from the payoff matrix, checked against bots with known repeat rates.
- 1,000-throw matches in the 1999 tournament and in the 2023 re-run.
verified.effect:
- Against the 1/3 baseline for repeating: each 0.01 drop in r below 1/3 adds 0.015 per throw to the counter-strategy's EV.
- r = 0.12 corresponds to 0.32 per throw. That is roughly 66% wins vs 34% losses among non-tied throws (my calculation).
verified.implication:
Track how often each opponent repeats their last hand.

- **Below about 25% (typical over-switcher):** throw the hand their last throw beats.
- **Above about 40%:** throw the hand that beats their last throw.
- **Yourself:** a true random device repeats 1/3 of the time. Do not 'correct' it.
verified.caveats:
- Human repeat rates in RPS depend on the setting and the previous outcome (C15), and are not established for tournament play.
- In short matches the estimate is noisy. With 9 transitions the standard error of r is about 0.16; with 20 it is about 0.10 (my calculation).
- The arithmetic assumes the two switch hands are equally likely, which is not true after wins and losses (C15).

verified.statement:
**Wong, Merholz & Maoz (2021).** UCLA undergraduates for course credit. Each part had 200 trials with a 500-ms response deadline. Against a computer that exploited patterns in choice history and in win/lose/tie sequences (Unaware n=51, Aware n=48; a further 42 Control participants faced a cyclic bot):
- In-game Lempel–Ziv complexity was, on average, statistically indistinguishable from Python's PRNG and higher than in pre-game generation.
- The gain did not transfer to post-game generation.
- In-game runs were longer than pre-game runs.
- Telling players explicitly to be random did not help.
- Players still lost: final scores were 75.8 and 78.8 from a start of 100, about −0.12 and −0.11 net per throw. Only 3 of 51 and 4 of 48 beat the computer.
- The paper does not show which patterns the computer exploited. The claim that 'the leaks are outcome-tied patterns, not frequencies' is therefore unsupported.

**Contrast:** Komai et al. (2022; 500 open-day visitors; 50 games against a GA/GP algorithm) found human RPS series clearly less complex than Mersenne Twister series.

**Morra:** expert players were more random than novices only inside Morra games, not in a standard random-number task (Delogu et al. 2020, N=18).

**Matching pennies:** better randomization in competitive play than in plain generation is reported only second-hand (Rapoport & Budescu 1992).
verified.evidence:
- **S24** (nature.com/articles/s41598-021-99967-6), Methods: 'required to press the appropriate key ... within 500 ms'; 'the participant and the computer started with 100 points each ... gained or lost 1 point for every trial they won or lost'; 'win/lose/tie patterns (e.g., win-stay-lose-switch)'.
- **S24** Results: 'Unaware 75.78 ± 17.63, Aware 78.83 ± 16.06, Control 140.10 ± 51.05'; '3 out of 51 (5.88%), 4 out of 48 (8.33%)'; 'in the Game part only ... statistically indistinguishable from those of Python's random-number generator'; 'significantly longer average run lengths during the Game and Post-Game parts in comparison to the Pre-Game'.
- **S39** Sec. 2: 'the randomness of the human RPS time series is lower than that of the pseudorandom series'.
- **S25** Methods (PMC7541701): 'Eighteen participants ... 9 expert players ... 9 beginners'.
verified.reliability:
- Peer-reviewed (Scientific Reports).
- Course-credit students under a speeded response deadline.
- The equivalence is a group-mean permutation test.
verified.design:
- **S24:** US undergraduates for course credit; 3 parts of 200 throws (pre-game random generation / game / post-game random generation); between-subject conditions (Unaware n=51, Aware n=48, Control n=42); human against a pattern-detecting algorithm.
- **S25:** 9 Sardinian Morra experts filmed at a tournament (including 2-vs-2 team games), against 9 US student novices.
- **S17:** lab study with professionals.
verified.effect:
- **Game vs pattern-detector:** about 10–12 pp net loss per throw.
- **Share who beat the computer:** 6–8%, against about 50% expected if they were truly random.
- **Complexity:** in the game, inside the 95% range of the computer generator.
verified.implication:
The pressure of a real game helps, but a typical person still loses about 10–12% of throws net to an algorithm. The leaks are patterns tied to outcomes (what you do after a win, loss or draw), not overall frequencies.

Randomness can become a practised habit, but only within the specific game: practise the actual 가위바위보 format against a pattern-detecting opponent (an app, or a teammate keeping notes).
verified.caveats:
- Students for course credit, not motivated competitors.
- Delogu et al. had N=18.
- I could not read the Rapoport & Budescu abstracts; their results are reported here second-hand.
- Guseva et al. date the paper 1992 but list the authors in the 1994 order.

verified.statement:
**Neuringer (1986), Experiment 1:** 7 Reed College undergraduates; binary key presses; $2.50/h plus a $15 bonus.
- All 7 were significantly non-random at baseline (60 trials × 100 = 6,000 responses each).
- With feedback on 5 statistics, all 7 became statistically indistinguishable from the random generator over their last 60 trials, after 166–483 trials of 100 responses, i.e. less than an average of 6 hours.
- Without feedback, only 2 of 7 stayed random. Failed tests fell from about 4 at baseline to about 1.

**Experiment 2:** 4 high-school students; 10 statistics; about 35 hours of practice. Concatenated output still failed chi-square and autocorrelation tests at lags 4–5.
verified.evidence:
- **S22** (JEP:Gen 115(1):62–75; gwern PDF):
  - '6,000 baseline responses'.
  - 'During the last 60 trials of the feedback condition, all subjects were statistically indistinguishable (p > .05) from the random generator on all five K-S tests'.
  - Trials to criterion: '216, 261, 171, 166, 483, 186, and 385'.
  - 'after less than an average of 6 hours'.
  - 'two of the seven subjects continued to perform randomly ... The average number of tests ... during original baseline was four; the average during this replication was one'.
  - 'all subjects failed the chi-square Lags 4 and 5 and autocorrelation Lags 4 and 5 tests'.
  - '35 hours'.
verified.reliability:
- Peer-reviewed, but with very small N.
- Binary choices with no opponent.
verified.design:
- Lab study of binary key-pressing generation with no opponent.
- Exp 1: Reed College students, paid $2.50/h plus a $15 bonus for meeting the 'random' criterion.
- Exp 2: 4 high-school students in a paid summer programme.
verified.effect:
- All participants moved from significant deviation to non-significant deviation on the tests they were trained on.
- Without feedback, only 29% (2 of 7) retained it.
verified.implication: Learning to be random by feel is possible but impractical before a tournament, and it decays without feedback. An external randomizer is the cheaper route. If you do train, use an app that scores you on repeats, alternations and patterns tied to outcomes.
verified.caveats:
- Very small N; binary choices with no opponent.
- Higher-order patterns persisted.
- Unclear whether this generalizes to three options under time pressure.

verified.statement:
Guseva et al. (2023): preregistered online study, n=388 Prolific participants, 1,000 binary choices each, €7/h with no performance pay.
- **Conditional entropy** (order 3, maximum 1 bit), median: 'as irregular/chaotic as possible' 0.94; 'mental coin toss' 0.92; 'random' 0.84; perceptual guessing 0.83; 'free choice' 0.75.
- **Effect size:** Kruskal–Wallis η²=0.20 (d≈0.99).
- **Run length:** the mental-coin condition came closest to the pseudorandom generator (1.88 vs 2.00).
verified.evidence:
- **S23** (frontiersin.org 10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1113654):
  - Table 3: 'Explicit Randomness (ER) 80 0.84 (0.25) ... Free Choice (FC) 73 0.75 (0.34) ... Irregularity (IR) 80 0.94 (0.10) ... Mental Coin Toss (MC) 85 0.92 (0.11) ... Perceptual Guessing (PG) 70 0.83 (0.15)'.
  - 'conditional entropy rate estimated at k = 3'.
  - 'large effect size =0.20 ... (transformed to Cohen's d = 0.99)'.
  - 'MC with a run length of 1.88'.
  - 'compensated with 7€ per hour'.
verified.reliability:
- Peer-reviewed, preregistered, large N.
- Binary choices, no opponent, no incentives.
verified.design:
- Online (Prolific); between-subject design across 5 instruction conditions.
- 1,000 binary choices (coin sides) per person.
- Paid €7/h with no performance pay.
- No opponent.
verified.effect:
- Conditional entropy: about +0.10 to +0.19 bits over 'random' or 'free' instructions.
- Kruskal–Wallis η² = 0.20 (reported as Cohen's d ≈ 0.99).
verified.implication: If you cannot use a device, frame each throw as 'as irregular as possible so an observer can't find a pattern', or as rolling an imaginary three-sided die. Avoid 'just pick freely', which was the least random condition.
verified.caveats:
- Binary, non-competitive and online.
- Not tested in RPS or in face-to-face play.
- How hard this is to exploit for a pattern-detecting opponent is unknown.

verified.statement:
- **Baddeley et al. (1998):** faster generation increased redundancy for both spoken digits and key presses, via 'a limited number of stereotyped response sets'. Concurrent recall, category fluency and digit-generation tasks reduced randomness.
- **Towse (1998):** spoken generation was strongly affected by response speed, unlike key-pressing.
- **Wagenaar (1972):** speed effects conflict (Teraoka vs Warren & Morin).
- **Duffy et al. (2024):** repeated hide-and-seek against a computer showed serial correlation but no strong link to cognitive load. There was some evidence that high-load subjects earned more.
verified.evidence:
- **S20** abstract (PMID 9854442): 'redundancy increasing with speed of generation for both the verbal generation of digits and the manual pressing of keys ... stereotyped response sets ... concurrent immediate serial recall decreases randomness'.
- **S21** abstract: 'oral random number generation is strongly affected by both response speed and response set size, in contrast to a random key-pressing task'.
- **S18** p.71: 'Teraoka (1963) found a decrease of nonrandomness with an increase of speed, whereas Warren and Morin (1965) found the opposite.'
- **S27** abstract (Crossref): 'we do not find strong evidence these are related to their available cognitive resources'; 'some evidence that subjects in the high load treatment earn more'.
verified.reliability:
- Peer-reviewed; abstracts only for S20, S21 and S27.
- Mostly non-competitive tasks.
verified.design:
- **S20:** 6 lab experiments; verbal and key-press generation with dual tasks.
- **S21:** 4 lab experiments.
- **S27:** lab hide-and-seek game against a computer, comparing high and low cognitive load.
- None involves RPS against a human.
verified.effect: Direction only; the abstracts give no effect sizes.
verified.implication:
Under fast pacing or nerves, unaided choices drift toward habits. Taking randomness out of your head entirely — a pre-generated sequence or a device you glance at — removes the dependence on concentration.

Also expect opponents under time pressure to reason more shallowly (C05).
verified.caveats:
- Mostly non-competitive generation tasks.
- The competitive-game evidence (S27) is null rather than positive.
- I read only abstracts for S20, S21 and S27.

verified.statement:
- **Dyson et al. (2016):** 31 students, 225 throws against a computer playing each hand 25 times per 75-trial block in random order. Participants switched more after losses and draws. After losses, switches were numerically more often 'downgrades' (Rock→Scissors); after draws, significantly more 'upgrades' (Rock→Paper). Each type tended to continue on the next throw. Win-stay was only numerical.
- **Wang–Xu–Zhou (2014):** 360 paid students. After a win, W0 (repeat) is 'considerably higher' than either shift. For win payoff a≥2, a loss is most often followed by a clockwise shift (R→S, S→P, P→R).
- **Zhou (2016):** W0 > T0 > L0.
- **Kikumoto & Mayr (2019):** 5 experiments, matching-pennies variant, N=56/40/44/100/38/25. Choices were model-based after wins and more stochastic after losses.
verified.evidence:
- **S31** (PMC4740902): '31 undergraduate students'; 'the computer played Rock, Paper and Scissors 25 times in a random order'; 'No significant differences ... following a win although numerically ... staying ... a loss more likely prompted item switching than staying (numerically in favour of item downgrading) and following a draw, participants were inclined to switch and specifically upgrade'.
- **S32**: 'her probability (W0) of repeating the same action ... is considerably higher than her probabilities (W− and W+) ... for payoff parameter a ≥ 2, if a player loses ... more likely to shift action clockwise (probability L−)'.
- **S09** Sec. 3.2: 'The empirical data reveal W0 > T0 > L0'.
- **S26** (PMC6812965) abstract and Methods for the Ns.
verified.reliability:
- Peer-reviewed lab studies.
- Effect sizes appear only in figures.
verified.design:
- **S31:** lab, about 31 participants (inferred from df), 225 rounds against a computer, course credit.
- **S32:** lab; 60 groups of 6; 300 rounds; win payoff parameter a ∈ {1.1, 2, 4, 9, 100}; real cash.
- **S26:** University of Oregon students (N = 56, 40, 44, 100, 38, 25 across experiments); simulated and human opponents; paid or course credit.
verified.effect:
- Direction only: the probabilities appear in figures that I could not read.
- Dyson et al.'s 'downgrade after loss' effect is described as numerical in their Results.
verified.implication:
The S31/S32 tendencies imply the following (my mapping):

- **Opponent just lost with hand X:** they will probably switch to the hand X beats (Rock → Scissors). Throw X again (Rock beats Scissors).
- **Opponent just won with X:** they will probably repeat X. Throw the hand that beats X.
- **Yourself:** a loss is when you are most predictable. Hand the next throw to your random device.
verified.caveats:
- Small effects; the evidence comes from labs in Canada/UK and China.
- Kikumoto & Mayr's 'more random after losses' partly contradicts the switch pattern in Dyson et al.; they measure different things.
- This angle only touches outcome-conditioned patterns; other angles cover them in depth.

verified.statement:
**Roshambull** (Batzilis et al. Table 5, first throws):
- Experienced players won 34.66%, drew 32.17% and lost 33.17% (+1.49 pp).
- A best response to the predictable part of play would have won 41.66% and lost 27.37% (+14.29 pp).
- Opponents did not exploit this predictability.

**Multi-Markov AI** (Wang et al. 2020): beat more than 95% of 52 paid Zhejiang students over 300 throws. The Multi-10AI net margins against 11 players were +8 to +73 (mean +35.6, i.e. +0.119 per throw).

**Human pairs** (Brockbank & Vul 2021; 58 dyads × 300 rounds): win differentials exceeded chance. They were predicted by stay/up/down transition biases (β=0.19, p=0.027) and by responses to the opponent's previous move (β=0.45, p=0.015).

**Match odds** if the edge held on every throw: +1.49 pp gives 51.6–51.7% best-of-3 and 52.1% best-of-5; +14.29 pp gives 65.3% and 68.9%.
verified.evidence:
- **S01** Table 5: 'Experienced Sample 34.66 32.17 33.17 1.49 ... Best Response to Predicted Play 41.66 30.97 27.37 14.29'.
- **S01** p.10: 'opponents are less likely to play rock when the actual expected payoff is high'.
- **S33** abstract and Table 5 (Multi-10AI: 10, 41, 8, 34, 73, 43, 48, 43, 59, 24, 9; mean 35.64).
- **S34** Sec. 4.2: 'transition: β̂ = 0.19, p = 0.027; opponent previous choice: β̂ = 0.45, p = 0.015'.
- **My recomputation:** best-of-3 at +1.49 pp = 0.5165; best-of-5 = 0.5206; at +14.29 pp, 0.6530 and 0.6886.
verified.reliability:
- Peer-reviewed.
- The AI result is over 300-throw sessions, much longer than tournament matches.
verified.design:
- **S01:** online human vs human, as in C04.
- **S33:** lab, Zhejiang University, human against AI, money incentive.
- **S34:** reanalysis of 116 participants in stable pairs, 300 rounds each; incentives not checked.
verified.effect:
Net per throw:

- Experienced humans: +0.015.
- Ideal best response: +0.143.
- AI vs human: about +0.12.

If the same per-throw edge held on every throw (my calculation), the chance of winning a match would be:

- At +1.49 pp: 51.7% best-of-3, 52.1% best-of-5.
- At +14.29 pp: 65.3% best-of-3, 68.9% best-of-5.
verified.implication:
In a team event, modelling is a team job. Have one teammate record each opponent's throws, stay/up/down transitions, and reactions to the previous throw, and brief the next player.

Expect gains in the low single digits of percentage points unless an opponent has a strong habit.
verified.caveats:
- The match probabilities assume the same edge on every throw.
- The AI result is against students over 300 throws, far longer than tournament matches.
- S01 covers first throws with visible histories only.

verified.statement:
- **Okano (2013, GEB 77(1):168–180):** two-person teams playing O'Neill's 4×4 game against teams chose frequencies consistent with equilibrium, while individuals played far from it. Teams were less heterogeneous in hide-and-seek. Teams beat individuals at above the equilibrium rate in one treatment but not the other.
- **Kugler, Kausel & Kocher (2012, WIREs Cogn Sci 3(4):471–482):** group decisions are closer to game-theoretic rationality.
- **Towse et al. (2016, PLOS ONE):** when pairs take turns building one random sequence, repetition avoidance persists and 'sequence stereotypy' spreads immediately between partners. Directing effort away from the shared task can help. Abstract-level evidence only.
verified.evidence:
- **S35** RePEc abstract: 'When teams play OʼNeillʼs 4×4 game against another team, the choice frequencies are consistent with equilibrium ... individuals against another individual play far from equilibrium ... teamsʼ behavior is less heterogeneous ... teams win at above the equilibrium rate in one treatment, but not in the other.'
- **S36** Crossref abstract: 'group decisions are closer to the game-theoretic assumption of rationality than individual decisions'.
- **S37** (PMC4792471) abstract: 'repetition avoidance occurs in dyadic as well as individual production settings ... immediate contagion of sequence stereotypy amongst the pairs'.
verified.reliability:
- Peer-reviewed; abstracts only (the Okano working paper was unreachable).
- Not RPS.
verified.design:
- **S35:** lab; 2-person deliberating teams against teams or individuals; O'Neill's 4×4 game and a hide-and-seek game.
- **S36:** narrative review covering about 25 years.
- **S37:** three lab studies in which pairs take turns generating one random sequence.
- None uses RPS.
verified.effect: Not reported in the abstracts.
verified.implication:
For 단체전:

- Decide the team's throwing plan together, and use a team-level random protocol (e.g., a shared die-roll list per member) rather than individual hunches.
- When members play in sequence, do not let one member's habits (such as avoiding repeats) spread to the others.
- Deliberating as a team appears to help in mixing games.
verified.caveats:
- Not RPS.
- The team effect may come from deliberation, which may not be allowed in live play.
- I read only abstracts.

verified.statement:
**Players react to an opponent's displayed first-throw history** (Batzilis et al. 2019):
- Opponents with a 42–100% Rock history drew Paper 46.58%, Rock 30.35% and Scissors 23.06%.
- Opponents with a 0–25% Rock history drew Paper 27.07% and Scissors 37.09%.
- A one-SD (0.176) rise in the opponent's historical Scissors share raised Rock by 4.2 pp for inexperienced players and by 9.4 pp for experienced players after their first 100 games.
- 47% of experienced players responded significantly.

**The 'eight times' figure is not supported by the authors' own tables.** The text says players react about 8× more to 'what I can beat' than to 'what beats me'. The regression coefficients imply:
- 4.4–7.0× for the pooled sample, across hands;
- only about 2.5× for experienced players.
So experienced players do weigh the risk of losing.
verified.reliability: - Peer-reviewed, very large N, but the setting is an on-screen history display with low stakes.
verified.design: Online field data as in C04 (millions of first throws, human vs human, displayed opponent histories, no money).
verified.effect: Paper rises from 27.07% to 46.58% (−6.3 pp to +13.2 pp relative to 1/3) as the opponent's historical Rock share rises.
verified.implication:
If opponents can watch your earlier rounds (spectating teammates or opponents in a team event), expect them to throw the hand that beats your most-shown hand. Counter one level up: if your visible history leans Rock, they will lean Paper, so throw Scissors.

Keep track of what each opponent has seen of you, and scout opponents' visible tendencies in the same way.
verified.caveats:
- In the app, history was shown on screen. Live opponents must remember it, which weakens the effect.
- First throws only.
- Low stakes.

verified.statement:
**Billings's fail-safe.** His Anti-rotn bot plays uniformly at random on any turn while its running score is below −trials/25, i.e. −4% of the match length (−40 in 1,000 turns). This is a per-turn condition, not a permanent switch. Billings judged it 'would have saved many entries thousands of points against stronger opposition', though it 'would not prevent a match loss'. RussRocker4, which lacked a bail-out, could have cut more than 1,000 points of losses and moved up to 3rd.

**Deviating only on significant evidence.** Biopic, Robertot and Boom deviated from random only on statistically significant weaknesses. They drew against very strong opposition, though Iocaine Powder and Phasenbott still beat them narrowly. In Lanctot et al. 2023 they combine low exploitability (36.7, 50.2 and 27.9 per 1,000) with returns of +196, +178 and +169, ranking 3rd, 6th and 4th on return minus exploitability.

**Random fallback.** Iocaine Powder's random 'predictor' makes it 'cut its losses' when it is being read. Egnor: 'any good strategy should have a random fallback'.

**RPS-specific test.** In McCracken & Bowling (2004), capping each bot's risk at the winnings it had already banked (ε-safe/SPS) significantly raised scores for 15 of 24 competition bots and significantly lowered none.
verified.evidence:
- **S04**: 'a simple fail-safe, set at 4% of the total match length ... if ( score < -trials/25 ) { return(random() % 3); } would have saved many entries thousands of points ... would not prevent a match loss'.
- **S03** (RussRocker4): 'Had he employed such a fail-safe, he could have reduced those losses by more than 1000 points, and moved into third place ahead of MegaHAL.'
- **S04**: 'Biopic, Robertot, and Boom, only deviate from random when there appears to be a statistically significant weakness'.
- **S06** Table 6: biopic 196.365/36.665; boom 169.119/27.928; robertot 177.767/50.154.
- **S05**: 'cuts its losses'; 'any good strategy should have a random fallback'.
- **M1** (McCracken & Bowling): 'Of the 24 players, 15 experienced a significant increase in score. Four players had a decreased overall score, but none of these reductions were significant.'
verified.reliability:
- Bot evidence from 1,000-throw matches: organizer reports, TMLR and an AAAI symposium paper.
- The human adaptation is untested.
verified.design: Design rules and observations from the 1999 tournament of computer programs (1,000-throw matches). No controlled human test.
verified.effect: Qualitative ('thousands of points' across tournaments). The trigger threshold is −4% of the match length.
verified.implication:
A human version, which is my adaptation and has not been tested on people:

- **Default:** random from a device.
- **Deviate:** only when a clear opponent habit appears, such as repeating far below or above 1/3 (C10), or post-loss switches (C15).
- **Revert:** go back to the device as soon as you fall behind, or right after a loss to an opponent who seems to anticipate you.
verified.caveats:
- The evidence is from bots in long matches. For best-of-3 human matches, the right trigger is unknown.
- Opponents who deliberately induce patterns (as Iocaine Powder did) can still edge out this approach.

verifier_added.statement:
**RPS-specific safe exploitation works.** The setup: round-robins of 24 RoShamBo-1999 bots plus a random player (1,000-game matches, 50 tournaments). Each bot's opponent model was wrapped in ε-safe strategies with Safe Policy Selection, where the allowed worst-case loss grows only with what the bot has already won above the safety value of 0.
- Total score rose significantly for 15 of 24 bots and fell significantly for none; 15 rose in rank.
- RussRocker4's losses to Iocaine Powder, Phasenbott and MegaHAL shrank from −519/−530/−94 to −14/−6/−5 per match. Its wins over weak bots were kept (189→222, 477→478, 992→992), and it rose from 11th to 4th.
- Mixing via Hedge instead significantly lowered the scores of 5 of the strongest players.
verifier_added.evidence:
- **M1** Table 3: 'RussRocker4 11 4 1583 2731 X'.
- **M1** Table 4(b): 'Iocaine Powder -519 -14 X; Phasenbott -530 -6 X; MegaHAL -94 -5 X; Inocencio 189 222; Knucklehead 477 478; Peterbot 992 992'.
- **M1** text: 'Of the 24 players, 15 experienced a significant increase in score ... none of these reductions were significant'; 'the random player placed 20th out of 25 competitors'.
- **M1** update rule: ε(t+1) ← ε(t) + f(t+1) + V(π(t), a−i(t)) − r*.
- **M1** on Hedge: 'dangerous to use with the strongest players'.
- URL: cdn.aaai.org/Symposia/Fall/2004/FS-04-02/FS04-02-014.pdf
verifier_added.study_design: Computer bots only, from the 1999 RoShamBo competition; 25 competitors; 1,000-game matches; 50 tournaments per condition; AAAI 2004 Fall Symposium.
verifier_added.effect_size:
- Significant score gains for 15 of 24 bots.
- About 500 points per 1,000 throws of losses removed against the top bots.
- No significant score losses.
verifier_added.strategic_implication:
- Exploit only with what you have already won: let the size of your deviation from the device's random throws grow with your current lead.
- Revert to random when you are level or behind.
- This is RPS evidence for C02 and C19, rather than evidence borrowed from poker.
verifier_added.caveats:
- Bots in long matches; untested in humans and in best-of-3.
- A workshop/symposium paper.

verifier_added.statement:
**Human RPS players tend to over-repeat, not over-switch.** In the largest human-vs-human RPS lab study (360 paid students, groups of 6, 300 rounds), players were more likely to repeat their previous hand than to shift to either other hand, which implies a repeat rate above 1/3.
- The effect is strongest at the lowest win payoff and 'still very significant even at a = 100'.
- When players did change hand, clockwise and counter-clockwise shifts were about equally likely.
- This contradicts the over-switching assumption carried over from tennis serves and random-generation tasks in C09 and C10.
verifier_added.evidence:
- **S32** Results: 'at each time the players are more likely to repeat their last action than to shift action either counter-clockwise (i.e., R → P, P → S, S → R ...) or clockwise (R → S, S → P, P → R). This inertial effect is especially strong at a = 1.1 and it diminishes as a increases.'
- **S09** Sec. 3.1: 'still very significant even at a = 100 ... the probability of shifting action in the counter-clockwise direction is almost the same as that of shifting in the clockwise direction.'
verifier_added.study_design: 360 Zhejiang University students; 59 analysed groups of 6; random pairwise matching each round; 300 rounds; win payoff a ∈ {1.1, 2, 4, 9, 100}; real cash.
verifier_added.effect_size:
- Direction only; the values are in figures.
- Repeat > each shift implies r > 1/3.
- Against a player with r=0.45, throwing what beats their last hand earns (3r−1)/2 = +0.175 per throw.
verifier_added.strategic_implication:
- Do not assume opponents over-switch; tally each opponent's stay/up/down counts.
- If repeats exceed about 40%, throw what beats their last hand.
- If repeats fall below about 25%, throw what their last hand beats.
verifier_added.caveats:
- Chinese students in a lab, with random re-pairing.
- Dyson 2016 (against a computer) found more switching after losses and draws.
- No data from tournaments or Korea.

verifier_added.statement:
**Scoring by match results favours unexploitable designs.** In Billings's 1999 'Best of the Best' division (match result only, with progressive elimination), defensive programs beat stronger margin-maximizers:
- A fixed De Bruijn sequence finished 3rd, losing only to Iocaine Powder and Phasenbott; it was 28th on points.
- RoShamBot, 'designed to win a match in the long run' and capped at +500 even against Always Rock, finished 4th (13th on points); it was unbeaten until Iocaine Powder arrived.
- Majikthise finished 5th (25th on points).
- MegaHAL fell from 3rd on points to 7th, and RussRocker4 from 4th to 8th.
verifier_added.evidence:
- **S03**: 'In the "Best of the Best" tournaments, only the match result (win, loss, or a draw) was used to determine the order of finish -- the magnitude of a win did not matter.'
- **S03** standings rows: 'RoShamBot 13 4'; 'Majikthise 25 5'; '* De Bruijn 28 3'; 'MegaHAL 3 7'; 'RussRocker4 4 8'.
- **S03**: RoShamBot 'cannot score more than 500 points out of 1000, even against Always Rock! ... it never lost a match'.
- **S04**: 'De Bruijn finished third in the "Best of the Best" series, losing only to Iocaine Powder and Phasenbott.'
verifier_added.study_design: Computer programs; 1,000-turn matches; six sets of 25 Best-of-the-Best tournaments versus 25 Open (points) tournaments.
verifier_added.effect_size: Rank changes of up to 25 places between the points scoring and the match-result scoring.
verifier_added.strategic_implication: In a 단체전 decided by match wins, robustness beats margin. Small edges that never expose you to a match loss are worth more than big exploitative leans.
verifier_added.caveats:
- Bots in long matches.
- De Bruijn's success relied on opponents over-fitting to apparent patterns.

verifier_added.statement:
**Two failure modes of pattern-hunting** (Billings's dummy bots):
- **Decoys:** a statistically balanced De Bruijn sequence 'naturally gives the appearance of certain tendencies', so over-zealous exploiters are 'continuously deceived and punished'. The stronger the pattern detector, the more susceptible it is.
- **Missing absences:** simple habits defined by the absence of a pattern are missed by sophisticated predictors. Against 'Always Switchin'' (never repeats; best counter +500 per 1,000), even some of the strongest programs managed only +350. Against Switch A Lot (12% repeats; maximum 320), the simple Anti-rotn bot, which counts only repeat/up/down rotations, 'scored close to the maximum', while Iocaine Powder and Phasenbott scored under +100.
verifier_added.evidence:
- **S04**: 'Every string will appear to contain patterns, even if it is random ... If the opponent is over-zealous in its exploitation of any perceived weakness, it will be continuously deceived and punished! The stronger the opponent is at detecting subtle patterns (that don't actually exist) the more susceptible it is'.
- **S04**: 'Even some of the strongest programs did no better than +350. This may be another indication that they are looking for patterns directly, rather than for the absence of patterns that should be present.'
- **S04**: 'The best exploiter was the simple Anti-rotn bot, which scored close to the maximum. In contrast, five of the strongest head-to-head players, including Iocaine Powder and Phasenbott, scored less than +100 points on average.'
verifier_added.study_design: Computer programs; 1,000-turn matches; 1999 competition.
verifier_added.effect_size: Simple stay/up/down tracking earned about 3× more against Switch A Lot than the top general-purpose predictors.
verifier_added.strategic_implication:
- Have a teammate tally each opponent's stay/up/down counts; that simple statistic catches habits that intuition misses.
- In short matches, do not chase apparent streaks: balanced-looking sequences can bait you.
verifier_added.caveats: Bots in long matches; humans read patterns differently.

verifier_added.statement: **Salience-driven choices are costly in zero-sum games.** In Rubinstein–Tversky hide-and-seek (four boxes, six experiments), seekers found hiders 32% of the time, against the 25% that the equilibrium mix guarantees. Seekers chose the 'least salient' central box even more often (46%) than hiders did (37%). A level-k model with a uniformly random L0 coincides with equilibrium, so such deviations require a salient anchor.
verifier_added.evidence:
- **S12** (Crawford et al. WP 2012, Sec. 8): 'Why then do hiders allow seekers to find them 32% of the time when they could hold it down to 25% by using the equilibrium mixed strategy? And why are the results role-asymmetric, with seekers choosing central A more often (46%) than hiders (37%)?'
- **S12**: 'Even a level-k model with a uniform random L0 coincides with equilibrium.'
verifier_added.study_design: Lab hide-and-seek data from six treatments, as summarized in a JEL review; zero-sum game with four locations.
verifier_added.effect_size: +7 pp detection rate (32% vs 25%) against hiders who followed the salient pattern.
verifier_added.strategic_implication:
- Any choice driven by an anchor that opponents can also guess creates an exploitable tilt. Examples: 'Rock is obvious', 'don't repeat', 'beat their favourite'.
- Edges arise only from salience. Without a read, use a device.
verifier_added.caveats: Not RPS; the figures come via a review, not the original paper.

verifier_added.statement:
**Most experienced Roshambull players show no frequency bias; their exploitable structure is in reactions.**
- Only 18% of experienced players (≥100 matches; n=7,758) had throw distributions significantly different from uniform (20% for their k0 play).
- About half (47%) responded significantly to opponents' displayed histories.
- Responses grew with the evidence: per SD of k1 payoff, k1-consistency rose 1.6 pp against opponents with fewer than 14 games and 14 pp against opponents with more than 46 games.
verifier_added.evidence:
- **S01** Sec. 2: '82% of experienced players have first throw distributions that do not differ from 1/3, 1/3, 1/3, but half respond to their opponents' histories'.
- **S01** Sec. 3: 'we reject uniform random play for 18% of experienced players'.
- **S01** Sec. 4.2: 'differs significantly from random uniform for 1252 players (20%)'.
- **S01** Sec. 4.6: '1.6 percentage points ... when opponents have played fewer than 14 games ... 14 percentage points ... when opponents have played over 46 games'.
verifier_added.study_design: Facebook Roshambull, 2007; first throws of best-of-3 matches; opponent histories displayed on screen; no money.
verifier_added.effect_size:
- 18% non-uniform in frequencies vs 47% reacting to information.
- Reaction size scales about 9× with the length of the opponent's history.
verifier_added.strategic_implication:
- Against experienced opponents, static hand-frequency leans (C06) have little to exploit.
- Read how opponents react to information: your visible history and previous outcomes.
- The longer opponents can watch you, the more they will react, so vary your visible tendencies.
verifier_added.caveats: Online, low stakes, with a history display; live play may differ.

verifier_added.statement:
**Efficient partial exploitation** (my derivation). Against an opponent who over-plays one hand X while the other two are balanced, the most efficient partial exploitation keeps X itself at 1/3 and shifts probability from the hand X beats to the hand that beats X.

Against a 36/32/32 Rock-leaning opponent, the mix R 1/3, P 1/3+ε, S 1/3−ε earns 0.08ε of expected gain at a worst-case loss of ε:
- 33/58/8: +2.0 pp at −25 pp.
- 33/67/0: +2.67 pp at −33 pp.

That is twice the efficiency of the symmetric leans 50/25/25 (+1.0 pp at −25) and 40/30/30 (+0.4 pp at −10). For small leans the trade-off is linear, not 'highly concave'.
verifier_added.evidence:
- **S04** formula: 'EV[x] = Pr[x+2] - Pr[x+1]'.
- **My calculation**, a grid over the simplex with exploitability defined as the opponent's best pure-response EV. Maximum EV at a given exploitability ε:
  - ε=0.05 → +0.40 pp at (0.333, 0.383, 0.283).
  - ε=0.25 → +2.00 pp at (0.333, 0.583, 0.083).
  - ε=1/3 → +2.67 pp at (0.333, 0.667, 0).
  - ε=1 → +4.00 pp (pure Paper).
  - (0.25, 0.5, 0.25) → +1.00 pp at exploitability 0.25.
- **S07** is the poker-only source of the 'highly concave' claim.
verifier_added.study_design: Exact expected-value arithmetic on the RPS payoff matrix against a known opponent mix.
verifier_added.effect_size: Twice the gain per unit of worst-case exposure compared with symmetric leans; absolute gains are at most +2–4 pp per throw.
verifier_added.strategic_implication:
- If you lean at all against a 'Rock-heavy' opponent, take Scissors out and add Paper; do not cut Rock.
- In general: drop the hand their favourite beats, add the hand that beats their favourite, and keep their favourite hand at 1/3.
verifier_added.caveats:
- Assumes the estimated bias is real; real biases are small (1–3 pp) and noisy.
- The worst case assumes an opponent who reads your lean.

dead_ends: Rapoport & Budescu (1992), 'Generation of random series in two-person strictly competitive games', JEP: General 121(3):352–363. The paper exists: DOI 10.1037/0096-3445.121.3.352 confirmed via Semantic Scholar metadata and Wong et al. (2021) ref. 2. I could not retrieve an abstract or full text (APA PsycNet only shows 'Loading…'; Semantic Scholar has no abstract). Its finding is reported here only second-hand (Guseva et al. 2023; Wong et al. 2021; Sanabria & Thrailkill 2009, PMC2648521).

Budescu & Rapoport (1994), 'Subjective randomization in one- and two-person games', J. Behavioral Decision Making 7:261–278. Title and year confirmed (Semantic Scholar; Wong et al. ref. 11), but no abstract or text was retrievable.

Towse & Neil (1998), BRMIC, 'Analyzing human random generation behavior: A review of methods used and a computer program for describing performance'. Title and year confirmed via Semantic Scholar, but the Springer PDF link returned HTML, so I did not read it. I used the Towse (1998) Br J Psychol abstract instead.

Billings (2000) ICGA Journal 23(1): 'Thoughts on RoShamBo' (pp.3–8) and 'The First International RoShamBo Programming Competition' (pp.42–50); Egnor 'Iocaine Powder' (pp.33–35). Existence and pages confirmed on icga.org, but the IOS Press pages returned 403 and the live ualberta pages return 404. I substituted the archived 1999 web reports by the organizer and Egnor's archived web explanation.

NYT, Carol Vogel (29 Apr 2005), 'Rock, Paper, Payoff: Child's Play Wins Auction House an Art Sale'. nytimes.com blocked both WebFetch and curl. The article's existence is confirmed by Batzilis et al.'s reference [31]. Secondary sources disagree on the children's quote and on the value at stake.

Palacios-Huerta (2003), Review of Economic Studies. No full text was accessible (LSE: 'Full text not available'; OUP blocked). The sample size often cited for it (1,417 kicks) appeared only in a search-engine summary and was not verified, so I do not use it.

Ganzfried & Sandholm, 'Safe Opponent Exploitation' (ACM TEAC 2015). I could not find the full text. arXiv:1603.03491, which looked like the right paper, is a different one (Ganzfried & Sun, 'Bayesian Opponent Exploitation in Imperfect-Information Games'). An AAMAS 2011 PDF by the same authors is yet another paper.

Kocher & Sutter (2005), Economic Journal (groups vs individuals in beauty contests). The Crossref lookup failed and I did not read it. I used the Kugler, Kausel & Kocher (2012) review abstract instead; its full text on LMU epub refused connections.

Shachat (2002) full text (Durham repository) returned 403. Search snippets attributed the statement that 'serial correlation is not reduced' when subjects use a randomizing device to a University of Arizona repository item (probably a dissertation), which also returned 403. Unverified.
Gauriot, Page & Wooders: I did not verify the published journal version. I read only the September 2016 SSRN working paper.

Lead 4 says Batzilis et al. give 'shares of RPS players at each level'. The paper actually reports the average share of THROWS per player at each level (k0 73.8%, k1 18.5%, k2 7.7%) and shows that most players mix levels. The Stahl & Wilson shares quoted there (24% L1, 49% L2, 27% Nash) are cited to Stahl & Wilson 1994 (JEBO), not 1995.
Crawford, Costa-Gomes & Iriberri (JEL 2013). I read the April 2012 working paper. The journal pagination (51(1):5–62) comes from a repository listing, not the article.

MPRA (mpra.ub.uni-muenchen.de) and core.ac.uk could not be reached or returned 403, so working-paper versions of Duffy et al. (cognitive load and minimax) and related papers could not be read beyond the abstract.

Zhang, Moisan & Gonzalez (2021), Games 12(3):52 (RPS beyond win-stay/lose-change). The CMU-hosted PDF returned HTML and MDPI blocked direct download, so I did not read it (it is peripheral to Angle C).

RPS-specific human stay/repeat rates with numbers in the text: Wang–Xu–Zhou (2014), Dyson et al. (2016) and Zhou (2016) give these only in figures. I found no exact repeat rate for tournament-style human RPS.
open_questions: No study tested human RPS players who pre-commit to an external random sequence (die, phone RNG, a pre-rolled list) in live head-to-head play. The zero-expected-loss guarantee follows from the minimax theorem, but whether people stick to the sequence, whether timing or gesture cues leak, and how opponents react remain untested.

The direction of human serial dependence in RPS seems to depend on the setting. Wang–Xu–Zhou found repeats more likely than shifts, especially when the win payoff is low. Classic random-generation tasks show repetition avoidance. Batzilis et al. found a weak negative correlation across first throws, and key-press tasks can show too FEW alternations. Which applies to Korean live 가위바위보 best-of-N matches is unknown, and short matches give too few throws to estimate an opponent's repeat rate reliably.

Level-k shares for one-shot, face-to-face opening throws with no visible history have not been estimated. The large-scale RPS estimates come from an online app that displayed opponent histories, and the CHC τ≈1.5 comes from non-RPS games.

The literature found does not address how specific 단체전 rules change optimal play: relay or winner-stays elimination, simultaneous team throws, captain decisions, or whether teammates may confer between throws. Okano's team advantage is for two-person deliberating teams in O'Neill's 4×4 game.

Whether stress or time pressure makes competitive play more or less predictable is unresolved. Classic generation tasks show more stereotypy under speed or load; a competitive game against a computer showed no load effect (Duffy et al. 2024); and time pressure produced shallower level-k in one study (Spiliopoulos et al.) but more equilibrium-like play in another (Lindner & Sutter).

Whether the population hand frequencies found elsewhere hold in Korea is untested: the lab bias toward Rock, the online bias toward Paper on first throws, and experienced players' first-throw mix (which makes Scissors slightly best).

Live visual cues, such as automatic imitation of an opponent's hand shape or tells while the hands come down, are outside this angle and could outweigh the small statistical edges (≤5 pp per throw) documented here.

condensed.angle: D. Face-to-face factors: imitation, reading hands, timing, speed, emotion/stress, cheap talk and priming

verified.statement: Cook, Bird, Lünser, Huck & Heyes (Proc R Soc B 2012, 279(1729):780-786; online 20 Jul 2011; 45 UCL adults, 14 analysed triads, 60 rounds per pair) found 36.3% draws (SD 4.6) when one player was blindfolded vs 33.3% (SD 5.0) when both were, a +3.0 pp difference. In logit models clustered by triad, the sighted player copied Scissors (b=0.266, p=.006 one-tailed; about 0.32 to 0.38) and Rock (b=0.245, p=.034; about 0.29 to 0.35) but not Paper (b=0.086, p=.298). Sighted players won 31.3% vs 32.4% for blindfolded players. The key paired test (t13=1.72) was reported as 'p = 0.05 one-tailed' but is p of about 0.055 (critical t=1.771), so it is not significant. The effect was not replicated (C2).
verified.evidence: PMC full text (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3248720/). Results: 'there was a greater number of draws in the blind-sighted (36.3%) than in the blind-blind (33.3%) conditions'; 'one-sample t-tests ... (t13 = 2.49; p < 0.025 (one-tailed))'; 'paired-samples t-test ... (t13 = 1.72; p = 0.05 (one-tailed))'. Table 4: draws 36.3 (4.6) vs 33.3 (5.0); blind wins 32.4 (4.1), sighted wins 31.3 (2.9). Table 5: rock 0.245 (0.134, p=0.034), constant -0.874; paper 0.086 (0.162, p=0.298), constant -0.677; scissors 0.266 (0.105, p=0.006), constant -0.737. Fig. 1 bars: P(sighted Scissors | blind Scissors) about 0.39. My calculation: one-tailed p for t13=1.72 is 0.0546. Logit-implied probabilities: 0.294 to 0.348, 0.337 to 0.356, 0.324 to 0.384. Design: 'presenting a clenched fist ... Following a count of three made by the umpire'; £5 plus '£2.50 win bonus' per 60-round match.
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed (Proc R Soc B). Small study: 14 triads analysed. Face-to-face, human vs human, with a weak incentive (Belot et al. estimated under 3 US cents per match to avoid imitation). Two direct replications failed.
verified.design: Tier: peer-reviewed lab experiment, face-to-face human vs human. 45 adults (23 F, mean age 24.9) at UCL's ELSE lab, none with economics training, split into random triads. One of the 15 triads was excluded, leaving 14, with the triad as the unit of analysis. Each pair played 60 rounds: two 20-round blind–sighted matches (roles swapped) and one 20-round blind–blind match. Players started from a clenched fist; an umpire counted three and announced gestures and outcomes. Pay: £5 show-up fee plus £2.50 for winning a 60-round match, nothing for a tied match. An extra 4 pairs played 80 rounds each, filmed at 60 fps.
verified.effect: Draws +3.0 pp over 1/3 (36.3% vs 33.3%). Model-implied copying (my calculation from the Table 5 coefficients): Scissors 0.324→0.384 (+6.1 pp), Rock 0.294→0.348 (+5.3 pp), Paper 0.337→0.356 (+1.9 pp, not significant). Sighted minus blind win rate −1.1 pp (descriptive only). The key paired test had t13=1.72 with reported p=0.05 one-tailed; the one-tailed critical value for t13 is 1.771 (cited by S2 and S3), so the test does not reach 0.05.
verified.implication: Even at face value, this copying is small. It produces draws (replays), not losses, and only works when the other hand appears first. You cannot exploit it without throwing off-beat. The cheap precaution: fix your hand before the final beat and do not track the opponent's hand while delivering yours.
verified.caveats: The numbers are transcribed accurately from the full text; 'low' refers to how robust the effect is. One small study (14 triads) with a marginal key test, not replicated (C2, C3). Belot et al. (S4) calculated that the incentive to avoid imitation was under 3 US cents per 60-game match. Published online 2011; print 2012, 279(1729):780–786.

verified.statement: Two direct replications found no extra draws. Aczel, Bago & Foldes (Proc R Soc B 2012, 279(1741):3231-3233; 114 Hungarians, 34 triads analysed) found 36.54% (SD 4.24) when one player could see vs 37.77% (SD 6.37) when both were blindfolded (t33=-1.02, p=.32). Ito (Psychologia 2017, 60(2):57-67; 42 Aichi students, 14 triads) found 34.2% vs 32.5% (t13=0.78, p=.45). Ito's random-effects mini-meta-analysis of Cook, Aczel and Ito gave Hedges' g=0.15, 95% CI [-0.36, 0.67], p=.56. Aczel's authors called their high blind-blind draw rate 'unexpected'. The observed Scissors over-play (36.6-36.8%) would raise expected draws only to about 33.5% under independent play, so it does not explain 37.77%. Belot et al.'s idea that the Aczel null came from 'bobbing' is contradicted by Aczel's report that Cook's players also bobbed.
verified.evidence: Aczel 2012 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3385727/) §3: 't33 = -1.02, p = 0.32 (two-tailed) ... blind-blind condition (M = 37.77, s.d. = 6.37) than in the blind-sighted condition (M = 36.54, s.d. = 4.24)'; scissors M = 36.76% and 36.64%. §4: 'The high level of draws in the blind-blind condition was unexpected in our study.' Endnote 1: 'personal communication with the authors established that the RPS game was played with participants bobbing their fists in time with the count (1-2-3), and as such we conducted our study employing the same technique.' Ito 2017 (https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/psysoc/60/2/60_57/_pdf) p.61: 't(13) = .78, p = .45 (two-tailed)'; Table 2 draws 34.2 (3.8) vs 32.5 (6.8); p.62: 'combined effect size of 0.15, 95% CI [-0.36, 0.67], p = .56'. Belot 2013 Discussion: 'in contrast with Cook et al., Aczel et al. required their subjects to bob'. My calculation: 0.3664^2 + 2(0.3168^2) = 0.335.
verified.reliability: Both replications are peer-reviewed, small (14-34 triads), face-to-face human vs human, with small cash or chocolate incentives. The mini-meta-analysis pools 3 small studies.
verified.design: Tier: peer-reviewed lab experiments, face-to-face. S2: 114 native Hungarian speakers (61 F, mean age 22.46); 4 triads discarded. Pay: a chocolate bar plus 300 HUF (about £1) to each block winner, nothing for ties. Players had to 'move their fists downwards then back to their chest on each count' ('bobbing'). S3: 42 Aichi University undergraduates in Japan (29 F, mean age 20.7), 14 triads. Pay: 1000 JPY plus 500 JPY per match won. Clenched hand at the chest, referee counted three, filmed at 120 fps.
verified.effect: Aczel: −1.23 pp (fewer draws when one player could see). Ito: +1.7 pp, not significant. Pooled g = 0.15, CI [−0.36, 0.67], which includes zero. Aczel's blind–blind draws were already 37.77% because Scissors was overplayed (36.76% and 36.64% in the two conditions).
verified.implication: Do not plan around 'opponents unconsciously copy my hand' (or 'I copy theirs'). The effect is not reliable across labs or in an East Asian sample (Japan).
verified.caveats: All three studies are small (14–34 triads). Belot et al. (S4) speculated that Aczel's bobbing procedure reduced asynchronies; this was not tested. Aczel argues the blind–blind condition, not 1/3, is the right baseline. Ito notes that some sighted players looked away.

verified.statement: Belot, Crawford & Heyes (PNAS 2013, 110(8):2763-2768; 54 Oxford students, 18 triads, 12x20 games, £5 plus 10p per win) tested a face-to-face open/closed-hand Matching Pennies game. Sighted players matched a blindfolded opponent 52.13% of the time when matching paid (p=.048 one-tailed) and 50.69% when mismatching paid (p=.29). The authors' calibration put automatic imitation at about 2.82% of games and intentional responding at about 1.44%. The automatic-imitation probit term was significant only in games 1-10 of a pairing (0.053, SE 0.028), not in the full sample (0.023, SE 0.021). Aczel et al. (JEP:HPP 2015, 41(4):1049-1062; 102 Hungarians, hidden video, 32 sessions) looked at trials where the sighted player moved at least 133 ms after the blindfolded one. Matching rose only under the match incentive (OR 1.28, p=.002 one-tailed), not the mismatch incentive (OR 1.07, p=.403). After controlling for previous-gesture biases, the match-incentive effect fell to OR 1.22 (p=.060), and a Bayes factor of 0.186 favoured no automatic imitation.
verified.evidence: Belot (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3581976/) Table 4: '52.13% (0.048) ... 50.69% (0.29)'; win 49.31% (0.29). Text: 'p = 52.13-50.69% = 1.44% and q = 2(52.13-50.00%) - p = 2.82%'. Table 5: full sample 0.023 (0.021); games 1-10 0.053 (0.028)**; games 11-20 -0.008 (0.032). Aczel 2015 accepted manuscript (https://spiral.imperial.ac.uk/handle/10044/1/32477) Results: 'OR = 1.28, Z(542) = 2.82, p = .002 (one tailed) ... OR = 1.07, Z(690) = 0.84, p = .403'; 'OR from 1.28 to 1.22 ... (OR = 1.22, Z(226) = 1.56, p = .060, one tailed)'; 'B(mismatching<matching)=0.186'. Introduction: 'Neither showed support for automatic imitation when regarding the whole sample ... After conducting six one-tailed t-tests on the split data, they found two significant results'.
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed, face-to-face, real per-game money. Belot's positive result rests on post-hoc early/late splits. Aczel 2015 has the larger sample and is video-coded; only the accepted manuscript was read.
verified.design: Tier: peer-reviewed lab experiments, face-to-face. S4: 54 Oxford students (21 F), 18 triads, 12 rounds of 20 games. Pay: £5 plus 10p per game won. One player blindfolded; an umpire counted three. S5: 102 Hungarian students (67 F, mean age 21.91), same protocol, 10 HUF per game. 32 triad sessions (7,680 trials) were recorded on hidden video and coded frame by frame.
verified.effect: Belot: +2.13 pp over 50% when matching paid; +0.69 pp (not significant) when mismatching paid. Automatic imitation in about 2.82% of games. Aczel 2015: OR 1.28 when matching paid; OR 1.07 (not significant) when mismatching paid.
verified.implication: Involuntary copying of a seen hand is tiny (a few % of throws) and fades after about 10 games. When people do see the other hand in time, they use it on purpose if it pays, which in RPS is exactly the late reaction that rules forbid. The take-away is the same as C1: commit before the beat.
verified.caveats: This is a two-gesture game, not RPS. Belot's explanation of the Aczel 2012 null via 'bobbing' is untested. For S5, only the accepted manuscript was read.

verified.statement: In the RPS blindfold studies, seeing the opponent's hand gave no win advantage: sighted players won 31.3% vs 32.4% for blindfolded players (Cook 2012) and 31.8% vs 34.0% (Ito 2017). These figures are descriptive and untested; Aczel 2012 reported no win rates. This is not true of every face-to-face blindfold study. In the two-gesture Matching Pennies game, sight helped when copying paid: sighted players won 52.13% (p=.05 one-tailed) when paid to match vs 49.31% when paid to mismatch (Belot 2013). Aczel 2015 likewise found more matching only under the match incentive (OR 1.28). Sighted players sometimes looked away: Aczel 2015 excluded 554 of 7,680 trials (7.2%) for averted gaze, and Ito saw participants 'occasionally' avert their eyes.
verified.evidence: Cook Table 4 and text: 'blind players actually won slightly more of the blind-sighted rounds (32.4%) than the sighted players (31.3%)'. Ito Table 2: blind wins 34.0 (3.5), sighted wins 31.8 (3.5); Discussion p.65: 'occasionally appeared to avert their eyes from their opponents' gestures'. Belot Table 4: win frequency 'Sighted with incentive to match 52.13% (0.05)'; 'Sighted with incentive to mismatch 49.31% (0.29)'. Aczel 2015: 'From the 7680 trials of the 32 remaining sessions, 554 were excluded from further analysis because of averted gaze'; 'some of the sighted players averted their gaze from the blind player's hand (for example facing away from the opponent or covering their own eyes with their hand)'.
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed, small, face-to-face. Win-rate differences in RPS were not formally tested.
verified.design: Same designs as C1–C3: face-to-face lab studies in the UK, Hungary and Japan with small cash incentives.
verified.effect: Sighted minus blind win rate: −1.1 pp (Cook), −2.2 pp (Ito), −0.69 pp vs 50% (Belot, paid to mismatch). These are descriptive; win rates were not formally tested. Gaze aversion: 554/7,680 = 7.2% of trials (my calculation).
verified.implication: Watching the opponent's hand at the moment of delivery has no demonstrated benefit and a possible small cost (copying leads to draws). Fixing your gaze elsewhere during delivery is a free precaution that stays within the rules.
verified.caveats: Win differences are small, untested, and the studies were not powered for them. Gaze aversion was observed, not manipulated.

verified.statement: Gaps between throws long enough to react to are rare. Cook 2012 filmed 4 UK pairs at 60 fps, 80 rounds each: the blindfolded player's gesture was identifiable first in 44.7% of rounds, and it led by more than 200 ms in 17.2%; pair asynchrony SDs were 137-249 ms. Ito 2017 (14 Japanese triads, 120 fps) analysed asynchronies 'in draws under the blind-sighted condition': the blindfolded player was first in 44.2% and led by more than 200 ms in 1.4%. In Aczel 2015's hidden-video Matching Pennies data, 81.52% of trials gave the sighted player no lead or a lead under 133 ms (mean -29 ms, SD 172 ms). Why Ito's long-lead tail was so small is unexplained; no study attributes it to a better-synchronised chant.
verified.evidence: Cook p.4: 'The blindfolded player initiated his or her gesture before the sighted player in 44.7 per cent of rounds, and this positive asynchrony exceeded 200 ms ... in 17.2 per cent of rounds'. Fig. 2 (image checked): means/SDs 0.875/220, 28.4/148, 10.1/137, -41.4/249 ms. Ito p.63: 'to assess the participants' response asynchronies in draws under the blind-sighted condition ... The blindfolded participant started the gesture before the sighted participant in 44.2% of rounds, and this positive asynchrony exceeded 200 ms ... in 1.4% of rounds.' Aczel 2015: 'in 81.52 % of the data either the blind players initiated the gesture later than the sighted players or the delay after their gesture was too short ... mean = -29 ms; SD = 172 ms'.
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed video measurements, face-to-face. Samples are small: 4 pairs in Cook, draws only in Ito. Frame rates limit precision.
verified.design: Tier: peer-reviewed lab video measurements, face-to-face human pairs. Cook: 4 extra pairs × 80 rounds. Ito: 14 triads. Aczel 2015: about 6,688 coded trials from 32 sessions. In all three, onset is the first frame in which the gesture can be identified.
verified.effect: A lead long enough to react to (>200 ms) occurred in 1.4%–17.2% of RPS rounds. A lead of at least 133 ms occurred in at most 18.5% of hand-game trials (100 − 81.52). Typical pair asynchrony SD was 137–249 ms.
verified.implication: Even before rules are considered, 'see the hand and react' is unavailable in more than 80% of throws. A well-synchronised chant (as in the Japanese sample) shrinks the window further.
verified.caveats: Video samples are small. Frame rates of 30–120 fps limit precision. Why Ito's long-lead tail was so much smaller is unexplained (procedure or culture).

verified.statement: Katsuki, Yamakawa & Ishikawa (HRI'15 Extended Abstracts, pp.117-118) report that a human hand takes about 60 ms to finish changing shape (measured with a 3000 fps camera). Their robot recognises the shape every 2 ms, starts moving about 30 ms after the human begins, and completes within 30 ms. Ito, Sueishi, Yamakawa & Ishikawa (IEEE CASE 2016, pp.891-896) used 500 fps vision with a 20 ms sign-forming time. The Yamakawa Lab page calls the system a '1 ms late-throw janken' (1ミリ秒の後出しじゃんけん) that people do not notice because human vision is 'about 30 fps'; that is the lab's own claim. It says version 2 recognises the hand before it is complete. Wei, Liu, Dollack & Perusquia-Hernandez (arXiv:2606.29423, marked 'Accepted by ACII2025'; 24 participants) detected forearm EMG onsets at least 800 ms before the gesture became visible. A classifier trained on posed gestures reached 53.6% on spontaneous ones (chance 33%). The 'tight hand = rock' tip (Farber 2015 blog) cites no data.
verified.evidence: Katsuki p.118: 'The shape of the human hand is recognized every 2 ms'; 'It took about 60 ms for the human player to finish changing their hand shape. The robot hand started moving about 30 ms after ... and completed its motion within 30 ms'; Phantom v640 at 3000 fps. Ito 2016: 'vision system with a high frame rate (500 fps)'; 'a sign-forming time of only 20 ms'. Lab page (http://www.hfr.iis.u-tokyo.ac.jp/research/Janken/index-j.html): '1ミリ秒の後出しじゃんけんを実現している．人間の目は30fps程度であるため'; 'バージョン2では，人間の「手」が完成する前に認識する'. arXiv abstract: 'EMG onsets could be detected at least 800 ms before the gesture's visible onset ... 53.6% for spontaneous gestures'; Comments: 'Accepted by ACII2025'. Farber: 'A tight hand, when raised often, ends in a rock.'
verified.reliability: Engineering demonstrations (an extended abstract and a peer-reviewed conference paper) with no human-performance statistics. EMG work: small conference paper. Hand-reading tip: blog, anecdotal.
verified.design: Tier: engineering demonstrations (HRI'15 extended abstract; IEEE CASE 2016) plus a lab web page. Timing was measured with a 3000 fps camera; no human-performance statistics or N were reported. EMG: unreviewed arXiv preprint with 24 participants in pairs. Hand-reading tip: blog (anecdotal).
verified.effect: Timing only: human shaping about 60 ms; machine recognition every 1–2 ms plus 20–30 ms to form the robot's sign.
verified.implication: Reading a hand while it forms is a machine-speed task, and the robot's '100% win rate' is itself a disguised late throw. No study shows that human eyes can use pre-shaping cues in real time, so don't spend attention on 'tells'.
verified.caveats: The 100% claims are demonstrations, not controlled trials. The EMG work is an unreviewed preprint and needs sensors. No peer-reviewed study of human observers reading RPS hand pre-shaping was found.

verified.statement: Fukunaga et al. (2005, 高次脳機能研究 25(3):242-250) cite Omori et al. (1999, Neurosci Res 33:317-323) for reaction times in a picture-cued 'late janken' task, measured to the start of the hand movement: tie (copy) 158.6±36.2 ms, win 224.7±39.3 ms, lose 323.0±73.7 ms. Beating was 66 ms slower than copying and losing 164 ms slower. Omori's abstract describes an fMRI hand-shape selection task in which six right-handed subjects responded to on-screen hand images under fixed win/lose/tie rules. The RTs are not in the abstract and were verified only through Fukunaga's citation.
verified.evidence: Fukunaga p.242 (https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/hbfr/25/3/25_3_242/_pdf/-char/ja): 'Omori ら（1999）は，絵を見てじゃんけん運動を開始するまでの反応時間は，あいこじゃんけん（158.6 ± 36.2 ms），勝ちじゃんけん（224.7 ± 39.3 ms），負けじゃんけん（323.0 ± 73.7 ms）の順に長くなると報告し'. Fukunaga's own study: '右利き健常人 9 名', fMRI. Omori 1999 abstract (PMID 10401985): 'six right-handed subjects were required to make one of three hand-shapes ... in response to the hand-shape images on a video screen, following one of the three predefined rules of win, lose, and tie.'
verified.reliability: Secondary citation in a peer-reviewed Japanese journal. The primary study is very small (N=6 per its abstract), uses static pictures and known rules, and is not a live game.
verified.design: Tier: peer-reviewed Japanese neuropsychology, secondary citation. A picture-cued reaction task, not a live game. Fukunaga's own fMRI study had 9 right-handed healthy adults and reports no reaction times.
verified.effect: Copying (a draw) is fastest. Beating is 66 ms slower and losing on purpose 164 ms slower than copying.
verified.implication: With the opponent's hand fully visible, it still takes about 225 ms just to start the beating hand. That is longer than normal throw asynchronies (C5), so 'see and beat' is only possible as an obvious late throw. Copying is the most automatic response to a seen hand, another reason not to watch it.
verified.caveats: The primary Omori et al. (1999) paper was not accessed, so N and procedure are unknown. Static pictures, not a moving hand.

verified.statement: The World RPS Society rules (archived 2017) say: 'The fist must remain in the closed position until the delivery of the final prime'; the player who starts priming 'is under the strict obligation to maintain a constant priming speed'; and 'Any throw not delivered prior to the hand crossing the 90-degree mark shall be considered a throw of rock.' In lab protocols, Cook's umpire prevented 'deliberately delayed gesture execution', Belot's umpires replayed games with any rule violation (6.24% of games), and Aczel 2015 replayed games with 'apparent asynchrony'.
verified.evidence: Wayback copy (https://web.archive.org/web/2017id_/http://worldrps.com/game-basics/the-official-rules-of-rock-paper-scissors/): 3.1.1, 3.2.0 and Approach 4.0 quoted verbatim; 6.3 'In the case of a stalemate ... the round must be replayed.' Cook Methods: 'The presence of an umpire also prevented cheating in the form of deliberately delayed gesture execution.' Belot Methods: 'to require players to replay any games in which violations were noted. (The umpire ordered a replay in 6.24% of the games.)' Aczel 2015 Methods: 'In the case of apparent asynchrony in the execution of the gestures, the umpire required the players to replay that game.'
verified.reliability: Organisational rules with no data, plus peer-reviewed lab procedures.
