verified.design: Tier: organization rules (World RPS Society; archived web page, no data) plus refereed lab procedures (peer-reviewed).
verified.effect: Replays for rule violations in a refereed hand game: 6.24% of games (Belot).
verified.implication: Any tactic that relies on seeing the other hand first is a late throw (늦게 내기 / 後出し). Under World RPS Society-style rules a late throw counts as Rock, which is predictable and beaten by Paper; refereed events replay or penalise it. Check your event's own rules on timing and the chant beforehand.
verified.caveats: No official Korean rule text was found, and local event rules may differ (for example, forfeiting instead of replaying). The current World RPS Society site returns 404, so the archived version was used.

verified.statement: Naber, Stoll, Einhäuser & Carter (PLoS ONE 2013, 8(8):e73302) used a modified, sequential RPS: the three options were spoken one at a time, 4 s apart, and the choice was made by button press. The opponent's peak pupil dilation followed the chosen option in 45 of 75 games (60% vs 33% chance). Ten naïve players who watched only eye videos performed at chance on average (t(9)=0.73, p=.48), although one of them did reach individual significance (37/75 wins, p=.003). Once told to look for peak dilation, they beat chance (t(9)=4.56, p=.001), and 7 of 10 were individually significant. The study tests pupil cues in an artificial sequential format. It does not test whole-face reading or simultaneous hand throws.
verified.evidence: PMC full text (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3753247/): 'In 45 out of 75 games, maximum pupil dilation followed the selected word'; 'naïve-eye condition ... indistinguishable from chance (t(9) = 0.73, p = 0.48) ... informed-pupil ... (t(9) = 4.56, p = 0.001)'; 'we found one individual in the naïve-eye condition that indeed increased their chance of winning significantly above chance (37/75 wins, p=0.003)'; '7/10 players reached significance'; 'presented ... in random order with 4-s intervals'; 'performance-dependent reward ($10-$20)'.
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed, small (3 filmed opponents, 10 players per condition), not live and not simultaneous.
verified.design: Tier: peer-reviewed lab experiment (PLoS ONE). Three 'opponents' were filmed in Marburg (eye video at 120 Hz in dim light, 25 games each against a computer). 30 'players' in Melbourne played against the recordings, with performance-based pay ($10–20). Not live and not simultaneous throws.
verified.effect: The pupil cue was correct 60% of the time vs 33% chance. Naïve players stayed at chance; instructed players were significantly above chance (exact win % is shown only in a figure).
verified.implication: Without special equipment and a one-option-at-a-time format, there is no evidence that players can read a throw from the face or eyes. Don't spend attention on it; keeping a neutral face costs nothing.
verified.caveats: Small n and an artificial set-up (spoken options, delayed button press). Does not transfer directly to simultaneous hand throws.

verified.statement: Against computer opponents, the next choice comes faster after losses and draws than after wins. Dyson 2021 Exp 1 (random bot, N=36): 457/438 vs 543 ms. Forder & Dyson 2016 (random bot, N=29 in the RT analysis): 555/505 vs 708 ms, with no RT difference between staying and switching (F<1). Dyson et al. 2018 Exp 1 (N=38, averaged over a random bot and a 60%-predictable bot): 435/397 vs 488 ms. Dyson et al. 2018 Exps 2-3 pooled, random bots: 552/504 vs 672 ms. Dyson 2024 (PBR, Exp 2, N=72): post-win RT was 671 ms with explicit WIN/LOSE feedback vs 515 ms without, while post-loss RT was 525 vs 530 ms, so the gap is mainly slowing after wins. Against exploitable bots the pattern reverses: Dyson 2018 Exp 2 had losses at 739 ms vs wins at 582 ms (not significant on its own), and Exps 2-3 pooled had 756 vs 611 ms (significant).
verified.evidence: Dyson 2021 (PMC7859242): 'both losses (457 ms) and draws (438 ms) yielded significantly faster RTs than wins (543 ms)'. Forder (PMC5034336): 'Main effects of condition, strategy ... (F < 1)'; '(708, 555 and 505 ms, respectively'. Dyson 2018 accepted manuscript (Sussex figshare file 41165141, 313,740 bytes): Exp 1 'Independently of the nature of the opponent, both losses (435 ms) and draws (397 ms) yielded subsequently faster RTs than wins (488 ms)'; Exp 2 'lose trials (739 ms) were now statistically slower than draw trials (508 ms) and statistically equivalent but numerically slower than win trials (582 ms)'; pooled 'against unexploitable opponents, RTs following wins (672 ms) were slower than those following losses (552 ms) or draws (504 ms) ... against exploitable opponents, RTs following losses (756 ms) were slower than those following wins (611 ms)'. Dyson 2024 published version (PMC11543769), Table 1: Post-Win 671 (58) / 515 (32); Post-Loss 525 (33) / 530 (35); 'Seventy-two individuals were analysed for Experiment 2'.
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed, one lab, keypress tasks against computers, modest or no performance pay (Dyson 2018 Exp 3 partly paid). Replicated within the lab.
verified.design: Tier: peer-reviewed lab experiments; keypress RPS against a computer playing an even, random mix. S13: N=36 per experiment (University of Alberta, course credit, 270 trials). S14: 36 Sussex undergraduates (29 in the RT analysis), course credit or £20 not tied to performance, 450 trials. S15: Exp 1 N=50 (38 analysed), £25 prize draw; Exp 2 N=40 (35 analysed), credit or £10. S16: Exp 2 about 72 participants, 2×66 trials, course credit (preprint numbers).
verified.effect: Post-loss minus post-win response time: about −53 to −153 ms against random opponents. Reversed (+157 ms) against exploitable opponents.
verified.implication: Speed tells you about mental state (less deliberation after losses and draws), not which hand comes next; the exploitable signal is the lose-shift pattern (C13). For yourself: after a loss, deliberately slow down before committing (C11).
verified.caveats: All from one lab (Dyson), using computer keypress tasks with modest or no incentives. In live play the chant sets the pace, so these differences can only show up as thinking time between rounds.

verified.statement: The evidence that slowing down helps is weak and mixed. (a) Dyson 2021 reports r=0.202, 'p=0.036' between post-loss slowing and win-loss rate in the 72 players of Exps 2-3 (about 4% of variance). With n=72, that r gives two-tailed p of about 0.089 (one-tailed 0.044). All three reported Fig. 2 p-values match n of about 108 instead, so the significance is doubtful. (b) A mandatory extra keypress (about 400 ms) did not change choices against a random bot (Exp 1). Against an exploitable bot (Exp 3) it cut lose-shift from 77.48% to 69.80% (repeat-after-loss 0.225 to 0.302, pooled across hands). However, win rate was lowest with the forced pause: 33.5% vs 35.1% with no pause and 37.3% with a voluntary pause. (c) Ivan et al. 2018 had 12 adults do serial subtraction during a two-option task: lose-shift fell as the enforced delay grew from 1 to 6.5 to 12 s (F(2,22)=17.1, p=3E-5), while win-stay did not change. (d) Baddeley et al. 1998 (abstract only) found that random-generation output becomes more patterned at faster generation rates; this is not a game.
verified.evidence: Dyson 2021 (PMC7859242): 'for the two experiments in which a model of opponent performance could be learnt (Experiments 2 and 3; n = 72) ... (i.e., post-error slowing; r = 0.202, p = 0.036)'; other Fig. 2 correlations 'r = 0.295, p = 0.002' and 'r = -0.103, p = 0.287'. My t-test computation (df=70): p two-tailed 0.089, 0.012, 0.389; with n=108: 0.036, 0.002, 0.289. Exp 1: 'the addition of an extra response per trial (approximately 400 ms) in the fixed credit condition did not change the distribution of participant responding'. Exp 3: 'no credit (77.48%) varying from fixed (69.80%)'; Table 2 lose-stay 0.225 vs 0.302; Table 1 Exp 3 win 0.351 / 0.373 / 0.335 (no / variable / fixed); 'increased in the variable credit condition relative to the fixed credit condition (37.28% vs. 33.49%)'. Ivan (PMC5852382): 'fixed intervals of either 1, 6.5, or 12 s ... F (2,22) = 17.1, p = 3E-5'. Baddeley abstract (PMID 9854442): 'redundancy increasing with speed of generation'.
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed. (a) is correlational, and its p-value is internally inconsistent. (b) comes from one experiment with 36 people against computers. (c) is a small two-option task done under load. (d) is a random-generation task, not a game.
verified.design: Tier: peer-reviewed lab experiments against computers. S13: 3 × 36 Alberta students, course credit. S17 Exp 2: 12 Lethbridge undergraduates doing serial subtraction while playing a two-option Matching-Pennies-type task against an adaptive computer, with pauses of 1, 6.5 or 12 s; course credit. S18: random-generation experiments (abstract only).
verified.effect: r=0.202 (r² about 0.04). With the forced pause, lose-stay moved 7.7 pp toward 1/3 (Exp 3 only). Pause effect F(2,22)=17.1 (exact probabilities only in a figure). My calculation: against the Exp 3 post-loss pattern without the pause, the counter-throw 'play the hand their losing hand beats' nets +0.15 wins per round; with the forced pause only +0.01.
verified.implication: If the format allows a pause between rounds, take a few seconds after a loss before the next chant and do not let the opponent rush you; expect only small gains. A rushed opponent who just lost is the most predictable (see C13).
verified.caveats: (a) is correlational, and the author's word 'causal' rests on it. (b) is inconsistent across opponent types. (c) is a two-option, small-n, non-RPS task under cognitive load. (d) is not a game.

verified.statement: Ivan, Banks, Goodfellow & Gruber (Front Integr Neurosci 2018, 12:9) had adults count backwards by 3 from 999 while playing a two-option competitive task against an adaptive computer that punishes patterns (n=8 with load vs 8 without). The loaded group showed 30-40% more lose-shift (t(15)=4.59, p=2E-4, d=1.77), while win-stay did not change. Children aged 5-9 without load (n=11, 40 trials) showed raised lose-shift like the loaded adults (p=.004, d=1.45); children aged 11-13 did not. Lose-shift did not drift across the quarters of the 180-trial session (p's=.14-.99). Baddeley et al. 1998 (abstract) found that simple counting did not reduce randomness in key-press generation, but serial recall, category generation, concurrent digit generation and a fluid-intelligence test did.
verified.evidence: Ivan (PMC5852382): 'serial subtraction of 3 starting from 999 ... (n = 8), while a control group did not have this additional cognitive load (n = 8)'; 'two-tailed t-test: t (15) = 4.59, p = 2E-4, d = 1.77'; 'younger children (Dunnett's ... p = 0.004; d = 1.45)'; 'quartiles of trial number ... no difference in either lose-shift (RM ANOVAs, p's = 0.14-0.99)'. Abstract: 'increased by 30%-40%'. Rewards were on-screen 'Win $10' text only; participants received course credit, toys or movie vouchers. Baddeley abstract: 'whereas simple counting has no effect on randomness, serial recall, semantic category generation, and concurrent digit generation have substantial effects, and a concurrent fluid intelligence test has the greatest influence'.
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed. Very small groups, a two-option (not RPS) tablet task against a computer, and no real money.
verified.design: Tier: peer-reviewed lab experiments. S17: University of Lethbridge undergraduates; Exp 1 had 8 with load vs 8 without. Children aged 5–9 (11 included) and 11–13. Tablet task against an adaptive computer, 180 trials (40 for young children); course credit, toys or vouchers. S18: random-generation experiments (abstract only).
verified.effect: Lose-shift 30–40% higher under load (exact proportions only in figures); d=1.77 for adults, d=1.45 for children aged 5–9.
verified.implication: Crowd noise, cheering, keeping score, or tracking several opponents' patterns at once may push players toward reflexive lose-shift. Keep your own load low by deciding a simple plan in advance and tuning out the crowd. Expect a distracted opponent who just lost to avoid repeating that hand.
verified.caveats: Two-option task, not RPS. Very small groups. Serial subtraction is far more demanding than a chant. Transfer to live team RPS is untested.

verified.statement: In keypress RPS against random bots, players repeated a hand they had just lost with only about 17-30% of the time (typically 21-23%; chance 33.3%) and split the rest almost evenly between the other two hands. The data are transitions relative to each player's previous hand, pooled across hands, not Rock-specific. After losing with any hand X: X 23.4%, the hand that beats X 38.5%, the hand X beats 38.2% (Dyson 2021 Exp 1, no-credit condition). The corresponding figures were 21.46%, 39.13% and 39.41% in Forder & Dyson 2016. Lose-shift (about 74-83% on average) did not change with point values (+2/-1 or +1/-2) or when the opponent changed (78.93% change vs 79.70% repeat, F(1,78)=0.29, p=.59). A forced pause did lower it to 69.8% (Dyson 2021 Exp 3). Win-stay was flexible: it rose from 35.92% to 48.44% when wins were worth +2 points (points were not paid), and fell from 44.02% to 38.21% when the opponent changed (F(1,78)=6.95, p=.010). Against a player who just lost, throwing the hand their losing hand beats nets about +0.15 (Dyson) or +0.18 (Forder) wins per round, computed from these computer-task rates.
verified.evidence: Dyson 2021 Table 2, Exp 1 no credit, Lose: Stay 0.234, Upgrade 0.385, Downgrade 0.382; Exp 3 fixed credit Lose stay 0.302; lose-shift averages 77.23/80.18/73.86%. Dyson 2016 (PMC4740902): downgrade '(e.g., Rock followed by Scissors)', upgrade '(e.g., Rock followed by Paper)'. Forder (PMC5034336): '(39.13%, 39.41% and 21.46%, respectively)'; '(48.44% versus 35.92% ...)'; 'did not change the frequency of the lose-shift heuristic'. Srihaput et al. PsyArXiv R1 file (https://osf.io/82y5e): 'Win-stay ... (44.02% versus 38.21%; F[1,78] = 6.951 ... p = .010)'; 'lose-shift ... (78.93% versus 79.70%; F[1,78] = 0.292 ... p = .591)'; Exp 1 had two item-biased opponents (12 Rock/3 Paper/3 Scissors). My calculation: 0.385-0.234=+0.151; 0.3913-0.2146=+0.177.
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed, mostly one lab (Dyson), keypress tasks against computers, Canadian and UK students, no performance pay.
verified.design: Tier: peer-reviewed lab keypress experiments against computers. S13: 3 × 36 Alberta students. S14: 36 Sussex students, 450 trials; point schemes +1/−1/0 (baseline), +2/−1/0 (win-heavy), +1/−2/0 (lose-heavy); points not paid. S19: 80 students (40 at Sussex with a £25 voucher lottery; 40 at Alberta for course credit), 288 trials against 8 avatar opponents playing a random mix, no performance pay.
verified.effect: Repeat-after-loss about 17–30% vs 33.3% (−3 to −16 pp). Repeat-after-win +12.5 pp when wins were worth double; −5.8 pp when the opponent changed. Opponent change shifted lose-shift by only −0.8 pp (not significant). My calculation: against 23.4/38.5/38.2, throwing the hand that the opponent's losing hand beats (they lost with Rock, so you throw Scissors) nets about +0.15 wins per round; +0.18 with Forder's numbers.
verified.implication: In team or relay formats, a player who just lost will likely avoid repeating that hand, even against a new opponent. The counter is to throw the hand their losing throw beats. A player who just won a high-stakes point is more likely than usual to repeat it. Avoid showing this pattern yourself: after a loss, repeating the same hand is fine.
verified.caveats: Mostly one lab, computer opponents and Canadian/UK students. The only live face-to-face evidence in the same direction is from a two-gesture game (C19). This mapping belongs mainly to the sequential-pattern angle and should be cross-checked there.

verified.statement: Dyson & Asad (npj Science of Learning 2021, 6:19; published version) re-analysed 145 of 148 players facing unexploitable bots (Exps 1-4). Switching on both of the next two throws ('restlessness') was less likely after a loss two rounds earlier (34.29%) than after a win (38.28%) or a draw (36.68%). The same held against unexploitable bots in Exps 5-10 (32.71% vs 36.76% vs 35.96%, n=175). Staying twice after a win ('win-calmness') appeared only against exploitable bots. There was no multi-round 'tilt' after losses.
verified.evidence: Published version (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8222288/): 'Of the initial sample of 148, 145 data sets (97.97%) were retained'; 'restlessness was significantly less likely following losses (34.29%) relative to both wins (38.28%) and draws (36.68%)'; Exps 5-10: 'restlessness was significantly less likely following losses (32.71%) relative to both wins (36.76%) and draws (35.96%)'; abstract: 'evidence of win-calmness (but not loss-restlessness) when wins could be maximised (exploitable opponents)'.
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed re-analysis of 10 computer-RPS experiments (n=357 overall), all with computer opponents.
verified.design: Tier: peer-reviewed re-analysis (npj Science of Learning 2021) of 10 computer-RPS experiments. Experiments 1–4: 152 participants, 149 retained. Experiments 5–10: 208 participants facing exploiting or exploitable opponents.
verified.effect: Switching twice in a row: 34.27% after a loss vs 38.09% after a win (−3.8 pp).
verified.implication: The exploitable effect of a loss is concentrated in the very next throw. Don't assume an opponent on a losing streak becomes steadily more erratic or more predictable.
verified.caveats: Numbers come from the PsyArXiv preprint, and the published title differs. Computer opponents. 'Restlessness' here means two consecutive switches in any direction.

verified.statement: Leder, Häusser & Mojzisch (Psychoneuroendocrinology 2013, 38(9):1503-1511) gave participants a group stress test (the Trier Social Stress Test for Groups). Stressed participants then chose higher numbers in a beauty-contest game, 'indicating less strategizing', and cortisol mediated the effect. In a quasi-experiment before a real exam, the same authors (J Econ Psychol 2015, 49:133-140) found that 'stress impaired strategic reasoning in the beauty contest game'. No RPS study that manipulated stress or arousal was found.
verified.evidence: 2013 abstract (Europe PMC): 'participants under stress chose higher numbers in the beauty contest game than non-stressed participants, indicating less strategizing. This effect was mediated by the stress-induced increase in cortisol.' 2015 abstract (RePEc, https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/joepsy/v49y2015icp133-140.html): 'waiting to attend an exam ... The results showed that stress impaired strategic reasoning in the beauty contest game.' My own searches found no RPS stress, mood or arousal manipulation.
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed; abstracts only; German samples; a non-RPS game that requires no randomising.
verified.design: Tier: peer-reviewed lab experiment (Psychoneuroendocrinology) and quasi-experiment (Journal of Economic Psychology). German samples; N not given in the abstracts; not RPS.
verified.effect: Not available from the abstracts.
verified.implication: Inference only: under competition stress, players may fall back on simple habits (lose-shift, a favourite hand) instead of second-guessing. Keep your own plan simple and decided in advance.
verified.caveats: Abstract only. The beauty-contest game needs no randomization, so transfer to RPS is untested.

verified.statement: No controlled experiment on announcing an RPS throw was found. The closest analog is Brocas & Carrillo (Quantitative Economics 2022, 13(2):825-862): a 3-location hide-and-seek game with locations of unequal value, in which the hider sent a cheap-talk message (228 children aged 7-16 plus 34 USC adults; tablets; points exchanged for toys or gift cards). Hiders were 'excessively truthful', seekers had 'a slight tendency to (correctly) believe hiders', and 'messages have a small impact on outcomes'. Adult seekers would have lost 7.4% of payoffs by always following the message, while school-age seekers would have gained 4.9-34.8%. The 'Telegraph Your Throw' tip comes from a 2006 World RPS Society article with no data.
verified.evidence: Brocas & Carrillo working paper (http://isabellebrocas.org/Research/Hide.pdf), abstract: 'Hiders are excessively truthful in the messages they send while seekers have a slight tendency to (correctly) believe hiders. In general, however, messages have a small impact on outcomes.' Appendix: 'the naïve average in the school-age groups would still be 4.9% to 34.8% higher than their actual gains. Only adults would lose 7.4% of payoffs by following the Farmers' suggestion every time in every location.' Walker (2006, archived): '4 - Telegraph Your Throw ... if you announce rock, your opponent won't play paper'.
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed (August 2021 working-paper version read). Mostly children; not face-to-face; not RPS. The tip is anecdotal.
verified.design: Tier: peer-reviewed lab experiment (Quantitative Economics 2022; working-paper version read). Tablets, anonymous pairs; a game that is not strictly zero-sum, with 3 locations of known but unequal value; tokens exchanged for toys or cash. S11 and S27: organization and blog advice (anecdotal).
verified.effect: Messages had a 'small' effect on payoffs; adults would lose 7.4% by always believing them. No RPS effect size exists.
verified.implication: Announcing is an untested ploy. In adversarial play, messages tend to be discounted or ignored, so expect little effect either way. If your team's rules allow talking, treat it as a low-value gimmick, not a strategy.
verified.caveats: The analog game differs (unequal location values, mostly children, no face-to-face talk). Absence of RPS evidence is not evidence of no effect.

verified.statement: No RPS priming effect has been published. The only RPS priming study found is a 2017 Marshall University student poster by J. A. Muncy (planned N=40). It asked participants about their shirt colour to prime Scissors and reports a protocol and hypothesis but no results. In a non-adversarial magic-trick setting (Pailhès & Kuhn, PNAS 2020, 117(30):17675-17679; N=90), verbal and gestural primes led 17.8% of viewers to name the 3 of Diamonds, vs 0 of 23 without primes and a 1/52 chance rate (about ninefold). Aczel et al. 2012's idea that the umpire's announcement primes the third gesture is an untested hypothesis.
verified.evidence: Marshall abstract page (https://mds.marshall.edu/colaconf/2017/day1/24): design and hypothesis only. Pailhès (PMC7395500): 'Overall, 17.8% of the participants chose the three of diamonds'; '(0 out of 23 named the three of diamonds; SI Appendix)'; 'the force resulted in a ninefold increase'. Aczel 2012 §1: 'both players could be easily primed to show the third gesture in the next round'.
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed PNAS study, but a 52-option, non-adversarial setting. The poster has no data.
verified.design: Tier: peer-reviewed (PNAS 2020; 90 participants watching a live or video performance; accepted manuscript read) plus a student poster without data and organization advice.
verified.effect: Card forcing: 17.8% vs 1.9% chance (1/52, my calculation). Not RPS.
verified.implication: Priming an RPS opponent is unproven. A motivated, adversarial opponent with only 3 options is a poor fit for magicians' forcing techniques. Don't rely on it; at most it is harmless.
verified.caveats: Absence of evidence. Card-forcing effects may not transfer to RPS, and priming research in general has replication problems (noted by S23).

verified.statement: Naber, Vaziri Pashkam & Nakayama (PNAS 2013, 110(50):20046-20050) ran a face-to-face touchscreen 'whac-a-mole' race (25 pairs). Within-pair reaction times correlated at r=0.85. When a confederate alternated slow and fast blocks, 20 players slowed down and sped up with him (t(19)=9.41), even though each hit earned money. In Exp 3, players still followed the reaction-time pattern of an invisible, replayed opponent whose hits were shown only through on-screen cues.
verified.evidence: PMC3864297: '[r(23) = 0.85; P < 0.001]'; 'reaction time: t (19) = 9.41, P < 0.001'; Exp 2 pay was '1 cent per target'; Exp 3: 'Players only mimicked reaction times and not the move distance.'
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed. Live, money-incentivised, but not RPS: it measures movement-speed matching, not choice.
verified.design: Tier: peer-reviewed lab experiment (PNAS); live touchscreen race; money for out-scoring the opponent. Not RPS.
verified.effect: Within-pair reaction-time correlation r=0.85; players followed the confederate's tempo, t(19)=9.41.
verified.implication: Inference: the opponent's or the chant-caller's pace can pull yours along. If you want thinking time after a loss (C11), you have to actively hold your own rhythm rather than match theirs.
verified.caveats: This is matching of movement speed, not of hand choice. Transfer to RPS throw selection is untested.

verified.statement: In two face-to-face open/closed-hand datasets, players repeated their previous gesture more after winning than after losing: OR=1.23 (Z(12655)=5.81, p<.001) in Aczel et al. 2015 (Hungary, 102 students) and OR=1.16 (Z(8205)=3.46, p<.001) in a re-analysis of Belot et al.'s Oxford data (54 students). Sighted players switched after losses and stayed after wins. Blindfolded players tended to repeat their own previous gesture (OR=1.08), mainly after wins, and showed no switching preference after losses.
verified.evidence: Aczel 2015 accepted manuscript: 'winners of the previous game tended to stay with their previous gesture more readily than losers, OR = 1.23, Z(12655) = 5.81, p < .001'; 'sighted players behaved as predicted by CR: they switched gestures when they lost, while they stuck to their previous gesture after winning'; Belot data 'OR = 1.16, Z(8205) = 3.46, p < .001'; blind players 'did not seem to have a preference for switching or remaining with the previous gesture when they lost'.
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed. Face-to-face, small per-game pay, two-gesture game. The odds ratios are modest.
verified.design: Tier: peer-reviewed lab experiments, face-to-face human vs human, small cash per game. Aczel 2015's Hungarian dataset (102 students) and a re-analysis of Belot 2013's Oxford dataset (54 students).
verified.effect: Odds of repeating after a win vs after a loss: 1.23 and 1.16. Proportions are not reported in the text.
verified.implication: The win-stay/lose-shift tendency in C13 is not just a computer-screen artifact; it shows up in live hand play. Applying it to face-to-face team RPS is reasonable, with caution.
verified.caveats: Two-gesture game, not RPS. The odds ratios are modest, and the blindfold manipulation itself changed behaviour.

verifier_added.statement: A forced pause made players less predictable after losses but did not raise their win rate. In Dyson 2021 Exp 3 the bot was exploitable (it over-played one hand, 46 of 90). A mandatory extra keypress each round (about 400 ms) cut lose-shift from 77.48% to 69.80%, yet win rate was lowest in that condition: 33.5%, vs 35.1% with no pause and 37.3% when players chose their own pauses (variable vs fixed differed, F(2,70)=4.80, p=.011). Against a bot that exploited the player's own bias (Exp 2), the forced-pause win rate was also lowest: 31.3% vs 33.1% and 33.4%.
verifier_added.evidence: Dyson 2021 Sci Rep 11:2859 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7859242/), Exp 3 Results: 'wins did significantly vary as a function of credit conditions [F(2,70) = 4.80, MSE = 0.003, p = 0.011 ...], and were increased in the variable credit condition relative to the fixed credit condition (37.28% vs. 33.49%; see Table 1)'. Table 1 outcome distribution, win: Exp 3 No 0.351, Variable 0.373, Fixed 0.335; Exp 2 No 0.331, Variable 0.334, Fixed 0.313. Lose-shift 'no credit (77.48%) varying from fixed (69.80%)'.
verifier_added.study_design: 36 University of Alberta students per experiment, course credit, 270 keypress RPS rounds against a computer (Exp 2: bot exploiting the player's item bias; Exp 3: bot with a 51% item bias). Credit condition varied within subjects.
verifier_added.effect_size: Win rate with the forced pause: -1.6 pp vs no pause (Exp 3) and -1.8 pp (Exp 2). Voluntary pause: +2.2 pp vs no pause (Exp 3). Lose-shift with the forced pause: -7.7 pp.
verifier_added.strategic_implication: Do not expect pausing after a loss to win you more rounds by itself. It may make your next throw less predictable, which matters only against an opponent who exploits lose-shift; it does not help you read the opponent.
verifier_added.caveats: Computer opponents and no performance pay. The forced pause also added an extra motor response. The Exp 3 bot did not punish lose-shift, so lower predictability could not pay off there.

verifier_added.statement: Slowing down after a loss marks successful exploitation, but it has not been shown to cause it. Against exploitable bots, players with higher win-loss rates slowed more after losses than after wins (r=.647, .577 and .575 in Exps 1-3 of Dyson et al. 2018). Against random bots the usual speeding after losses appeared (Exps 2-3 pooled: wins 672 ms, losses 552 ms, draws 504 ms). The authors call the data 'correlational rather than causal'.
verifier_added.evidence: Dyson, Sundvall, Forder & Douglas 2018 accepted manuscript (Sussex figshare item 23456759, file 41165141): 'individual win-lose rates were plotted against RT differences between lose and win trials during exploitation conditions in Experiment 1 (r = .647, p < .001), Experiment 2 (r = .577, p < .001) and Experiment 3 (r = .575, p = .001)'; 'Although the data are correlational rather than causal in nature'; pooled ANOVA: 'against unexploitable opponents, RTs following wins (672 ms) were slower than those following losses (552 ms) or draws (504 ms)'.
verifier_added.study_design: University of Sussex. Exp 1: N=50 (38 analysed), prize draw. Exp 2: N=40 (35), course credit or £10. Exp 3: N=40 (30), points converted to money at 10p per point in high-value blocks. Keypress RPS against random and exploitable bots.
verifier_added.effect_size: r of about .58-.65 between post-loss slowing and win-loss rate against exploitable bots. Against random bots, post-loss RT was 120 ms faster than post-win RT.
verifier_added.strategic_implication: Players who have a working model of the opponent naturally slow down after an unexpected loss. Use the gap after a loss to recall the opponent's recent throws rather than simply waiting; MF1 shows that waiting alone did not help.
verifier_added.caveats: Correlational, and reverse causation is plausible: for a player who is winning, losses are rare and draw attention (an orienting account discussed in Dyson 2024). Computer opponents.

verifier_added.statement: In live play, choices track the opponent's previous gesture in a goal-directed way, and this sequential bias can masquerade as automatic imitation. In Aczel et al. 2015, sighted players paid to match tended to replay the opponent's previous gesture, and those paid to mismatch avoided it (three-way interaction OR=1.83, p<.001; same pattern in Belot's Oxford data, OR=1.64, p<.001). Blindfolded players repeated their own previous gesture mainly after wins (OR=1.14, p=.015). Once these biases were controlled, the remaining online-matching effect (match incentive, lead of at least 133 ms) shrank to OR=1.22 (p=.060), and a Bayes factor of 0.186 favoured no automatic imitation.
verifier_added.evidence: Aczel et al. 2015 accepted manuscript (https://spiral.imperial.ac.uk/handle/10044/1/32477): 'significant three-way interaction between the task and role of the player and the outcome of the preceding game, OR = 1.83, Z(12646) = 4.19, p < .001'; Belot dataset 'OR = 1.64, Z(8196) = 4.44, p < .001'; 'tendency of blind players to stick with their previous gesture is mostly present when they have won in the preceding game, OR = 1.14, Z(3110) = 2.42, p < .015'; 'OR from 1.28 to 1.22 ... p = .060, one tailed'; 'B(mismatching<matching)=0.186'. Belot Table 5: full-sample automatic-imitation coefficient 0.023 (SE 0.021), not significant.
verifier_added.study_design: 102 Hungarian students; 34 triad sessions, 32 analysed; hidden video; 10 HUF per game won. Re-analysis of Belot's 54 Oxford students. Face-to-face open/closed-hand Matching Pennies.
verifier_added.effect_size: Odds ratios of 1.14-1.83 for history-dependent choices. The residual online-imitation effect is not significant once history is controlled.
verifier_added.strategic_implication: Face-to-face, the usable information is the opponent's previous throw and its outcome, not the hand in motion. Track history (what they threw and whether they won); don't try to read or react to the hand at delivery.
verifier_added.caveats: Two-gesture game, not RPS. Only the accepted manuscript was read. History effects are modest in size.

verifier_added.statement: In Ivan et al. 2018, mental load rather than speed drove the extra lose-shift. Adults doing serial subtraction and children aged 5-9 took longer per trial than unloaded adults (F(3,45)=4.37, p=.008; children d=1.28, loaded adults d=1.02), yet showed more lose-shift. Win counts did not differ (F(3,45)=1.61, p=.199). Within the loaded group, a longer gap after feedback reduced lose-shift (decay over 1-12 s).
verifier_added.evidence: Ivan et al. 2018 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5852382/): 'the groups with increased lose-shift responding have an increased mean trial duration over the first 40 trials (one-way ANOVA; main effect of group: F (3,45) = 4.366, p = 0.008 ...). The 5-9 years old and cognitively loaded adults tend to be slower than the non-counting adults (... children: p = 0.012, d = 1.28; +load adults: p = 0.028, d = 1.02)'; 'the number of wins was not affected by load or age (F (3,45) = 1.61, p = 0.199)'; decay: 'F (2,22) = 17.1, p = 3E-5'.
verifier_added.study_design: University of Lethbridge. First 40 trials compared across unloaded adults, loaded adults, 5-9-year-olds (n=11) and 11-13-year-olds. Two-option tablet task against an adaptive computer; course credit, toys or vouchers.
verifier_added.effect_size: d of about 1.0-1.3 for slower trials in the high-lose-shift groups; d=1.39-1.45 for their raised lose-shift.
verifier_added.strategic_implication: Slowing your pace will not protect you if your attention is taken up. Lower your load by pre-deciding a simple plan and ignoring the crowd and the score. A distracted opponent may lose-shift even when moving slowly.
verifier_added.caveats: Small groups, a two-option (not RPS) task, and fictitious money. The between-group link between slowness and lose-shift is confounded with load and age.

dead_ends: Lead 1 (Cook et al.): the citation checks out (online 20 Jul 2011, print 2012, Proc R Soc B 279(1729):780–786). One correction to common summaries: the key blind–sighted vs blind–blind test (t13=1.72, 'p=0.05 one-tailed') falls below the one-tailed critical value of 1.771 (S2, S3). Two direct replications (Hungary, Japan) and a mini-meta-analysis found no effect.

Lead 2: no peer-reviewed study was found that tests whether human observers can predict an RPS throw from early arm or hand movement or from pre-shaping during the countdown (temporal-occlusion designs). Only machine systems exist: the University of Tokyo janken robot and an EMG preprint. The robot lab gives about 60 ms for a human hand to form its shape; no study gives a lead time that human eyes can use.

Lead 3: the Dyson (2021) title is correct ('...against exploiting and exploitative opponents'; the lab page says 'exploitable'). The idea that lose-shift responses are themselves faster is not supported: Forder & Dyson 2016 found a strategy main effect of F<1. Dyson (2024) reinterprets post-loss speeding as post-win slowing. Dyson's (2021) 'causal' wording rests on a correlation of r=0.202.

Lead 4: no RPS study was found that manipulated stress, arousal or emotion (e.g., the Trier Social Stress Test, cortisol, skin conductance, induced anger) and measured predictability. The nearest evidence is cognitive load in a two-option task (S17) and stress studies using the beauty-contest game (S21).

Lead 5: no controlled experiment on announcing throws, cheap talk or bluffing in RPS was found. No RPS priming study with results was found; the Marshall University 2017 student poster gives only its protocol. 'Talk Paper Scissors' (a phone RPS game) reports no data. 'Telegraph your throw' and 'Suggest a throw' trace back to a 2006 World RPS Society article by G. Walker with no data.

Lead 6: nothing was found on handedness, alcohol, audience or social pressure in RPS, and no data on chant-start effects (e.g., Japanese '最初はグー'). On fatigue, there is only Cook's speculation and the absence of any drift across session quarters in Ivan et al. Belot's claim that 'bobbing' (Aczel 2012 procedure) reduces asynchrony is an untested conjecture.
The current World RPS Society rules page (worldrps.com) returns 404; the 2017 Wayback Machine copy was used. Its '29.6% scissors in competition play' figure is unsourced.
Omori et al. (1999), the primary source of the late-janken reaction times (158.6/224.7/323.0 ms), was not accessed; the values come from Fukunaga et al. (2005).

Kayhan et al. 2022 (face-to-face fNIRS hyperscanning RPS) reports no behavioural accuracy for predicting the opponent in the main text. Moerel et al. 2025 (EEG hyperscanning) seated players in separate rooms, had no performance bonus, and found no behavioural predictability difference between match winners and losers. Neither was usable for face-to-face strategy claims.

Full texts not available: MDPI (Srihaput et al. 2020) returned 403, so PsyArXiv preprint numbers were used. Dyson & Asad 2021 was published under a different title than the preprint read. The Aczel et al. 2015 publisher PDF was not accessed; the Imperial Spiral accepted manuscript was used.
No official Korean rule text on late throwing (늦게 내기) was found. Korean academic work found covers only the probability of team RPS formats (Cho 2019), not player behaviour.

Not read: Hofree et al. 2012 (ICDL; facial mimicry of an android in an RPS-like setting) and Short et al. 2010 (HRI; robot that cheats by changing its gesture after seeing the human's). Both are peripheral to choice strategy.
open_questions: Does any copying or draw effect appear among Korean players, and does it matter under the tie-replay rules typical of team events, where draws cost nothing?
Does a deliberate pause of several seconds between rounds reduce lose-shift in live human-vs-human RPS? Ivan et al.'s pause effect comes from a two-option task done under cognitive load.
Do crowd noise, team cheering or score-keeping act as cognitive load that increases lose-shift in live team competitions?
Does announcing a throw ever change opponents' throw frequencies or win rates in RPS between adults? No data exist.

How does the team format change which face-to-face effects matter: simultaneous multi-player throws (e.g., Cho 2019) vs relay one-on-one matches where opponents change between rounds (relevant to Srihaput et al.)?
Are experienced or expert players less prone to lose-shift and to copying? Belot's early-vs-late games result suggests copying fades after about 10 games against the same opponent.

Are there visible pre-shaping cues (fist tightness, finger movement) that humans could learn to read within the roughly 60 ms hand-formation window, and could that ever be done within the timing rules?

Do the post-loss speed and lose-shift effects, measured mostly in one lab (Dyson) with computer opponents and little money at stake, hold up in live, incentivised human-vs-human RPS beyond the two-gesture hand game?

condensed.angle: E. Team formats: Korean 단체전 rules, multi-player RPS math, group decisions, scouting/observation, opponent switching, team coordination

verified.statement: Cho (2019, Korean J. Applied Statistics 32(2):277-289) names two formats as the most common (가장 보편적인) ways to pick one of two teams by RPS. (1) One representative per team plays 1:1. (2) Members play in a set order and the winner keeps playing until one team has no players left (a winner-stays relay). The paper offers (3), all members of both teams throwing at once, only as another possible method (다른 방법으로는 ... 생각해 볼 수 있다). Format 3 is decided by rule I (the team with more winners wins; equal counts mean the winners replay) or rule II (a team wins when every winner of a throw is its member; otherwise only the winners replay). Its conclusion says four players throwing at once to pick sides in doubles has become common (보편화). Cho (2010, KJAS 23(6):1217-1224) says club doubles usually send one captain each to play 1:1, and that all four players 'sometimes' (더러) throw together to remove the psychological burden on the representative. The context is deciding which team attacks first or which side it takes before a sports match, not an RPS tournament.
verified.evidence: Cho 2019 PDF (https://koreascience.kr/article/JAKO201919341608265.pdf), pp. 277-278: '가장 보편적인 방법은 대표로 한명씩 나온 두 명의 승부에 따라 결정하는 방식과 모든 참가자가 한명씩 순번을 정해서 이긴 사람이 계속하여 어느 한 팀에 가위바위보게임에 참가할 사람이 더 이상 없는 경우 상대팀이 이기는 방식이 있을 수 있다. 다른 방법으로는 전체가 동시에 참여하는 방법을 생각해 볼 수 있다.' §2.2 defines 승부결정방법 I and II as stated. 결언, p. 288: '요즈음 각 두 명씩 벌이는 복식경기에서 4명이 동시에 가위바위보게임을 통하여 진영을 결정하는 것은 보편화 되어 있다.' The abstract describes using RPS 'before the main game to determine which team will begin first'. Cho 2010 PDF (https://koreascience.kr/article/JAKO201007049666093.pdf), p. 1217: '각 팀의 주장격인 사람이 1명씩 나와서 가위바위보를 통하여 공격 팀을 결정하곤 한다 ... 이러한 심리적인 요소를 제거하기 위해 더러 동호인의 복식경기에서는 4명 모두가 동시에 가위바위보를 하여 승부를 결정하곤 한다.' Cho 2020 (p. 579) repeats the list and mentions tennis doubles.
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed Korean statistics journal (single author, three related papers). The format descriptions are introductory assertions with no survey data.
verified.design: Combinatorial probability papers (no participants), Korea. The formats are described in the introduction and conclusion.
verified.effect: Not applicable (descriptive).
verified.implication: First confirm which format and tie rule the event uses. Representative, relay and points formats reduce to 1:1 bouts, where the team levers are ordering and scouting (C9, C10, C13). Simultaneous formats under rule II reward coordination within the team (C6).
verified.caveats: The prevalence statements are the author's assertions, not survey data. Rules at a specific event may differ.

verified.statement: Korean and Japanese wiki and guide sources describe several recreational group RPS formats. (a) A leader plays everyone at once. In one version, losers and tied players are eliminated: Librewiki defines 가위바위보 단체전 as one person presenting a hand and everyone who ties or loses being eliminated, and a Japanese party guide (45mix) uses the same rule. In a slower variant, only losers are eliminated. (b) In 징검다리 가위바위보 (playland.kr), each team has 5-6 players; the bout winner keeps running, the loser leaves the field and the losing team sends its next runner, and the first team to occupy the opposing base wins. (c) 삼세번 means best two of three (Encyclopedia of Korean Culture). (d) For large groups, players split into subgroups (Korean Wikipedia) or play 'XX 내면 탈락' (Namu Wiki). These are anecdotal sources, not official rulebooks.
verified.evidence: Librewiki (https://librewiki.net/wiki/가위바위보), 변칙 section: '단체전(한 사람이 대표로 가위/바위/보 중 하나를 제시하여, 그것에 비기거나 지면 탈락하는 방식)'. 45mix (https://45mix.net/jyankentaikai/): 'リーダーひとり対、子ども全員でじゃんけんをします。' 'じゃんけんに負けた子と、あいこの子は、その場に座ります。' and the slower variant 「じゃんけんに負けた子だけ座る」. playland.kr: '참여인원은 팀당 5-6명 정도를 추천드립니다'; '이긴 주자는 이어서 달려가고, 진 주자는 경기장 밖으로 나갑니다'; '상대팀보다 먼저 상대팀의 본진을 점거하면 승리합니다'. Encykorea E0000295: ''삼세번'이라 하여 세 번 계속해서 두 번 이상 이기는 것으로 정하기도 한다'. Namu 변형 가위바위보: ''XX 내면 탈락, 가위바위보!'로 변형시키는 경우도 있다'. Korean Wikipedia (raw wikitext): '세 명 이상이서 할 때에는 모두 같은 모양을 내거나, 가위, 바위, 보가 모두 다 나오면 비긴다' and '사람이 많은 경우, 나누어서 하는 것이 편리하다.'
verified.reliability: Community wikis, an encyclopedia entry and recreation guides: anecdotal, with no prevalence data.
verified.design: Wiki, encyclopedia and game-guide web pages from Korea and Japan; no data.
verified.effect: Not applicable (descriptive).
verified.implication: The tie rule changes the whole plan. Against a random host, each player survives a round with probability 1/3 when ties eliminate (rule A) and 2/3 when only losses do (rule B); see C7 and C8. Under 'XX 내면 탈락', throwing the hand that loses to the banned hand is weakly dominant. For example, if Rock is banned, Scissors beats the only other legal hand, Paper. In the stepping-stone relay, running speed also decides where bouts happen, so the elimination maths in C9 applies only loosely.
verified.caveats: These are anecdotal wiki and guide sources, not official rulebooks, and prevalence is unknown. A search snippet described '일당백 가위바위보' (only those who beat the leader stay standing; with few people only losers sit), but its Daum blog page is defunct and could not be opened.

verified.statement: WRPSA's standard match is best of 3 ('first to 2 decisive-round wins'), with ties replayed 'as many times as it takes'. The 2019 PBR Rock Paper Scissors Indy Championship (USA) used teams of exactly three. Each member played a best-of-three head-to-head, each individual win scored one team point, and the first team to two points advanced ('Structure your team order accordingly'). The final used longer 'best of three of five' battles. Stalemates were replayed with no limit, play used a three-prime shoot, and non-sanctioned throws meant automatic disqualification.
verified.evidence: WRPSA (https://wrpsa.com/how-to-play): 'Same throw = Tie - Play again. As many times as it takes.'; 'Best of 3 WRPSA standard match: first to 2 decisive-round wins.' PBR Indy rules (https://mokbpresents.com/rock-paper-scissors-indy/official-rules/): 'Teams will consist of exactly three members per team.'; 'Each preliminary round will consist of a 'best of three' head to head competition of each team member (3 head to head individual battles, best of three each). Each individual winner will score one point for his/her team. First team to win two points wins the match ... Structure your team order accordingly.'; '6.3 In the case of a stalemate ... the game must be replayed. There are no limits to the number of stalemates'; 'Any use of Dynamite, Bird, Well, Spock ... will result in automatic disqualification. Three prime shoot (i.e., 1,2,3, then deliver your throw on 4).'
verified.reliability: Official event and organization rule pages (USA), not Korean. Descriptive only.
verified.design: Organization and event rule pages (USA); no data.
verified.effect: Not applicable (descriptive).
verified.implication: When ties are replayed, a tie costs nothing, unlike host games where a tie can eliminate you. In points formats the team levers are who plays and which matchups you can scout, not the batting order as such (C10).
verified.caveats: Rules are specific to these events and are not Korean. I found no World RPS Society or USA RPS League team rules.

verified.statement: With n players throwing independently and uniformly, a round is decisive (exactly two hand types shown) with probability 3(2^n-2)/3^n: 0.667 for n=2 and n=3, 0.519 (n=4), 0.370 (5), 0.255 (6), 0.116 (8), 0.052 (10) and 0.0009 (20). The expected throws until the first decisive round are 1.5, 1.5, 1.93, 2.70, 3.92, 8.61, 19.3 and 1108. If losers retire, the expected rounds to a single winner are 4.49 (n=5), 24.35 (n=10) and 1142.9 (n=20), growing like (1/3)(3/2)^n (Maehara & Ueda 2000; Fuchs, Hwang & Itoh 2017).
verified.evidence: Independent recomputation (c4_multi.py) by brute force for n=2..8 matches the formula exactly. The recursion gives E[W_5]=4.4857, E[W_10]=24.3496, E[W_20]=1142.90 and E[W_30]=64201 against (1/3)(1.5)^30=63917. Fuchs et al. (arXiv 1507.08145, p. 4) tabulate E(Y_n) = 1.5, 2.25, 3.21, 4.49, 6.22, 8.65, 12.1 for n=2..8 and state 'E(Y_n) ~ (1/3)(3/2)^n'. Section 3 says 'for p1 = p2 = p3 = 1/3, we have ρ = 2/3 and ν = 3 and one recovers the main result from [31]'. Maehara & Ueda abstract (Cambridge Core, JAP 37(2):601-605): '(2/3)^n W_n is asymptotically ... exponential distribution with mean 1/3'. Cho 2010 p. 1221: '6!/4! × 3 + 6!/(2!3!) × 6 + 6!/(2!2!2!) + 3 = 543' out of 729. Cho 2019 Table 2.2: p00 = 39/81. Namu §9 prints the equivalent form (2^n-2)/3^(n-1).
verified.reliability: Exact mathematics, backed by two peer-reviewed probability papers (JAP) and Cho's counts. Assumes independent uniform throws.
verified.design: Mathematical derivation, exact enumeration in Python, and peer-reviewed probability papers.
verified.effect: The decisive-round probability falls from 0.667 (2-3 players) to 0.255 (6) and 0.052 (10).
verified.implication: Formats where many people throw at once mostly produce ties, which is why organizers switch to host-vs-everyone or subgroups. In simultaneous team-vs-team play with 3 or more per side, expect several throws per decision (C5), so a coordination plan has to cover several throws.
verified.caveats: Assumes independent, uniform throws. Correlated throws (imitation, herding) change tie rates. I found no paper that prints '3(2^n-2)/3^n' verbatim; it follows from Fuchs et al.'s definitions and matches Cho's counts.

verified.statement: When all members of both teams throw at once, the expected number of throws to a decision grows quickly with team size. Under rule I (more winners wins) it is 1.5 (1v1), 33/14≈2.36 (2v2) and 972/217≈4.48 (3v3) (Cho 2010). Under rule II (a team wins when only its members win) it is 2 (2v1), 41/14≈2.93 (2v2) and 75/28≈2.68 (3v1) (Cho 2019). The exact values for 3v2 and 3v3 under rule II are 57/14≈4.07 and 5031/868≈5.80; Cho 2019 prints ≈3.93 and either 5.78 or 5.49.
verified.evidence: I independently recomputed every value by exact recursion over all hand profiles (c5_cho.py): rule II (2,1)=2, (2,2)=41/14, (3,1)=75/28, (3,2)=57/14, (3,3)=5031/868; rule I (2,2)=33/14, (3,3)=972/217. Monte Carlo with 400k games gave 4.071 for (3,2) and 5.791 for (3,3). Cho 2019 PDF: Table 2.4 gives (0,1)=6/243 and (1,0)=9/243, while eq. 2.11 weights 103/28 by 9/243 and 55/14 by 6/243. Result 2.4 gives 9909/2520, Result 2.5 gives 150579/26040≈5.782604, and the derivation of eq. 2.14 gives 9531/1736≈5.49. Cho 2010 eqs. 2.2 and 2.4 give 99/42≈2.36 and 34992/7812=4.48.
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed combinatorics with internal arithmetic errors; my recomputation is exact and confirmed by simulation.
verified.design: Combinatorial derivation (Cho) plus my own exact rational recursion over all hand profiles.
verified.effect: 3v3 simultaneous play takes ≈4.5 throws (rule I) to ≈5.8 throws (rule II), against 1.5 for 1v1.
verified.implication: Simultaneous formats run long, which gives intra-team coordination (C6) more throws to work with. Do not build a plan around a single throw.
verified.caveats: Assumes independent random throws. Cho 2019's (3,2) and (3,3) figures appear to contain transcription or arithmetic errors.

verified.statement: Derived result (exact recursion plus Monte Carlo). In simultaneous team-against-team RPS, coordination within the team matters under both of Cho's rules once a team has 3 or more members, and the orientation of the split is what counts. With 2 per side under rule II (a team wins when only its members win), showing two different hands wins 0.583 against an independently random team. Herding on one hand wins 0.333, and against a herding team the two-hand split wins 0.75. With 2 per side under rule I (more winners wins), every composition gives 0.50. With 3 per side, the sweep's random-orientation 2+1 split gives 0.576 under rule II and 0.50 under rule I. The best composition is two members on a hand X and one on the hand X beats (Rock-Rock-Scissors, Paper-Paper-Rock or Scissors-Scissors-Paper), with X chosen at random. It wins 0.684 (rule II) and 0.6875 (rule I) against a random team, and 0.875 (rule II) or 0.50 (rule I) against a herding team. The reverse orientation (two on X, one on the hand that beats X) wins only 0.469 (rule II) or 0.3125 (rule I). With 4 per side, 3 on X plus 1 on the hand X beats wins 0.779 (rule II) and 0.859 (rule I). Herding on one hand gives 0.25 (rule II, 3v3) against random play. A team showing all three hands forces endless ties.
verified.evidence: My exact recursion (c6_coord.py) reproduces the sweep's numbers for its own strategies. Rule II, 2v2: same 0.50/0.25/0.333, different 0.75/0.50/0.583. Rule II, 3v3: same 0.5/0.1875/0.25, different 0.8125/0.5/0.576. Rule I gives 0.5 for all three. An optimisation over all compositions (c6_opt.py) shows that the best composition against a random team is RRS-type: 3v3 rule II 175/256=0.6836, rule I 11/16=0.6875; RRP-type gives 0.469 and 0.3125; 4v4 RRRS-type gives 0.779 and 0.859. Monte Carlo (200k games): rule I 0.6876, rule II 0.6837. Hand check for rule I (our R,R,S against 3 random players): the throw is decisive only if no opponent shows Paper (8/27). Rock then wins, with our 2 winners against their k Rocks: k≤1 is a win (4/27), k=2 is a 2v2 replay worth 0.5 (3/27), and k=3 is a loss (1/27), giving (4+1.5)/8 = 0.6875. 3v3 payoff matrix (c6_matrix.py), BEAT row against SAME/BEAT/LOSE/random-orientation/independent: rule I 0.5/0.5/1.0/0.75/0.6875; rule II 0.875/0.5/0.75/0.625/0.684. BEAT is a best response to itself among these strategies (0.5). Rules are as defined in Cho 2019 §2.2 and Cho 2010.
verified.reliability: Exact mathematics verified two ways (exact enumeration and simulation). No human data; assumes the opponent's throws are independent of ours.
verified.design: Exact probability computation and simulation, assuming the opponent's throws are independent of ours. No human data.
verified.effect: +8.3 percentage points (2v2) and +7.6 points (3v3) over 50% against random opponents; herding costs 16.7 and 25 points.
verified.implication: If the event uses the 'only one team has winners' rule, agree before each throw that no two teammates show the same hand and that the team never shows all three. Choose the hand pair with a random device, such as a die. Under 'more winners wins', coordinating within the team gives nothing.
verified.caveats: This is derived, not tested on people. It needs the rules to allow secret coordination, and it assumes opponents cannot predict which pair of hands you will use. Rule variants change the results.

verified.statement: Derived result. Against a uniformly random host, a team that needs at least one member standing after k rounds should split its surviving members evenly across R/P/S every round. Under rule A (only those who beat the host survive): n=10, k=2 gives 1.000 (even split), 0.692 (independent) and 0.111 (herding); n=20, k=3 gives 0.741, 0.530 and 0.037. Under rule B (beating or tying survives): n=5, k=4 gives 0.827, 0.667 and 0.198; n=10, k=5 gives 0.959, 0.756 and 0.132. An exhaustive dynamic programme over all allocations finds the even split optimal for n=3, 5, 10, 20 and k=1-5. Expected survivors are the same for every strategy.
verified.evidence: Independent exact DP (c7_host.py) reproduces every cell the sweep lists: rule A n=3 k1 .704/1/.333 ... n=20 k5 .079/.082; rule B n=3 k2 .829/1.000 ... n=20 k5 .941/1.000. In every case the optimum equals the even split. Independent play gives 1-(1-3^-k)^n under rule A and 1-(1-(2/3)^k)^n under rule B; herding gives (1/3)^k and (2/3)^k.
verified.reliability: Exact mathematics. Assumes the host's hand is independent of the team's plan and that the rules allow pre-assigned hands.
verified.design: Exact calculation. Assumes the host throws uniformly at random and independently of the team's plan.
verified.effect: Up to +31 percentage points (rule A, n=10, k=2) and +20 points (rule B, n=10, k=5) over independent play.
verified.implication: In 사회자 vs 전원 formats where the team needs at least one survivor, assign hands in advance so survivors are spread evenly over R/P/S, and re-split the survivors every round. Never let teammates converge on a 'popular' hand.
verified.caveats: Derived, not empirical. The rules may forbid coordination. With an even split, at least ⌊m/3⌋ of m survivors remain under rule A, and at least m-⌈m/3⌉ under rule B, whatever the host throws. If the host is predictable, concentrating on the counter-hand could do better but is riskier.

verified.statement: Derived result (simulation). In a last-one-standing game against a uniformly random host, where a round that would eliminate everyone is replayed, a team that splits its surviving members evenly over R/P/S every round produces the final survivor more often than its head-count share. With 10 of 40 players: about 0.30 (ties eliminate) or 0.29 (only losses eliminate), against a 0.25 share. With 10 of 100: about 0.11, against 0.10. With 3 of 30: about 0.106, against 0.10. Independent play reproduces the head-count share.
verified.evidence: My own simulation (c8_crowd.py, 100k games per cell, SE ≈0.0014 at 0.25 and ≈0.001 at 0.10): 40/10 ties-out 0.3019 and losses-only 0.2906; 100/10 0.1105 and 0.1081; 30/3 0.1068 and 0.1059. Independent play: 0.2497, 0.2495, 0.0981, 0.1007, 0.0982, 0.1002. These agree with the sweep's 0.303, 0.290, 0.109, 0.107, 0.106 and 0.105 within simulation error.
verified.reliability: Monte Carlo verified independently. No human data.
verified.design: Monte Carlo simulation. Assumes a random host and that the other participants play independently.
verified.effect: Relative gain of about +5% to +21% over the head-count share; larger when the team is a bigger fraction of the room.
verified.implication: Coordination still helps when the prize is 'last one standing', but much less than when the goal is 'any survivor after k rounds' (C7).
verified.caveats: Simulation only. Results depend on the void-round rule and on the host being random. Other teams coordinating would erode the gain.

verified.statement: Derived result. If each bout is won with constant probability p (ties replayed), a winner-stays relay between two teams of n is the same as a best-of-(2n-1) series: P(win) = P(Bin(2n-1, p) ≥ n). At p = 0.50/0.52/0.55/0.60, a relay gives 0.500/0.537/0.593/0.683 for n=3, 0.500/0.549/0.621/0.733 for n=5 and 0.500/0.558/0.644/0.771 for n=7. A points format (each pair plays once) gives 0.500/0.530/0.575/0.648 for n=3, 0.500/0.537/0.593/0.683 for n=5 and 0.500/0.544/0.608/0.710 for n=7. One representative playing best-of-3 wins p²(3-2p): 0.530, 0.575 and 0.648. Batzilis et al.'s experienced-player first-throw rates (34.66% wins, 33.17% losses, p≈0.511) give 0.527 for a 5-person relay; their model best response (41.66%/27.37%, p≈0.604) gives 0.741.
verified.evidence: Exact binomial sums (c9_relay.py), with a Monte Carlo relay simulation for n=5, p=0.55 giving 0.6196 against an exact 0.6214. Batzilis et al. 2019 Table 5 (PDF via https://knowledge.uchicago.edu/records/jfcf3-13r07): 'Experienced Sample 34.66 32.17 33.17 1.49'; 'Best Response to Predicted Play 41.66 30.97 27.37 14.29'. Cho 2020 Theorem 2.2 independently derives the number of relay bouts as a race to m wins, P(N=i)=C(i-1,m-1)(1/2)^(i-1).
verified.reliability: Exact mathematics. The illustrative p comes from a large peer-reviewed field dataset (online first throws, no money).
verified.design: Exact calculation, with per-bout p illustrated from a field dataset (S15).
verified.effect: A 5-person relay turns p=0.55 into 0.621 and p=0.60 into 0.733. A realistic experienced-player edge (p≈0.511) gives only 0.527.
verified.implication: Formats with more bouts amplify a real edge, but if everyone plays randomly every format is 50:50. Measured human edges are tiny, so structural levers (C6-C8) and avoiding exploitable habits matter more than 'reading' skill.
verified.caveats: Assumes p is constant and bouts are independent. Batzilis's rates come from first throws in online play with no money; in-person edges may differ.

verified.statement: Derived result. In a winner-stays relay, the batting order does not change the team's win probability when bout probabilities follow a Bradley-Terry strength model, or when each player has the same edge against every opponent. Across 200 random 3-5-player cases the largest spread across orders was 4.4×10^-16. Order can matter when edges are matchup-specific. Example: one member has a 0.65 edge only against y1, and y1 leads the other team. The team then wins 0.556 when that member goes first and 0.509 when they go last; averaged over a random opposing order, every order gives 0.531. With several matchup-specific edges, order can still matter even when the opposing order is unknown: in 3v3 with bout probabilities between 0.35 and 0.65, the effect is up to about 1.7 points, and with extreme edges about 18 points. So order matters mainly, not only, when the opposing order is known. With realistic RPS edges (about 1-2 points per bout), order effects are negligible.
verified.evidence: My own recursion (c10_order.py): BT max spread 4.44e-16, per-player uniform edges give no spread, and the single-edge example reproduces 0.5563, 0.5094 and 0.5312 averaged. Arbitrary matrices with a known opposing order reach a spread of 0.65 (entries 0.05-0.95). With the opposing order averaged out, the spread reaches 0.185 (entries 0.05-0.95, n=3-4). In c10_example3.py (3v3, entries 0.35-0.65) our-order averages range from 0.5497 to 0.5666. In 2v2, order never matters once the opposing order is averaged.
verified.reliability: Exact mathematics. No empirical data on matchup-specific RPS edges.
verified.design: Exact calculation.
verified.effect: Zero effect without matchup-specific information. Up to about ±5 percentage points in the scouting example, and up to 39 points in arbitrary matrices.
verified.implication: Do not agonize over batting order unless you hold opponent-specific scouting and can see or predict the opposing order. If you have both, place the member with the matchup edge where they will face that opponent.
verified.caveats: Derived, not empirical. Assumes bout outcomes are independent of history; momentum and tilt are not modelled.

verified.statement: Across economics experiments, small groups that deliberate choose closer to game-theoretic predictions than individuals do (Charness & Sutter 2012; Kugler, Kausel & Kocher 2012). In beauty-contest games, groups were not smarter per se but learned faster, and outperformed individuals when the two competed (Kocher & Sutter 2005). With three-person teams (Sutter, Czermak & Feri 2013, N=192), Nash play was about 50% against about 40% for individuals (49.30% vs 40.97%), and the estimated share of strategic types was 62% against 40%. None of these studies used RPS.
verified.evidence: RePEc abstract (https://ideas.repec.org/a/aea/jecper/v26y2012i3p157-76.html): 'groups are more likely to make choices that follow standard game-theoretic predictions, while individuals are more likely to be influenced by biases, cognitive limitations, and social considerations.' PubMed 26301530: 'results are quite consistent in revealing that group decisions are closer to the game-theoretic assumption of rationality than individual decisions.' RePEc ESI 2004-09: 'groups are not smarter decision makers per se, but ... they learn faster than individuals. When individuals compete against groups, the latter significantly outperform the former in terms of payoff.' Sutter et al. PMC4047612: 'Based on a total of 192 experimental participants, we find that teams play Nash-strategies in about 50% of cases, while individuals ... only about 40%'; Table 1 text '(49.30% vs. 40.97%; p<0.05)'; 'the estimated probability to play strategically is 62% for teams, but only 40% for individuals'; 'teams of three subjects each ... sat together in a sound-proof cabin'; '30 Euro Cents for each experimental point'.
verified.reliability: Two peer-reviewed reviews and two peer-reviewed lab studies (the Sutter et al. full text was read). None uses RPS, and the main lab evidence comes from dominance-solvable games.
verified.design: Two reviews (abstracts only) and one lab experiment. Sutter et al. 2013: N=192, 3-person teams versus individuals in one-shot normal-form games with belief elicitation, paid 30 euro cents per point. Kocher & Sutter 2005: beauty-contest lab experiments (details not read).
verified.effect: Nash play about +10 percentage points for teams; strategic-type share 62% against 40%.
verified.implication: Letting the team deliberate on a throw, or on the plan, should reduce obvious biases and make predictable opponents easier to exploit. In RPS against a random opponent, though, rationality guarantees only 1/3-1/3-1/3, not an edge.
verified.caveats: I read only the abstracts of three of the four sources. None tests RPS. The games studied are mostly dominance-solvable or social-preference games.

verified.statement: Okano (2013, Games Econ. Behav. 77:168-180) studied repeated zero-sum games with a unique mixed equilibrium, the class RPS belongs to (RPS itself was not tested). Two-person teams that discussed each choice face to face matched minimax in O'Neill's 4×4 game at the decision-maker level, while individuals did not. The treatments were separate: 36 teams played other teams and 36 individuals played other individuals, over 15 practice and 150 paid rounds. Data were analysed through round 132 after a computer problem. A winning team earned 100 yen, split between its members, and a winning individual earned 50 yen. When teams played individuals, teams won above the equilibrium rate in one treatment but not the other. Teams' hide-and-seek play was less heterogeneous than individuals'. In a 5×5 Rapoport-Boebel game (Okano 2017 working paper; Osaka University, 2011-2012; separate treatments of 56 teams in 28 pairs and 40 individuals in 20 pairs; 120 rounds), hypothesis tests found teams consistent with minimax only in rounds 1-60. Model selection, however, found the minimax model fitted individuals' aggregate play best in both halves and teams' play in rounds 61-120. At the decision-maker level, minimax was the best model for about half of both teams and individuals. Runs tests rarely rejected serial independence for either group; for action C, 5.4% of teams and 10.0% of individuals over rounds 1-120.
verified.evidence: Okano 2013 RePEc abstract: 'When teams play O'Neill's 4×4 game against another team, the choice frequencies are consistent with equilibrium ... at the decision-maker level. In contrast, individuals against another individual play far from equilibrium ... The hide-and-seek game experiment reveals that teams' behavior is less heterogeneous than individuals. When teams play O'Neill's game against individuals, teams win at above the equilibrium rate in one treatment, but not in the other.' Okano 2014 WP §2 (SDES-2014-12): 'Subjects played 15 times for practice and 150 times for real money. Because of a computer problem in the 133rd round, Okano (2013) uses the data through the 132nd round'; '36 teams (72 students) in the team treatment and 36 individuals (36 students) in the individual treatment.' Okano 2017 WP (SDES-2017-18) abstract: 'Based on model selection, the aggregated behavior of teams in the first half is best fitted by a belief-based learning model, whereas that of teams in the second half and that of individuals in both halves are best fitted by the minimax model. At the decision-maker level, the minimax model is best for about half of the teams and individuals.' §2: '112 subjects participated in the team treatment. Consequently, we have 56 teams (28 pairs). The remaining 40 subjects (20 pairs)'. Table 5 (runs test): C 5.4% vs 10.0%.
verified.reliability: One peer-reviewed lab study (GEB) plus two working papers (one later published in AEL). Japanese students, modest yen incentives, games other than RPS, small samples.
verified.design: Japanese university students. Okano 2013/2014: 2-person teams with free face-to-face discussion versus individuals, fixed pairs, O'Neill 4×4 game, yen per win. Okano 2017: Osaka University, 2011-2012, 112 students in 56 teams against 40 individuals, 5×5 Rapoport-Boebel game, 120 rounds, 200/120 yen per team win plus a 1400 yen show-up fee.
verified.effect: Teams were statistically consistent with minimax while individuals were not (p-value based). Evidence of teams beating individuals is mixed (1 of 2 treatments).
verified.implication: A pair that jointly decides throws may keep its hand frequencies balanced and hard to exploit early on, but the benefit fades over long matches. For long sequences, use an external randomizer rather than relying on discussion.
verified.caveats: These are not RPS (4×4 and 5×5 games with unequal equilibrium mixes). Two of the three sources are working papers. The team advantage was not robust over time.

verified.statement: Batzilis et al. (2019, Games 10(2):18) analysed 2,636,417 best-of-3 Roshambull matches played on Facebook from 23 May to 14 August 2007 (340,213 users). Before each match, players saw a 'scouting sheet' of the opponent's history, and they used it. A one-SD rise (0.176) in the opponent's past first-throw Scissors share raised P(Rock) by 4.2 points for inexperienced players and by 9.4 points for experienced players who had already played 100 games. Coefficients on opponent history were significant for 47% of experienced players, and reactions were stronger when the opponent's history was longer. Experienced players (7,758 with at least 100 matches) won 34.66% and lost 33.17% of first throws (net +1.49). A model-based best response to predicted play would have won 41.66% and lost 27.37%.
verified.evidence: PDF (UChicago repository, games-10-00018-v2.pdf). §1: '340,213 users'; 'best-two-out-of-three matches for prestige points known as 'creds''; 'a 'scouting sheet' with information on the opponent's history of play'; 'Our dataset contains 2,636,417 matches ... between 23 May 2007 ... and 14 August 2007'; '7758 'experienced' players'. §3: 'a standard deviation increase in the opponent's historical fraction of scissors (0.176) increases the probability that an inexperienced player plays rock by 4.2 percentage points ... for an experienced player who already played at least 100 games, the increase is 9.4 percentage points'; 'statistically significant for 47% of experienced players'. Table 5: Full 33.8/32.4/33.8; Experienced 34.66/32.17/33.17; Best Response 41.66/30.97/27.37. Table 12 text: increases of 1.6, 9 and 14 percentage points by opponent history length (<14, 14-46, >46 games).
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed. A very large field dataset of human-against-human online play with no money at stake; analysis covers first throws only.
verified.design: Large online field dataset (Facebook 'Roshambull', 23 May to 14 August 2007), human against human, no money; analysis of first throws.
verified.effect: Experienced players' wins were +1.3 points over 1/3. The model-based best response would win +8.3 points over 1/3 and lose 6.0 points less.
verified.implication: Scouting has real but limited value. Record opponents' (or the host's) throws on a shared team sheet, especially opening throws, and share them with the next player. Weight what you see by sample size: a handful of throws is mostly noise.
verified.caveats: Online, low stakes, first throws only. The best-response figure uses a regression fitted on massive data and is not achievable live. Effects of individual-level histories are noisy.

verified.statement: In Dyson et al. (2020, Biological Psychology 149:107778; bioRxiv 571257), 'observe' trials were trials where the computer chose the participant's response; this is not scouting. In Experiment 2 (n=36, Sussex, £25 prize draw, 480 trials), the exploitable opponent followed a rule on 80% of trials that was beaten by 'downgrading', that is, throwing the hand one's previous hand beats. Participants downgraded on 55.19% of trials after a trial they had chosen themselves and on 49.90% after an observe trial (Tukey HSD p<.05; baseline 33.3%). Against the strategic bot they won 49.63%, lost 21.62% and drew 28.75%. Against the random bot, play was near equilibrium whatever the previous trial type.
verified.evidence: bioRxiv full text (https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/571257v1.full), read via WebFetch. Experiment 1: 'participants initiated each trial with a fourth button and had no control over the response selection.' Experiment 2: '480 trials of RPS split into two, counterbalanced opponent conditions (random, strategic)'; '80% of the time (96 trials per block)'; '60 play and 60 observe trials'; '36 individuals'; 'prize draw to win £25'; ethics at the University of Sussex; 'downgrade [select item that would have been beaten by your previous play]'; '(49.63%, 21.62%, 28.75%, respectively)'; 'the optimal downgrade option fell when the previous trial was an observe relative to a play trial (49.90% vs. 55.19%; Tukey's HSD test, p < .05)'.
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed lab EEG study, n=36 per experiment, computer opponents, weak incentives.
verified.design: Lab EEG study at the University of Sussex. Experiment 2: n=36, 480 trials against computer opponents (random, or exploitable on 80% of trials), prize draw of £25.
verified.effect: The exploiting response fell from 55.19% to 49.90% (-5.3 points) after a non-chosen trial; both are well above the 33.3% baseline.
verified.implication: Watching outcomes you did not choose, such as a teammate's bouts, is no substitute for an explicit, written pattern. In relays, hand the incoming player a concrete instruction (for example, 'their winner tends to repeat; throw the counter') rather than relying on impressions from watching.
verified.caveats: Computer opponents and low incentives. Numbers come from the preprint. This does not test whether watching a human opponent's earlier games improves prediction; that remains untested here.

verified.statement: Srihaput, Craplewe & Dyson (2020, Games 11(3):25; N=80; computer opponents playing randomly) found that changing opponents weakens win-stay but not lose-shift. After a win, players repeated the winning hand on 44.02% of trials when the same opponent came next and 38.21% when a different opponent came next (pooled ANOVA p=0.010; baseline 33.3%). After a loss they shifted on 78.93% (opponent change) and 79.70% (opponent repeat) of trials (p=0.591; baseline 66.7%). Experiment 1 showed 41.88% vs 34.17% (p=0.026) and Experiment 2 showed 46.17% vs 42.24% (not significant). If a staying relay winner repeats with p≈0.38 and splits the rest evenly, the counter-throw wins about 38% and loses about 31% (derived).
verified.evidence: PDF via the MDPI CDN (https://mdpi-res.com/d_attachment/games/games-11-00025/article_deploy/games-11-00025.pdf). §2.1: '80 individuals ... 40 (Experiment 1) ... University of Sussex ... 40 (Experiment 2) ... University of Alberta'; 'A £25 Amazon voucher was randomly allocated to one participant in Experiment 1; course credit was allocated in Experiment 2.' §2.3: '288 trials'; '72 ... opponent repeat pairs ... (72) ... opponent change pairs'; 'All opponents played MS'; Experiment 1 item-biased opponents (12 R/3 P/3 S). §3: '(44.02% versus 38.21%; F[2,78] = 6.951, MSE = 0.019, p = 0.010, ηp2 = 0.082)'; '(78.93% versus 79.70%; F[1,78] = 0.292 ... p = 0.591'; '(41.88% versus 34.17%; t[34] = 2.322, p = 0.026)'; '(46.17% versus 42.24%; t[34] = 1.350, p = 0.185)'. Discussion: 'computerized (rather than human) opponents' and no financial incentive.
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed (MDPI Games), N=80, computer opponents, no performance pay.
verified.design: N=80: 40 at Sussex (£25 voucher lottery) and 40 at Alberta (course credit). 288 RPS trials against 8 computer avatars playing randomly (Experiment 1 had 2 item-biased avatars); 72 opponent-repeat and 72 opponent-change trial pairs.
verified.effect: Win-stay +10.7 points over baseline with the same opponent and +4.9 points with a new opponent. Lose-shift about +12-13 points over 66.7%, unaffected by opponent change.
verified.implication: In a winner-stays relay, the staying winner always faces a new opponent but still repeats the winning hand somewhat more than 1/3 of the time. The incoming teammate, who saw that hand, can lean to the hand that beats it. If the other two hands split evenly, that first throw wins about 38% and loses about 31%, a small edge. In points or best-of-3 formats against the same opponent, the opponent's lose-shift (rarely repeating a losing hand) persists.
verified.caveats: Computer opponents and no pay. The split between the two shift directions is not reported here; other studies report directional shifts that would change the best counter. The 38% vs 31% edge is my derivation.

verified.statement: Cook et al. (2012, Proc R Soc B 279:780-786) found that seeing the opponent's hand while throwing produces involuntary imitation, not wins. In face-to-face play with one player blindfolded, draws rose to 36.3%, against 33.3% when both were blindfolded. Sighted players copied the blind player's Rock (b=0.245, p=0.034) and Scissors (b=0.266, p=0.006) but not Paper (b=0.086, n.s.). Sighted players won 31.3% of rounds and blind players 32.4%. Participants were 45 adults, and 14 triads were analysed; each triad played 9 matches of 20 rounds on an umpire's count of three.
verified.evidence: Author-hosted PDF (https://users.ox.ac.uk/~ascch/Celia's%20pdfs/91%202011%20Cook%20et%20al%20RPS.pdf). 'Forty-five healthy adults (23 females)'; 'nine matches of RPS, each comprising 20 individual rounds'; Table 4: blind wins 32.4%, sighted wins 31.3%, draws 36.3%; blind-blind draws 33.3%; Table 5: rock 0.245 (p 0.034), paper 0.086 (0.298), scissors 0.266 (0.006); 'blind - sighted condition (t13 = 2.49; p < 0.025 (one-tailed))'; payment '£5' plus 'the player who achieved the greater number of wins within each 60-round match would receive an additional £2.50 win bonus'.
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed lab study, small sample (14 triads), face-to-face, small stakes.
verified.design: Lab study at UCL ELSE. 45 adults, 14 triads analysed, each triad playing 9 matches of 20 rounds face to face to an umpire's count of three. Paid £5 plus a £2.50 bonus per match won.
verified.effect: Draws +3.0 points over 1/3; sighted players gained no win advantage (-1.1 points against the blind players).
verified.implication: In host-against-everyone games where a tie eliminates you (rule A), looking at the host's hand as you throw may make you copy it and raise your elimination rate. Commit to your pre-assigned hand (C7) and do not try to react to what you see.
verified.caveats: Tested in 1:1 play, not with one host and a crowd. Small sample (14 triads). The effect is modest.

verified.statement: Towse et al. (2016, PLoS ONE 11(3):e0151306) found that when two people take turns building one 'random' digit sequence (digits 1-10), each avoids repeating the partner's last response. Immediate repetitions averaged 2.4 per 200 responses in real pair sequences, against 20.5 in composites of the same people's solo sequences and 19.8 expected by chance (Experiment 1, 40 undergraduates in 20 pairs). In Experiment 3 (33 Kyoto pairs), telling pairs to ignore their partner raised true-pair repetitions to 10.4 (cooperate: 1.5; composite: 21.5) but did not reach randomness ('neither makes you random').
verified.evidence: PMC4792471 full text. Table 1, Immediate Repetition (RD1): 1.10 (slow), 1.05 (fast), 1.15 (paired), 9.91 (ideal for 100); true pairs 2.4 (1.88), composite 20.5 (3.17), ideal 19.8 (4.41).
