Table 3, Ignore Group RD1: true pairs 10.4, composite 21.5; Cooperate: 1.5 and 20.8. 'Ignoring your partner is a better strategy than cooperating with them, but neither makes you random on most performance dimensions.' Experiment 3: 'Sixty-six (Kyoto University) ... 33 pairs ... (16 pairs) ... cooperate ... (17 pairs) ... ignore'.
verified.reliability: Peer-reviewed lab study (PLoS ONE) with replication across countries, modest N, non-RPS task.
verified.design: Experiment 1: 40 undergraduates (Colorado Boulder and Lancaster) in 20 pairs, generating digits 1-10 at a metronome pace, alone (100 responses) or taking turns (200). Experiment 3: Japanese pairs (16 told to cooperate, 17 told to ignore the partner).
verified.effect: Immediate repetitions in real pairs were about 12% of the chance level (2.4 against 19.8 per 200 responses).
verified.implication: Teammates who play in turn against the same host or opponent may unconsciously avoid the hand a teammate just used, which makes the team's sequence predictable. Use pre-generated random assignments (dice, a phone RNG) instead of reacting to teammates.
verified.caveats: The task was digit generation (10 options), not RPS (3 options). Applying it to RPS team play is an extrapolation.

verifier_added.statement: Derived result. In simultaneous team-against-team RPS (all members throw at once) under either of Cho's rules, a 3-person team's best pre-agreed composition is two members on hand X and one on the hand X beats (R-R-S, P-P-R or S-S-P), with X drawn secretly at random each throw. Against an independently random team it wins 0.6875 under rule I (more winners wins) and 0.684 under rule II (only one team has winners). The reverse orientation (two on X, one on the hand that beats X) wins only 0.3125 and 0.469. The sweep's random-orientation split gives 0.50 and 0.576, and herding gives 0.50 and 0.25. For 4-person teams, 3 on X plus 1 on the hand X beats wins 0.859 (rule I) and 0.779 (rule II). For 2-person teams, rule I is 0.50 whatever the team does, and rule II gives 0.583 with two different hands. If both teams use this composition the match is 50:50, and among the strategies checked the composition is a best response to itself.
verifier_added.evidence: Exact rational recursion over all hand profiles (c6_opt.py, c6_matrix.py) and Monte Carlo with 200k games (rule I 0.6876, rule II 0.6837). Exact values are 11/16 and 175/256. 3v3 payoff rows for the composition against SAME/BEAT/LOSE/random-orientation/independent: rule I 0.5/0.5/1.0/0.75/0.6875; rule II 0.875/0.5/0.75/0.625/0.684. Hand check for rule I (R,R,S against 3 random players): decisive only when no opponent shows Paper (8/27); win if at most 1 opponent shows Rock (4/27), a 2v2 replay worth 0.5 if 2 do (3/27), a loss if all 3 do (1/27), giving (4+1.5)/8 = 0.6875. Rule definitions from Cho 2019 §2.2, Cho 2010 §2.2 and Cho 2020 §2.
verifier_added.study_design: Mathematical derivation (exact enumeration and recursion) plus simulation. Assumes the opposing team throws independently of us and cannot predict X. No human data.
verifier_added.effect_size: 3v3: +18.75 points (rule I) and +18.4 points (rule II) over 50% against a random team. That is +10.8 points over the sweep's recommended split under rule II (0.684 vs 0.576) and +18.75 points under rule I, where the sweep said coordination gives nothing.
verifier_added.strategic_implication: If the 단체전 has all members throw at once, a 3-person team should agree on 'two on X, one on the hand X beats' and pick X by a hidden die roll or a pre-generated list before each throw, never using the reverse orientation. Under rule I an opponent who learns X can win by all showing X, so keep X secret. In 2v2 under 'more winners wins' nothing helps.
verifier_added.caveats: The mathematics is exact, but practical value depends on the format being simultaneous, on rules allowing pre-agreed plans, and on the opponent not coordinating the same way, which makes it 50:50. A team of 3 or more showing all three hands stalls the game, and organisers may forbid that.

verifier_added.statement: The 한국가위바위보협회 (Korea RPS Association) published official match rules, archived on rpskorea.co.kr in March 2008. Ties are replayed with no limit ('무승부는 없습니다'). Only the right hand may be used, with standard hand shapes: scissors uses the index and middle fingers at 30-45°, and thumb-index scissors are banned. Players show their hand on the referee's '보'. The standard match is '3세트 2선승제 (1세트=3게임 / 1게임=3판 2선승제)', which the referee may change with both players' consent. After 10 or more ties ('mirror play'), a 1-minute strategy timeout is allowed. Calls or any kind of signal from trainers or spectators can lead to disqualification, and talking with the opponent, trainers or officials during a match is banned. The association's 'CARD 가위바위보' preliminaries gave each player 10 cards (3 Rock, 3 Paper, 3 Scissors, and 1 joker that beats all three; joker against joker is a tie), and every card had to be used. In the button version players start with 3 buttons and need at least 4 to qualify; in the most-wins version they need at least 5 win stamps. No team (단체전) rules appear.

(상황에 따라 양선수의 동의아래 심판의 결정으로 변동 가능합니다.)'; '만약 계속 비기게 되면 이런 상황을 'mirror play' 라고 하는데 ... (총10회 이상 비길 경우 /작전타임1분)'; '트레이너들 또는 구경꾼들에 의하여 행해지는 구호 또는 다양한 방법의 신호는 자격 박탈을 초래할 수 있습니다'; '경기 중 경쟁자(상대선수), 트레이너, 대회관계자와의 대화 및 교류는 금합니다.' rps06.html: '총 10장(가위:3장/바위3장/보3장/조커1장)'; '조커카드의 경우 가위,바위,보 카드 어떤 것이든지 이기며, 조커카드끼리의 승부는 무승부다'; '경기 종료 후 카드를 1장이라도 보유한 게이머는 탈락'; '캠페인 버튼을 4개 이상 보유한 게이머는 예선을 통과'; '5개 이상의 '승'도장'.

verifier_added.effect_size: Not applicable (rules).
verifier_added.strategic_implication: Ask whether the event follows KRPSA-style rules. If it does, live signals from teammates on the sidelines risk disqualification, so share scouting notes between bouts, not during them. Ties cost nothing. In a card format, track which of the opponent's 10 cards remain, including the single joker; that dominates strategy there.
verifier_added.caveats: This is a 2008 archive from a small association whose Korean Wikipedia article is uncited; current events may use different rules. It contains individual rules only, with no team rules. These are the only Korean 'official' RPS rules found.

verifier_added.statement: Two sources the sweep already cites contain rule details that matter for team play but were not reported. (a) The 2019 PBR Indy team rules ban 'verbal or written prompting or assistance' from trainers or spectators during play, but state that 'hand signals are permitted'. Any throw not delivered before the arm crosses the 90-degree mark 'shall be considered a throw of Rock'. (b) The Encyclopedia of Korean Culture records that a player who throws late after glimpsing the other's hand is counted as the loser ('늦게 낸 사람을 진 것으로 친다'), and that players sometimes turn away and throw over the shoulder to prevent this.
verifier_added.evidence: PBR rules (https://mokbpresents.com/rock-paper-scissors-indy/official-rules/), ADJUDICATION: 'No verbal or written prompting or assistance (hand signals are permitted) may be rendered by trainers or spectators during the competition. Failure to comply could result in disqualification.' Delivery rule: 'Any throw not delivered prior to the hand crossing the 90-degree mark shall be considered a throw of Rock.' Encykorea E0000295: '이 놀이를 할 때 남이 내는 것을 얼핏 보고 나서 뒤늦게 내는 꾀를 부리기도 하는데, 이 경우 늦게 낸 사람을 진 것으로 친다. 이를 막으려고 각각 돌아서서 어깨너머로 손을 내밀기도 한다.'
verifier_added.study_design: Event rules (USA, 2019) and a national encyclopedia entry (Korea). No data.
verifier_added.effect_size: Not applicable (rules).
verifier_added.strategic_implication: Rules on sideline help differ by event: PBR allowed hand signals while KRPSA (MF2) banned signals, so confirm before planning any live signalling. Hesitating to react to the opponent's hand is penalised, either as Rock or as a loss. This supports committing to a pre-planned hand (C16).
verifier_added.caveats: Rules are specific to each event or custom. Neither source is a Korean 단체전 rulebook.

verifier_added.statement: Cho (2020; full text, which the sweep read only as an abstract) compares, for m players per side, the winner-stays relay (method I), simultaneous 'more winners wins' (II) and simultaneous 'only one team has winners' (III). Mean throws to a decision are 3.75 / 2.36 / 2.93 for m=2 and 6.19 / 4.49 / 5.78 for m=3; the exact values for m=3 are 6.19 / 4.48 / 5.80. In the relay, the number of decisive bouts N has P(N=i) = C(i-1,m-1)(1/2)^(i-1) for i=m..2m-1 (for m=3: 1/4, 3/8, 3/8). The relay is therefore a race to m bout wins, which independently confirms C9. Several printed variances are wrong: the relay values of 3.00 and 5.20 should be 39/16≈2.44 and 1143/256≈4.46, and method III for m=2 should be 631/196≈3.22, not 3.42.
verifier_added.evidence: Cho 2020 PDF (https://koreascience.kr/article/JAKO202033564390558.pdf). Theorem 2.2: P(N=i) = (i-1)!/((m-1)!(i-m)!)(1/2)^(i-1). Result 2.1: E(Y2)=15/4. Result 2.2: E(Y3)=99/16. Table 2.5: means 1.50/1.50/1.50, 3.75/2.36/2.93, 6.19/4.49/5.78. The derivation gives 11664/2604 = 4.48, but Result 2.4 prints 11684/2604. My exact check (cho2020_var.py, with Monte Carlo of 300k-400k games): relay mean 6.1875, variance 4.4648 (MC 4.48); rule I m=3 mean 4.4793, variance 12.73; rule II m=3 mean 5.7961, variance 14.92 (MC 14.96).
verifier_added.study_design: Combinatorial derivation (peer-reviewed), checked by my exact recursion and simulation.
verifier_added.effect_size: A 3-a-side relay averages about 6.2 throws, against about 4.5-5.8 for simultaneous formats and 1.5 for 1v1.
verifier_added.strategic_implication: A 3-person relay involves more throws, so more chances to observe the opponent's staying player, but also more time. Plan scouting and time budgets accordingly. The paper's means are reliable but its variances are not.
verifier_added.caveats: Assumes uniform independent throws. The paper is framed around deciding which team starts first.

verifier_added.statement: In Sutter, Czermak & Feri (2013), the teams' higher rate of Nash play (49.30% vs 40.97%, p<0.05) came from the 10 games in which one player had a dominant strategy. In the games where neither player had a dominant strategy, the class RPS belongs to, there was no significant difference between teams and individuals.
verifier_added.evidence: PMC4047612, Results: 'teams are significantly more often playing the Nash-strategy than individuals (49.30% vs. 40.97%; p<0.05). ... These differences between individuals and teams are mainly driven by the 10 games with a dominant strategy. Only in D-games teams are significantly more often playing Nash, and less often playing Pareto, while there is no significant difference between individuals and teams in the ND-games where neither player has a dominant strategy.'
verifier_added.study_design: 192 participants at the MPI Jena lab, 18 one-shot normal-form games (10 with a dominant strategy), 3-person teams talking in sound-proof cabins, 30 euro cents per point, beliefs elicited.
verifier_added.effect_size: Overall +8.3 points of Nash play for teams; no significant difference in the non-dominance games.
verifier_added.strategic_implication: Do not expect team deliberation in itself to improve RPS throws. The group-rationality advantage that C11 relies on is concentrated in games with dominant strategies. Spend team effort on structural levers instead: format-specific coordination (MF1, C7), randomisation devices, and shared scouting notes.
verifier_added.caveats: One study. Its non-dominance games are not mixed-strategy games like RPS, and the lack of a difference may reflect low power.

verifier_added.statement: Derived result. In simultaneous elimination among peers with no host (everyone throws, and when exactly two hands show, the winners continue until one player remains), a coordinated 3-person subgroup among 10 players makes the final survivor a teammate with probability 0.450 if it shows two on X and one on the hand X beats. The head-count share is 0.300; a random-orientation two-hand split gives 0.349, independent play 0.300 and herding on one hand 0.125. In 'pick one loser' games (losers continue until one remains), herding on one hand makes a teammate the final loser with probability only 0.125, against a 0.300 share. Namu Wiki describes this kind of collusion: when three of four players match hands, the fourth is effectively left in a 1:1 game. It suggests splitting into pairs as the countermeasure.
verifier_added.evidence: Exact recursion (peer_elim3.py) for N=10, t=3, winner mode: herd 0.125, beat 0.450, lose 0.249, random split 0.349, independent 0.300. Loser mode mirrors this: herd 0.125, beat 0.249, lose 0.450. Monte Carlo with 200k runs (peer_mc.py), loser mode: herd 0.1249, split 0.3499, independent 0.3005. For N=6, t=3, winner mode gives beat 0.684 and split 0.576, the same as Cho's rule II for 3v3. Namu 가위바위보 §4.3 (via WebFetch): '4명이서 패자1인을 정할 때 3명이 미리 짜서 하나로 맞춘다면 나머지 1명이 불리해진다'; '2명씩 나누어서 패자와 패자끼리 다시 가위바위보를 시킨다면 승부 조작을 막을 수 있는 길이다'.
verifier_added.study_design: Exact derivation and simulation assuming the other players throw independently, plus an anecdotal community wiki.
verifier_added.effect_size: Winner mode: +15 points (0.450 vs 0.300). Loser mode: -17.5 points of exposure (0.125 vs 0.300).
verifier_added.strategic_implication: The right coordination depends on the objective. If the format rewards the last survivor, use the 2+1 split where X beats the single hand. If it punishes the last loser, herd on one hand. Check whether such coordination against non-team players is allowed.
verifier_added.caveats: Derived, not tested with people. Organisers may ban collusion or neutralise it by splitting players into pairs. Other teams coordinating would erode the gain.

dead_ends: No official rulebook for a Korean '가위바위보 단체전' competition was found online. Searches with Korean keywords (단체전 규칙, 대회 방식, 체육대회, 사회자, 릴레이) returned only wiki pages, recreation guides and school-game blogs. 한국가위바위보협회 exists according to an uncited Korean Wikipedia article (founded 2004; contests in 2005 and a Korea championship in August 2011), but no team rules were found.

Japanese じゃんけん団体戦 rules: found only party and children's leader-against-everyone guides (45mix) and search summaries of martial-arts style 勝ち抜き戦 (winner-stays) and 点取り戦 (points) formats; no official janken team rulebook.
World RPS Society and USA RPS League team or match rules could not be located (both appear defunct). The WRPSA page and the PBR Indy 2019 rules were used instead.

Lead 4 mismatch: in Dyson et al. (2020, Biological Psychology 149:107778) the 'observation' condition means the computer selected the participant's response (reduced responsibility). It does not test whether watching an opponent's earlier games improves prediction. In Experiment 2, a preceding observe trial reduced the optimal downgrade response against an exploitable bot (49.90% vs 55.19%).
Lead 5 confirmed as Srihaput, Craplewe & Dyson (2020) Games 11(3):25, DOI 10.3390/g11030025, with 80 participants (not a larger sample). Opponents were computer avatars, with no performance pay.

Lead 3 confirmed: Kocher & Sutter (2005) EJ 115(500):200-223; Charness & Sutter (2012) JEP 26(3):157-176; Kugler, Kausel & Kocher (2012) WIREs Cogn Sci 3(4):471-482. Only abstracts were accessible; PDFs were blocked (AEA 403, CESifo/ifo bot challenge, LMU and MPG unreachable).
No laboratory experiment comparing teams (jointly deciding) with individuals in RPS itself was found. The closest are Okano's O'Neill 4×4 and Rapoport-Boebel 5×5 zero-sum games.

Lead 2: no source prints '3(2^n-2)/3^n' verbatim. It follows from the inclusion-exclusion definitions in Fuchs, Hwang & Itoh (2017) and matches Cho (2010)'s 543/729 six-player tie count and Cho (2019)'s 39/81 four-player tie probability; I verified it by enumeration. Asymptotics: Maehara & Ueda (2000), JAP 37(2):601-605.

Cho (2019) internal inconsistencies: E(Z3:2) is reported as 9909/2520 (≈3.93) but is exactly 57/14 (≈4.07), because eq. 2.11 swaps two weights from its own Table 2.4. E(Z3:3) is given as 150579/26040 (≈5.78) in Result 2.5 and 9531/1736 (≈5.49) in the derivation; the exact value is 5031/868 (≈5.80).

A '일당백 가위바위보' (leader against everyone) description appeared only in a search-engine snippet from a defunct Daum blog (m.blog.daum.net); the page could not be opened. The equivalent Japanese rule was verified on 45mix.net.
No Korean-population behavioural RPS dataset was found; Korean news coverage concerned foreign studies (e.g., a 2025 Western Sydney EEG study).
Okano (2013) GEB full text (ScienceDirect 403), the Osaka University working paper expss08e7 (403) and Cho (2020) KJAS 33(5) full text were not accessible.
open_questions: Which exact format and tie rule the user's event uses: team against team (representative, relay, points, or all-at-once rule I or II), or everyone against a host (ties eliminate or not, void rounds when everyone is out). The optimal team plan differs sharply between these (C6-C9).
Whether the event allows teammates to coordinate throws secretly. The coordination gains in C6-C8 depend on it.
Whether a staying relay winner facing a new human opponent who saw their last throw repeats it more or less than the 38% measured against computer avatars (C15), and in which direction they shift.
How human hosts in leader-against-everyone games deviate from random (repetition avoidance, opening-hand bias). No data on host sequences was found.
Whether automatic imitation (C16) raises tie and elimination rates when many players face one host whose hand is visible.
Whether teams that discuss each throw in RPS are less predictable than individuals over long matches. The evidence comes from other zero-sum games and fades over time (C12).
How large the realistic per-bout edge is in live, in-person team RPS against strangers. Field data suggest only about +1.5 points net per first throw for experienced online players (C13).

sources.notes: Full PDF from koreascience.or.kr (JAKO201919341608265). Author is at Dept. of Statistics, Inje University. The introduction lists Korean team formats; the paper defines rules I and II and derives expected game counts. My exact recomputation confirms (1,1), (2,1), (2,2) and (3,1). It does not confirm (3,2) or (3,3). Eq. 2.11 weights (3,1) by 9/243 and (2,2) by 6/243, but the paper's own Table 2.4 gives 6/243 and 9/243. # RPS strategy brief: quantitative model

**Conventions**
- **Edge** is P(win) − P(loss) per throw, in percentage points (pp).
- **q** is P(win | decisive throw). Ties are always replayed.
- **X** is the opponent's previous hand. **X+** is the hand that beats X (Rock → Paper). **X−** is the hand X beats (Rock → Scissors).
- **Opponent state W/T/L** is the opponent's own previous outcome. W means they won, which means we lost.
- **Rule notation "a/b/c"** gives our throw after the opponent's win / tie / loss.
- **"Upper bound"** means the opponent behaves exactly like the population-average table and does not adapt.

---

## Key numbers the synthesis should quote

| # | Number | Source of parameters |
|---|---|---|
| K1 | **First-throw base rates.** Paper nets +2.8 pp [95% CI +2.7, +2.9] against 5.0M online openers. Experienced players' openers favour Scissors instead (+2.0 [+1.8, +2.1]; Paper −0.2). An edge on the first throw only adds just 0.25×e1 to a Bo3 match: +2.8 pp becomes 50.7%. | baserates:C01 |
| K2 | **All-throw Rock excess.** Always throwing Paper nets +2.8 to +4.9 pp in 9 datasets: Zhejiang labs, Western labs, AU pairs, JP live hands and the Batzilis proxy. It nets −2.7 [−4.8, −0.7] in US dyads and −2.0 in UK live play. Hungarian live play had a Scissors excess (36.8%). | C04, A4, B1, C18, MF03, C05, C11 |
| K3 | **Being watched matters more than base rates.** If your visible openers are ≥42% Rock, opponents open Paper 46.6%, so Scissors nets **+16.2 pp**. If your Rock share is 0–25%, Rock nets +10.0. | sequential:D1, foundations:C18 |
| K4 | **Upper bound from exploiting the opponent's conditional pattern** (best response to its own population, long run). Zhejiang a=2: +17.2 pp/throw, Bo3 0.659. Western labs: +10.9 to +13.4, Bo3 0.59–0.61. US/AU fixed pairs: +8.2 / +6.9, Bo3 0.567 / 0.564. Halving the opponent's biases roughly halves these. If only the after-loss bias exists: +1.9 to +6.3 pp, Bo3 0.514–0.544. | A1, C2, B1, B2, MF5, C1 |
| K5 | **The best response flips sign between populations.** The Zhejiang best response loses 6.4 pp/throw against AU pairs. "Always X−" (the US/AU best response) loses 18.7 pp/throw against Zhejiang a=2. | A1, C1, C2 |
| K6 | **Only one robust per-state rule.** Of 63 per-state rules (each state: X+, X, X− or random; all-random excluded), only **X+/X−/X−** is non-negative against all 7 full-session tables. Its minimum is +0.4, mean +7.0 (West +8.5, Zhejiang +3.2). In rounds 1–20 it scores −0.3 [−3.8, +3.3] (US), +1.7 (AU) and +3.1 (ZJ). Bo3 ranges 0.498–0.610. In words: if they just won, beat their hand; otherwise throw the hand their last hand beats. In your own terms: after a loss or tie, throw the hand your last hand beats; after a win, throw the hand that beats your last hand. | all conditional tables |
| K7 | **After a tie.** In fixed-opponent and Western data, X− wins: +5.4 [+1.2, +9.7] AU and +5.8 [+2.4, +9.1] US (Rock–Rock → Scissors), and +8.0 to +12.6 in Western labs. In Zhejiang data X+ wins: +19.8 at a=2, shrinking to +5.5 when a tie pays nothing (a=∞). In rounds 1–20 no response is distinguishable from 0 (CI ±6–9 pp). | MF01, B1, B2, A1, C08, MF02, MF2 |
| K8 | **Format amplification.** At q=0.55: Bo3 0.575, Bo5 0.593, 5-a-side relay 0.621, 7-a-side relay 0.644, 5-member points format with Bo3 bouts 0.638. Realistic edges are small: experienced online players' realised +1.49 pp gives q=0.511 and Bo3 0.516. | team:C3, C9, foundations:C16 |
| K9 | **Host game: coordinated even split is exactly optimal.** Rule A (only winners survive), n=10, k=2: 0.692 → 1.000. Rule A, n=20, k=3: 0.530 → 0.741. Rule B (ties also survive), n=10, k=5: 0.756 → 0.959. Herding gives (1/3)^k or (2/3)^k. | team:C7 |
| K10 | **Our exploitability.** A deterministic rule gives Bo3 P(win) = 0.000 against an opponent who knows it. Following a rule with probability p costs exactly −p per throw (Bo3 0.168 at p=0.5). In 300-round sessions humans recovered about 50% of the theoretical maximum against simple transition bots and 14–18% against outcome-conditioned bots. The task's example rule ("beat the previous winning hand") is the 14% type. | sequential:D4, MF1 |
| K11 | **P(simultaneous n-player round is decisive)** = 3(2^n−2)/3^n: 0.667 (n=2–3), 0.370 (n=5), 0.052 (n=10). | team:C4 |
| K12 | **Simultaneous 3v3 team throw.** Composition "2 on X + 1 on the hand X beats" wins 11/16 = 0.6875 (rule I) and 175/256 = 0.684 (rule II) against an independent team. The reverse orientation gives 0.3125 / 0.469. | team:C6/MF1 |
| K13 | **Relay challenger lean** (throw the hand that beats the champion's last winning hand) gives +7.3 pp on that throw, using the Western new-opponent win-stay of 38.2%. Against Zhejiang-like champions it gives +28.1. Effect on a 5-a-side relay: 0.540 / 0.520 (single-throw / Bo3 bouts) or 0.652 / 0.577. | sequential:B4, team:C15, A1 |

## Explicit assumptions

1. All exploitation edges are upper bounds. They assume a non-adapting opponent equal to the population-average table. Heterogeneity (sequential:B5) and adaptation (D3) shrink them. The ×0.5 shrink is equivalent to a 50/50 mixture of table-followers and uniform players, exactly so for per-state edges.
2. Opponents are first-order: the next move depends only on their own last hand and outcome. Table rows not summing to 1 (e.g., A1 W row = 1.001) were renormalised.
3. In match simulations the first throw is uniform for both players and ties are replayed. "Only after-loss bias" means the opponent plays uniformly after its wins and ties.
4. Clustering:
   - First-throw CIs are multinomial Wald.
   - "Adj." CIs use ICC ρ = 0.0166, the larger of the values implied by the reported pair-cluster bootstraps (Moerel 0.0066, Brockbank 0.0166). Wang 2014's player SDs imply about 0.024.
   - m (throws per player) is total throws ÷ players.
   - Rounds 1–20 bootstraps ignore within-player clustering.
5. Derived inputs:
   - Forder & Dyson Paper share = 100 − R − S.
   - Dyson 2022 = mean of 3 conditions, with n = 40×360.
   - Cook n = 14 triads × 9 × 20 × 2.
   - Aczel R = P.
   - Yoshizawa after-tie repeat = overall repeat (22.75%), shifts split evenly.
   - B4 champion shifts split evenly.
   - Dyson 2021 used the Exp 1 no-credit column, the only complete W/T/L table.
6. Formats (Section 4) use a constant q and independent bouts. The relay lean affects only the first throw of each bout.
7. The host is uniform and independent of the team plan. In the sensitivity check the host follows the JP live marginals.
8. The informed opponent knows both the rule and the state. α comes from 300-round sessions against 90% bots, which is longer than tournament bouts. The KL detection horizon assumes the observer already suspects the specific rule, so real detection is slower.
9. The rule selection in 2b is in-sample over 7+3 tables. No Korean data exist, so whether Korean opponents behave like the Zhejiang or the Western tables is the key unknown.

## Methods (one line each)

- **First throw:** exact W/T/L permutations, multinomial-variance Wald CIs, design-effect inflation; small-n rows cross-checked with a percentile bootstrap.
- **Conditional play:** 3-state Markov chain over the opponent's last outcome; stationary edge by linear solve; Bo3/Bo5 by an absorbing chain. Validated by Monte Carlo: Bo3 P(win) within 0.002, long-run edge within 0.2 pp.
- **Robustness:** brute force over all 64 per-state rules; parametric multinomial bootstrap (4,000 draws) for rounds 1–20.
- **Formats:** exact binomial sums; the relay was also solved by DP.
- **Host game:** exact rational DP over survivor allocations; decisive probability by exhaustive enumeration up to 3^10 profiles.
- **Team vs team:** exact rational recursion over all hand profiles.
- **Exploitability:** mixed-policy Markov chain with an informed best-responder; KL-divergence detection horizon.

gaps.gap: Is the 'repeat-prone' Zhejiang pattern an East Asian trait, and do sequential edges already appear in the first ~10 throws? The verified set had no non-Chinese East Asian sequential data and no short-horizon replication.
gaps.why_it_matters: The verified set's main fork is whether opponents are repeat-prone or repeat-averse. In the Zhejiang samples, stay rates were 0.41-0.44 and win-stay 0.47-0.53, so the best reply after a win or tie is X+. In UK, Canadian, US and Australian samples, stay is about 0.28, so the best reply is X-. Every 'react to their last hand' rule flips sign between these two groups. Korean opponents are East Asian, no Korean dataset was accessible, and MF2 suggested the first 1-20 throws are close to random. A large public Japanese dataset that also records the opponent's moves can settle much of this.

findings.statement:
Japanese players (n=500) were repeat-averse, unlike the Zhejiang samples. Data: Komai et al.'s public dataset, 50 keyboard games per player against a GA/GP program.

Repeat rate:
- Overall 28.2% (per-player 95% CI 26.9-29.6%).
- 349 of 500 players were below 1/3.
- Throws 2-10: 26.5%.

Next throw after each outcome (repeat / upgrade / downgrade):
- After a WIN (n=8,187): 30.5% / 35.2% / 34.2%. Upgrade means won with Rock -> Paper; downgrade means Rock -> Scissors.
- After a TIE (n=7,790): 27.7% / 36.1% / 36.2%.
- After a LOSS (n=8,522): 26.5% / 33.6% / 39.9%.

Next throw after a loss, by losing hand:
- Lost with Rock (n=2,634): Scissors 43.8%, Rock 28.9%, Paper 27.3%.
- Lost with Scissors (n=3,305): Paper 42.0%, Rock 34.9%, Scissors 23.1%.
- Lost with Paper (n=2,583): Scissors 38.3%, Rock 33.4%, Paper 28.3%.

There was no win-stay, and downgrading after a loss was the most common response. This matches the Western fixed-pair pattern and Yoshizawa's 22.8% Japanese field repeat rate, not the Zhejiang lab.
findings.evidence:
Komai, Kurokawa & Kim 2022, Sec. 2: 'The target RPS time series comprises data acquired from 500 people who played 50 consecutive RPS games. The RPS time-series data were obtained from participants attending open days at the Tokyo University of Technology from 2017–2019. Here, each subject played against an RPS algorithm using GA and GP [31,32], and the human RPS time-series data were obtained by the player's own operations using the keyboard. Note that all subjects played the RPS game after understanding the purpose of the experiments, and the goal of the player was to win the RPS game.'

Appendix: 'Xt ... is the t-th hand sign (i.e., rock, scissors, paper = 0, 1, 2)'. The appendix's example series is identical to Human_hand_data/1.csv.

Data availability: 'https://github.com/kuro-lab/RPSdata'. The repository README says '数字が、人が出した手の系列とその人と対戦したプログラムが出した手の系列に対応している', i.e. each file number pairs a human's series with the program's series.

My analysis covered all 500 human files and the 500 matching program files: 499 sessions of 50 games and one of 49. Scripts: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-baemanjin-orca-projects-----/9282a235-4fc4-4c50-add0-37a1d5aaa853/scratchpad/scripts/komai_analysis.py and komai_extra.py.

Coding check: under the stated coding, the program's most-played hand (Rock, 37.0%) beats the humans' most-played hand (Scissors, 35.1%), and the program nets +0.014 per throw (SE 0.007). Under the reversed cyclic coding the adaptive program would be a net loser.
findings.study_design:
Japan, Tokyo University of Technology open days, 2017-2019. 500 visitors; age and sex not reported. 50 consecutive keyboard RPS games against an adaptive GA/GP program. Subjects knew the purpose and aimed to win; no incentive reported.

Tier: public raw data from a peer-reviewed paper. The conditional tables are my secondary analysis.
findings.effect_size:
Relative to 1/3:
- Overall repeat: -5.1 pp (throws 2-10: -6.8 pp).
- Win-stay: -2.8 pp. Tie-stay: -5.6 pp. Lose-stay: -6.8 pp.
- Downgrade after a loss: +6.6 pp.
- Lost with Rock -> Scissors: +10.5 pp.
findings.strategic_implication:
In a fixed bout, assume East Asian opponents (and so, plausibly, Korean ones) are repeat-averse.

Best replies in this sample after the opponent LOSES:
- They lost with Rock: throw Rock (+0.165 per throw). It beats their likely Scissors and loses only to Paper (27.3%).
- They lost with Paper: throw Rock (+0.100).
- They lost with Scissors: throw Paper (+0.118).

Do not throw the hand that beats the hand they just lost with.
findings.caveats:
- The opponent was a computer program, its play may have shaped the transitions, and subjects knew it was a program.
- No stakes. Visitor demographics are unknown (likely many high-school students).
- Keyboard input, not hand gestures.
- Japanese, not Korean.
- The repository does not label the digits (Ganzfried notes this), so the hand mapping rests on the paper's appendix plus my consistency checks.
- The hand-specific replies are shaped by this sample's Scissors excess (35.1%).

findings.statement:
Rule tested: X-, 'throw the hand the opponent's last hand beats'. Their Rock -> your Scissors; Paper -> Rock; Scissors -> Paper. In the Japanese data it was positive after every opponent outcome and from the second throw on. The opposite rule X+, 'beat their last hand', was negative everywhere.

Per-player means, all throws (SE):
- After their WIN: X- +0.061 (0.015); X+ -0.047 (0.015).
- After a TIE: X- +0.089 (0.013); X+ -0.099 (0.014).
- After their LOSS: X- +0.084 (0.013); X+ -0.139 (0.014).

Throws 2-10 only (SE about 0.025):
- X-: +0.082 / +0.126 / +0.106 after win / tie / loss.
- X+: -0.096 / -0.107 / -0.153.

Unconditional 'always X-': +0.067 (SE 0.011) overall and +0.098 (0.017) in throws 2-10.

Same rule in throws 2-10 of other datasets:
- US dyads: +0.059 (SE 0.032; repeat 29.8%).
- Australian pairs: +0.095 (SE 0.043; repeat 26.8%).

Cournot check: players threw the hand that beats the program's previous hand 35.6% of the time (+2.3 pp). The counter, 'throw what your own last hand beats', netted only +0.036 (SE 0.008).
findings.evidence:
Japan (komai_edges.py, komai_cournot.py):
- Pooled values after win / tie / loss: X- +0.047 / +0.084 / +0.071; X+ -0.037 / -0.084 / -0.135.
- n = 8,187 / 7,790 / 8,522 transitions; throws 2-10: n = 1,612 / 1,462 / 1,426.

US and Australia (early_xminus.py):
- US: rps_v1_data.csv, 58 complete 300-round dyads, 116 players.
- Australia: OpenNeuro ds006761 events, 31 pairs, 62 players, 480 games each.
- All-round values reproduce the verified C1 counterfactuals (US +0.080 vs C1 +0.079; AU +0.072 vs C1 +0.073), which validates the parsing.
findings.study_design:
Secondary analysis of three public raw datasets:
- Japan: 500 visitors vs a program, 50 games, no pay.
- USA: UCSD students in stable online human dyads, 300 rounds, course credit.
- Australia: Western Sydney adults in stable human pairs, 480 games, flat AUD 60.
findings.effect_size:
- X-: +6 to +13 pp per throw (random play earns 0).
- X+: -5 to -15 pp.
- Upper bound if the edge held on every decisive throw (my arithmetic, ties about 32%): decisive-throw win share 55-57%, best-of-3 win about 57-61%.
findings.strategic_implication:
From the second throw of a bout, lean toward (do not commit to) X- as the default reply to the opponent's last hand: their Rock -> your Scissors, Paper -> Rock, Scissors -> Paper. It is the only reactive rule that was positive from the start in the Japanese, US and Australian data.

It is negative against Zhejiang-like repeaters (verified C2: -0.161 and -0.110). Switch to X+ only against an opponent with a clearly observed repeat habit: with few transitions the estimate is noisy (verified C10: SE about 0.16 after 9 transitions).
findings.caveats:
- The counterfactuals assume the opponent does not react to your rule. Humans read a 90% fixed habit within about 7-10 throws (Gap 3), so use X- as a lean, not a fixed rule.
- The Japanese players faced a program.
- The early-round US estimate is borderline (z about 1.8).

findings.statement:
After a tie, Japanese players mostly switched away from the tied hand.

Next throw after a tie:
- Tie on Rock (n=2,774): Scissors 41.3%, Paper 31.4%, Rock 27.3%.
- Tie on Paper (n=2,449): Scissors 39.5%, Paper 30.8%, Rock 29.7%.
- Tie on Scissors (n=2,567): Rock 38.0%, Paper 36.8%, Scissors 25.2%.

'Throw the hand the tied hand beats' (Rock-Rock -> Scissors, Paper-Paper -> Rock, Scissors-Scissors -> Paper):
- Net +0.041 / +0.087 / +0.128 by tied hand.
- +0.084 pooled; +0.114 in throws 2-10.

The Zhejiang a=2 rule, 'beat the tied hand' (Rock-Rock -> Paper, Paper-Paper -> Scissors, Scissors-Scissors -> Rock):
- Net -0.140 / +0.011 / -0.116.

Exception, two consecutive ties on the same hand (n=1,037): players repeated that hand a third time 39.7% (upgrade 31.2%, downgrade 29.0%). After such a double tie, 'beat the tied hand' was the better reply (+0.107 vs -0.085).
findings.evidence:
Tie breakdown by tied hand: komai_analysis.py.

komai_doubletie.py:
- After two consecutive ties on any hands (n=2,516): stay 0.305, up 0.352, down 0.343.
- After two ties on the same hand (n=1,037): stay 0.397, up 0.312, down 0.290.

Edges: 'hand the tied hand beats' = P(up) - P(stay); 'beat the tied hand' = P(stay) - P(down).
findings.study_design: Same Japanese dataset as G1-F1: 500 players against a program, 50 games each.
findings.effect_size:
- After a single tie: +4 to +13 pp for 'hand the tied hand beats'; -14 to +1 pp for 'beat the tied hand'.
- After a same-hand double tie: third repeat is +6.4 pp over 1/3.
findings.strategic_implication:
For immediate tie replays in a knockout:
- After the first tie, throw the hand the tied hand beats: Rock-Rock -> Scissors, Paper-Paper -> Rock, Scissors-Scissors -> Paper.
- If the same hand ties twice in a row, the opponent is showing a repeat habit, so beat that hand (e.g., Paper after two Rock-Rock ties).

This independently supports the fixed-pair Western evidence (MF01/MF7) over the Zhejiang a=2 rule (C08), and contradicts the WRPS 'Double Run' rule (eliminate a doubled hand).
findings.caveats:
- These ties were against a program.
- The double-tie cell pools players and selects people who had just repeated (a repeat-prone subset). It reflects that selection, not a reaction to ties as such, so its confidence is lower.

findings.statement:
Japanese players kept cycling.
- After an upgrade (Rock -> Paper), the next move was another upgrade (Paper -> Scissors) 47.9% of the time (n=8,386).
- After a downgrade (Rock -> Scissors), the next was another downgrade (Scissors -> Paper) 48.1% (n=8,828).
- After a repeat (X, X), a third X followed 35.8% (n=6,785).

Ganzfried's nonparametric test on the same 500 sequences found frequency bias rare and serial dependence common:
- At alpha=0.05, the chi-square test rejected uniform hand frequencies for 36 players (7.2%).
- The runs test rejected serial independence for 210 players (42%).
- With Bonferroni at alpha=0.025, 195 players (39%) were inconsistent with independent uniform play.
findings.evidence:
Second-order transitions: komai_analysis.py.

Ganzfried, arXiv:2312.10695v2, Sec. 3:
- 'The data consists of 50 consecutive plays of the game from 500 different human subjects'.
- '(though it is not stated which integer corresponds to which action)'.
- 'With α = 0.025 our overall test concludes that 500 − 305 = 195 (39%) of the subjects are following strategies inconsistent with the target strategy'.
- Table 1 at α=0.05: X1 = 14 (both tests significant), X2 = 22 (chi-square only), X3 = 196 (runs only), X4 = 268 (neither).
- 'our chi-squared test rejected uniform frequencies of play for 7.2% of the subjects'.
- Footnote 3: 'https://github.com/kuro-lab/RPSdata'.
findings.study_design: Same Japanese dataset. Ganzfried is a preprint applying a combined chi-square and runs test to each player.
findings.effect_size:
- Continued cycling: +14.6 / +14.8 pp over 33.3% (Western samples: +10 to +13 pp).
- Third repeat: +2.5 pp.
- Detectable serial dependence in 42% of players vs detectable frequency bias in 7.2%.
findings.strategic_implication:
Watch sequences, not hand counts.
- After an opponent goes Rock -> Paper, expect Scissors and throw Rock.
- After Rock -> Scissors, expect Paper and throw Scissors.
- Never treat a hand thrown twice as eliminated.
findings.caveats:
- Pooled over players, so part of the effect reflects stable individual preferences for one direction.
- Sessions were only 50 throws.
- The opponent was a computer.
- Ganzfried's runs test does not by itself say whether players had too many or too few runs. My repeat rate (28.2%) points to over-alternation.

findings.statement: I found only one Korean adult RPS study: Baek et al. 2013 (KAIST/Keimyung), with 50 healthy adults and 48 patients with schizophrenia. Its abstract says the tendency 'to choose the best response against the opponent's previous choice' (beat their last hand) in the two-person game was a patient bias, 'distinct from those of the healthy subjects'. No percentages for the healthy subjects were accessible.
findings.evidence:
PubMed abstract (PMID 23017652), retrieved via NCBI E-utilities: 'The aim of this study was to examine the response randomization of 48 schizophrenic patients and 50 healthy subjects in one- and two-person rock-paper-scissors games. Here we found that the schizophrenic patients exhibited non-random biases distinct from those of the healthy subjects (i.e., stereotypic switching in the one-person game and the tendency to choose the best response against the opponent's previous choice in the two-person game).'

The full text on ScienceDirect returned HTTP 403.
findings.study_design: Korea. 50 healthy adults and 48 patients. One-person (random generation) and two-person RPS; the abstract does not state the opponent type. Peer-reviewed: Psychiatry Research 207(3):158-163.
findings.strategic_implication: There is no Korean evidence that ordinary adults habitually 'beat the opponent's last hand'. That fits X+ being weak elsewhere, but the study gives no Korean base rates. The Japanese data (G1-F1 to G1-F4) remain the closest proxy.
findings.caveats: Abstract only; the comparison is clinical; no numbers for healthy subjects.

gaps.gap: Opening throw and overall hand shares: do they differ by population (East Asian vs US), by setting (live hands vs screen) and by gender? The verified opener advice conflicts, 'always Paper' rests on screen data, and gender claims rest on self-report.
gaps.why_it_matters:
In best-of-3 bouts with replayed ties, the first throw is a large share of all throws and has no history to react to. The verified set gives conflicting openers:
- Paper first: Yoshizawa, C06.
- Scissors against experienced players: Batzilis.
- MF04: openers are 'unstable'.

It also proposes a +3 pp 'always Paper' default that rests mostly on screen-based labs, and has only self-report evidence on gender.

findings.statement:
In the 500 Japanese sessions, Paper was rarely thrown first.
- First throw: Rock 40.4% (202), Scissors 39.2% (196), Paper 20.4% (102; bootstrap 95% CI 16.8-24.2%). Chi-square(2)=37.7, p<0.001.
- Shares converged after the opener. Throw 2: Rock 31.2%, Paper 32.4%, Scissors 36.4%. Throws 3-5: each hand between 29% and 37%.

Net value of each opener against this mix:
- Rock: +18.8 pp (beats Scissors 39.2%, loses only to Paper 20.4%).
- Paper: +1.2 pp.
- Scissors: -20.0 pp.

This closely matches the independent Japanese online self-report (verified C14: first throw Scissors 42.0%, Rock 37.4%, Paper 20.6%; n=1,000).
findings.evidence:
My script komai_extra.py on the kuro-lab/RPSdata human files, using the coding in Komai et al. 2022, Appendix (rock, scissors, paper = 0, 1, 2). Output lines:
- 'throw 1 R 0.404 P 0.204 S 0.392 n 500'
- 'first-throw Paper share 95% CI 0.168-0.242'

The Toint 2023 values are as verified in Angle B C14.
findings.study_design: Japan. First game of 500 keyboard sessions against a program, before any information about the opponent. Compared with an online self-report survey of 1,000 Japanese adults (Angle B).
findings.effect_size: At the opener, relative to 1/3: Paper -12.9 pp, Rock +7.1 pp, Scissors +5.9 pp.
findings.strategic_implication: Against Japanese-like openers, Rock is the strong first throw (+19 pp). Whether Korean openers look like this is unknown (see G2-F2).
findings.caveats:
- Keyboard play against a program; possible interface or key-layout effects are not reported.
- Japanese chant conventions may shape openers in Japan but not in Korea.
- The first throw of a 50-game session may differ from a one-off live opener.

findings.statement:
US students' openers were the mirror image: Paper most, Rock least.

Pooled first throws across Brockbank & Vul's three public datasets (n=586): Paper 42.7%, Scissors 30.2%, Rock 27.1% (chi-square(2)=23.8, p<0.001). Paper led in each dataset separately:
- Human dyads: 44.2% (n=120).
- Fixed-pattern bots: 40.9% (n=252).
- Adaptive bots: 43.9% (n=214).

Against this mix, opening Scissors nets +15.6 pp and Rock -12.5 pp. That is the reverse of the Japanese sample (Rock +18.8, Scissors -20.0).

Other opener evidence:
- Moerel's Australian first games favoured Scissors (46.9%; verified MF04).
- Batzilis's 5.0 million Facebook openers were near-uniform (Paper 34.8%).
- A Korean wiki says, without a source and hedged ('~고 한다'), that Koreans mostly open with Paper: '가위/바위는 손 모양이 복잡하기에 대체로 처음에는 보를 많이 낸다고 한다.'
findings.evidence:
Script us_first_throws.py on rps_v1_data.csv (round 1, all players) and on rps_v2_data.csv and rps_v3_data.csv (round 1, is_bot = 0). Excluded rows (none or blank): 4, 17 and 13.

Rock / Paper / Scissors shares:
- v1: 0.333 / 0.442 / 0.225.
- v2: 0.254 / 0.409 / 0.337.
- v3: 0.257 / 0.439 / 0.304.
- Pooled: 0.271 / 0.427 / 0.302 (chi2 23.78).

Korean claim: Namu Wiki '가위바위보', section 4.1 통계, read via WebFetch.
findings.study_design:
- USA: UCSD undergraduates, course credit, online; first round of 300-round sessions against a human or a bot.
- Australia: as in MF04.
- Korea: community wiki claim with no data.
findings.effect_size: US openers relative to 1/3: Paper +9.4 pp, Rock -6.2 pp. The best opener (Scissors) gains +15.6 pp.
findings.strategic_implication:
The best opener flips sign between populations: Scissors against US-like openers, Rock against Japanese-like ones. With no Korean data, do not commit to a fixed opener.
- Randomize it with a device.
- Have teammates tally opponents' first throws in early bouts.
- If openers look Paper-heavy (as the Korean wiki claims), lean Scissors. If they look Paper-poor (the Japanese pattern), lean Rock.
findings.caveats:
- These are first throws of long computerised sessions, not live one-shot openers.
- US participants in v2/v3 may have known the opponent was a bot.
- The Korean claim is hearsay.

findings.statement:
Neither live hand play nor the Japanese screen sample showed a Rock excess.

Live, refereed, face-to-face Japanese RPS (Ito 2017: 42 Aichi students, 14 triads, 9 matches x 20 rounds per triad):
- Rock 33.1%, Paper 33.3%, Scissors 33.6% overall.
- No significant difference: ANOVA F(2,26)=0.09 with one player blindfolded, 0.01 with both.

Japanese screen data (Komai; 24,999 throws): Rock 32.2%, Scissors 35.1%, Paper 32.7%. So 'always Paper' would lose 2.9 pp per throw and 'always Rock' would gain 2.4 pp.

The other two live samples agree: Cook (UK, 32.4/33.3/34.4) and Aczel (Hungary, Scissors 36.7%). None of the three live samples has the Rock excess that the Paper default relies on.
findings.evidence:

Text: 'No significant main effect of the gesture was found for either the blind-sighted condition, F(2, 26) = .09, p = .91 ... or the blind-blind condition, F(2, 26) = .01, p = .98'.

Method:
- 'Forty-two undergraduate students (13 male, 29 female, Mage = 20.7 ...)'.
- 'Following a count of three given by the referee, the participants simultaneously displayed their gestures'.
- Pay: '1000 JPY', plus 'a bonus of 500 JPY' for each match won.

Komai shares: komai_analysis.py, 'human marginals R 0.3217, S 0.3511, P 0.3272, N 24999'.
findings.study_design:
- Ito: Japan, live face-to-face triads with a referee and a blindfold manipulation; cash per match won.
- Komai: Japan, screen play against a program.
findings.effect_size:
- Live Japanese shares: all within 0.3 pp of 1/3.
- Japanese screen: Scissors +1.8 pp, Rock -1.2 pp.
findings.strategic_implication: Do not use 'always Paper' as a default in live Korean play. A fixed lean toward one hand is worth a few pp at most, and its direction depends on the population.
findings.caveats:
- Ito's blindfolds may have changed choices.
- The unit of analysis is the triad (n=14); hand shares are averages of triad percentages.

findings.statement:

- Paper: +1.3 pp (CI -0.3 to +2.9).
- Scissors: -0.6 pp (CI -2.5 to +1.3).

First valid throw:

The direction matches the Japanese self-report (women Scissors 46.9%, men Rock 42.4%) and the WRPS claim 'males lead with Rock', but it is not significant.

findings.strategic_implication: Gender is not a usable signal for overall play. At most it is a weak hint for openers (women: Scissors, so answer Rock; men: Rock, so answer Paper), and not strong enough to override randomizing.
findings.caveats:
- The opener samples are tiny.
- Western sample.
- For some players the first valid throw came in game 2 because they did not respond in game 1.

gaps.gap: How quickly do human opponents detect and punish a fixed throwing habit, and how quickly can a tracker exploit human habits? The verified set did not analyse adaptation over the first few throws.
gaps.why_it_matters:
A team event mixes very short bouts with repeated exposure to the same people.
- A best-of-3 with replayed ties lasts about 3-6 throws.
- Exposure repeats through relay rematches, the opponents' teammates watching, or the Korean association's 3 sets x 3 games x best-of-3 format.

Whether a deliberate lean such as X- is safe depends on how many throws an opponent needs to read it. The verified D3, D4 and MF1 report only 300-round averages.

findings.statement:
Humans needed about 7-10 throws to start beating a habit followed 90% of the time. Data: Brockbank & Vul 2024, Exp 1, raw data (220 complete 300-round games).

Against the two self-transition bots (n=63 games):
- 'Always throw the hand your own last hand beats': Rock -> Scissors -> Paper -> Rock.
- 'Always upgrade': Rock -> Paper -> Scissors.

Human net per throw (95% CI):
- Throws 1-3: +0.016 (-0.082 to +0.113).
- Throws 4-6: +0.090 (-0.036 to +0.216).
- Throws 7-10: +0.274 (+0.160 to +0.388).
- Throws 21-30: +0.346. Throws 31-50: +0.367.

Pooled over all four simple-transition bots (adding 'beat the human's last hand' and 'copy the human's last hand'; n=127 games):
- +0.052 (n.s.), +0.121 (CI +0.030 to +0.212) and +0.199 (CI +0.117 to +0.281) in throws 1-3, 4-6 and 7-10.
- +0.312 by throws 21-30.

The 'copy the human's last hand' bot was exploited only from throws 21-30 (+0.253).
findings.evidence:
My scripts v2_learning.py and v2_pooled.py on rps_v2_data.csv (269 games, 220 complete).

Bot behaviour, verified from the data (v2_botcheck.py):
- prev_move_negative: downgraded its own hand 90.4% of the time.
- prev_move_positive: upgraded 90.5%.
- opponent_prev_move_positive: beat the human's previous hand 89.6%.
- opponent_prev_move_nil: copied it 90.3%.

Design, as verified in D4 (Cross et al. 2025): 'The bot opponents chose moves according to different sequential dependencies with 90% probability'.
findings.study_design: USA: UCSD undergraduates, course credit, online. 300 rounds against one bot that follows a pattern 90% of the time; points +3 / 0 / -1. Measure: net per throw ((wins - losses) / throws) per game, averaged over games.
findings.effect_size:
- Throws 1-3: +1.6 pp (n.s.).
- Throws 7-10: +27.4 pp.
- Throws 21-50: +35 to +37 pp per throw (random play earns 0).
findings.strategic_implication:
A fixed habit of choosing your next hand from your last one is essentially safe for the first ~3-6 throws against a given opponent, but gets read by about throw 7-10.
- Inside a single short bout, rule-based leans (e.g., G1's X-) are low-risk.
- Randomize with a device when you meet the same opponent again, in long formats (3 sets x 3 games x best-of-3), or after the opposing team has watched several of your throws.
findings.caveats:
- The bots were 90% deterministic. A human lean of 50-60% would be detected more slowly.
- US students playing on a screen.
- The early bins are small (63-127 games x 3-4 throws).
- Detection by watching rather than playing was not tested.

findings.statement:
Habits that depend on the previous outcome were read slowly and poorly. Two bots followed such a habit 90% of the time (n=61 games):
- 'Stay after a win, upgrade after a loss, downgrade after a tie'.
- 'Upgrade after a win, downgrade after a loss, stay after a tie'.

Human net per throw:
- Throws 1-3: +0.049 (n.s.).
- Throws 4-6: +0.148.
- Throws 7-10: +0.037 (n.s.).
- Throws 11-30: about +0.12.
- Throws 31-50: +0.037 (n.s.).
- Throws 201-300: only about +0.21.
findings.evidence:
v2_pooled.py, 'outcome_conditioned (2 bots) games 61':
- Throws 1-3: +0.049 (CI -0.090 to +0.188).
- 4-6: +0.148 (+0.020 to +0.275).
- 7-10: +0.037 (-0.073 to +0.147).
- 11-15: +0.125. 16-20: +0.118. 21-30: +0.115.
- 31-50: +0.037 (-0.030 to +0.104).

Late bins (v2_learning.py), throws 201-300: +0.221 and +0.210 for the two bots.

Bot behaviour, verified from the data:
- win_nil_lose_positive: stayed 89.4% after wins, upgraded 89.7% after losses, downgraded 90.3% after ties.
- win_positive_lose_negative: upgraded 90.9% after wins, downgraded 91.1% after losses, stayed 89.7% after ties.
findings.effect_size: +4 to +15 pp per throw and inconsistent, against +27 to +37 pp for simple transition habits by the same stage.
findings.strategic_implication: If you vary your next hand according to the previous outcome (verified C2-style responses), opponents are unlikely to read it within a bout. The habits to avoid are plain 'after X I throw Y' sequences.
findings.caveats: Same as G3-F1. The early +0.148 bin may be chance (its CI lower bound is +0.02).

findings.statement:
Adaptive bots that counted human patterns exploited humans almost immediately; bots that tracked only base-rate transitions never did. Data: Brockbank & Vul 2021 raw data, 196 complete games. Each bot always throws the counter to the human's most likely next hand.

The three bots conditioning on the last two moves, or on outcome x previous transition, were ahead from the first 10 throws (n=72 games). Human net per throw:
- Throws 1-10: -0.112 (95% CI -0.187 to -0.038).
- Throws 11-20: -0.056 (n.s.).
- Throws 21-30: -0.086.
- Throws 31-50: -0.118.
- After that: -0.10 to -0.13.

Bots tracking only the human's transition base rates (n=49 games):
- Never significantly ahead (throws 1-10: -0.029, CI -0.097 to +0.040).
- Counter-exploited from about throw 51 (+0.078), reaching +0.148 in throws 101-300.
findings.evidence: My script v3_pooled.py on rps_v3_data.csv (227 games, 196 complete). The bot labels and the per-bot overall means match verified D3 (e.g., opponent_prev_two_moves +36.9 per 300 rounds).
findings.study_design: USA: UCSD undergraduates, course credit, online. 300 rounds against one of 8 adaptive bots; points +3 / 0 / -1; 10-s limit per round.
findings.effect_size: Against the best trackers, humans lost a net 11 pp per throw in throws 1-10 and about 10-13 pp thereafter.
findings.strategic_implication: A teammate who tallies an opponent's (last hand, outcome) -> next hand pairs could, in principle, gain within a handful of throws; unaided players cannot (G3-F1, G3-F2). This supports giving one team member the job of scorer.
findings.caveats:
- The early bins are small and include round 1 (pure chance) and bot start-up behaviour.
- The bots compute exact counts, which humans cannot.
- Long sessions.

gaps.gap: Korean format variants (가위바위보 하나빼기, i.e. 'rock-paper-scissors minus one', and 묵찌빠): how should they be played? The verified set covers standard RPS only.
gaps.why_it_matters:
Korean team events may use 하나빼기 (shown in Squid Game season 2; Namu Wiki: '오징어 게임(시즌 2)에서 하나빼기 버전이 등장한다'). 묵찌빠 is a common Korean decider. In both, the equilibrium differs from 1/3-1/3-1/3:
- In 하나빼기, the pair you show first can make you a +1/3 favourite or underdog.
- In 묵찌빠, winning the opening throw makes you a 2/3 favourite.

Applying standard-RPS advice to these games would be wrong.

findings.statement:
하나빼기 (show two hands, then withdraw one) has an exact solution.

Stage 1, choosing a pair:
- Show two different hands. Showing the same hand twice is weakly dominated.
- The three pairs form their own RPS cycle, each beating the next by +1/3: {Rock+Paper} beats {Rock+Scissors}, which beats {Paper+Scissors}, which beats {Rock+Paper}.
- So choose the pair uniformly at random.

Stage 2, keeping a hand:
- Same pair on both sides: keep the hand that wins inside the pair (Rock+Paper -> Paper; Rock+Scissors -> Rock; Paper+Scissors -> Scissors). The result is a tie.
- Different pairs (they always share exactly one hand): each player keeps the shared hand with probability 2/3 and the other hand with 1/3.
- The favourite is the player whose extra hand beats the shared hand. The favourite wins 4/9, ties 4/9 and loses 1/9 (+1/3 per game).

Example: you show Paper+Scissors and the opponent shows Paper+Rock, so Paper is shared and your Scissors beats it. You are favoured. You keep Paper 2/3 and Scissors 1/3; they should keep Paper 2/3 and Rock 1/3.
findings.evidence:
Wizard of Odds, 'Rock Paper Scissors Minus One' (updated 3 Aug 2026):
- 'Triangle plays paper and scissors. Circle plays paper and rock.'
- 'Triangle should play scissors with probability 1/3 and paper 2/3. Circle should play rock with probability 1/3 and paper 2/3.'
- 'Triangle wins = 4/9 = 44.44%, Tie = 4/9 = 44.44%, Circle wins = 1/9 = 11.11%'.

Talwalkar, Mind Your Decisions (6 Jan 2025):
- 'Play PR, SR, SP with equal chance.'
- '...play that option with a 2/3 chance and the other with a 1/3 chance.' (the option common to both pairs)
- 'pick the stronger hand out of the two options (in PR pick P, in SR pick R, and in SP pick S).'

My exact rational solution of all nine 2x2 subgames (variants_math.py) reproduces these values. It gives the stage-1 value matrix [[0, 1/3, -1/3], [-1/3, 0, 1/3], [1/3, -1/3, 0]] (rows and columns R+P, R+S, P+S). Against a uniform opponent every pair earns 0. A double such as Rock+Rock scores -1 / 0 / -1 against best responses.
findings.study_design: Game-theoretic analysis from math blog and organisation pages, plus my exact computation. No human data.
findings.effect_size: In stage 2 the favoured pair wins 44.4%, ties 44.4% and loses 11.1% (+33.3 pp net). The game value is 0 when stage 1 is randomized.
findings.strategic_implication:
- Pick your pair with a device: uniform over the three pairs.
- After seeing both pairs: if they are the same, keep the hand that wins inside the pair. If they differ, keep the shared hand 2/3 of the time (e.g., with a die: 1-4 keep the shared hand, 5-6 keep the other).
- A human bias toward the 'safe' shared hand, or toward 'my extra hand', can be exploited.
findings.caveats:
- Assumes zero-sum scoring with ties replayed.
- The POST (Pe-Aguirre) argues that mutual 'loss aversion' in Squid Game's lethal setting means perfect play 'always results in a draw'. That framing does not apply to a tournament.
- I found no study of how humans actually play 하나빼기.

findings.statement:
묵찌빠: an ordinary RPS throw decides the first attacker. Then 'The defender loses if they play the same move as the attacker' and 'If not, the one who wins become the attacker and repeat it until they produce the same move.'

If both players throw uniformly at random in each exchange, the attacker's win probability V satisfies V = 1/3 + V/3 + (1-V)/3, so V = 2/3. Uniform play is an equilibrium: the attacker's payoff matrix for an exchange is circulant, so every pure choice earns 2/3 against a uniform opponent.

Winning the opening throw is therefore worth a 2/3 chance of winning the game.
findings.evidence: Rules quoted from Wikipedia, 'Muk-jji-ppa'. Exact check (variants_math.py): the attacker's value is 2/3, and each pure choice by the attacker or the defender yields 2/3 against a uniform opponent.
findings.study_design: Rules from an encyclopedia; the equilibrium is my own derivation. I found no human data and no published analysis.
findings.effect_size: The winner of the opening throw has a 66.7% chance of winning the game (vs 33.3% for the loser); before the opening throw it is 50%.
findings.strategic_implication:
In 묵찌빠:
- Put every evidence-based lean (openers, Gap 2) into the opening RPS throw.
- Then randomize uniformly in the exchanges.
- As defender, any habit of avoiding or matching the attacker's previous hand can be punished.
findings.caveats:
- Assumes the defender loses only by matching the attacker, and that calls and throws are simultaneous. House rules on call-before-throw timing could allow late reactions.
- The derivation is mine, not published, though it is checked by exact computation.

contradictions:
**After a tie (the most consequential conflict).**
- Zhejiang a=2 data (A1/C08): opponents repeat the tied hand 43% of the time, so beat it (Rock-Rock -> Paper, +0.20).
- Fixed-opponent data with no tie reward point the other way: throw the hand the tied hand beats. Western pairs (MF01/MF7) give +0.05 to +0.13. The new 500-player Japanese data give +0.084 overall and +0.114 in throws 2-10, while 'beat the tied hand' scores -0.14 to +0.01. Ogawa's classroom null (C13) was confounded by its comparison.
- Reconcile: the Zhejiang tie response tracks the tie payoff. Repeat rates fall from 0.80 when a tie pays like a win to 0.34 when ties pay 0 (MF02), alongside random re-matching and long 40-s sessions.
- In a knockout replay the tie is worth nothing and the opponent is fixed, so default to Rock-Rock -> Scissors, Paper-Paper -> Rock, Scissors-Scissors -> Paper. Only after a second identical tie does the evidence favour beating the tied hand (39.7% third repeat in Japan).

**Win-stay and relay champions.**
- One side: Angle C (C15) and Angle E (C15) imply 'a winner repeats, so throw what beats their winning hand'. Support: Zhejiang 0.528, Zhejiang vs AI 0.469, Dyson computer labs 0.36-0.44, relay computer avatars 38.2%.
- Other side: human fixed pairs (US 0.322, Australia 0.262) and the Japanese sample (0.305) show no win-stay. There, 'beat the winner's hand' loses (Australia -0.110, Japan -0.047).
- Reconcile by setting: win-stay appears with computer avatars and in reward-heavy or re-matched labs, and grows late in long sessions (MF2). Against people in a fixed bout, the safer reply after an opponent's win is the hand their winning hand beats (Japan +0.061, Australia +0.103).

**Over-switching vs over-repeating.**
- Angle C C09/C10 (tennis serves, random-generation tasks): humans switch too often.
- Angle C MF2 and Angle A A1 (Zhejiang): repeats exceed each type of switch.
- The new data side with over-switching in fixed-opponent play across four countries including Japan: repeat 28.2% overall; 0.265-0.298 in throws 2-10 for Japan, Australia and the US. Japanese field data show 22.8%.
- Reconcile: the repeat-prone samples are the Zhejiang lab protocols plus Eyler's single cell, which is known only second-hand. They do not show that East Asians in general repeat.

**Opening throw.** The candidates conflict:
- 'Paper first': Yoshizawa; Angle C C06, +2.8 pp against Facebook openers.
- 'Scissors against experienced players': Batzilis.
- US students open Paper-heavy (42.7%), so Scissors gains +15.6 pp.
- Japanese players open Paper-poor (20.4% observed, 20.6% self-reported), so Rock gains +18.8 pp.
- Moerel's first games are Scissors-heavy (46.9%).
- Ogawa found no first-throw effect, and a Korean wiki claims Koreans open with Paper.

Reconcile: openers depend on population and context, and the best opener even flips sign across samples. Without Korean data, randomize the opener and scout opponents' first throws.

**Rock excess and 'always Paper'.**
- Rock excess: screen labs (Zhejiang 35.7%, Moerel 35.3%, Dyson 35.6%) and Japanese field tallies (35.0%).
- No Rock excess in live refereed play: UK 32.4%, Japan 33.1%; Hungary shows Scissors 36.7%.
- Scissors excess in some screen samples: US dyads 34.6%; Japanese Komai 35.1%, where 'always Paper' scores -2.9 pp.

Reconcile by interface (Zhejiang's Rock button was left-most), live fist-pumping, and population. Any fixed hand default is worth about 3 pp at most and has the wrong sign in several samples.

**Short horizon.**
- MF2 (Angle A) concluded the first 1-20 throws are close to random.
- Pooled over outcomes, repeat-aversion is present from the second throw. 'Always X-' in throws 2-10: Japan +0.098 (SE 0.017, n=500), Australia +0.095, US +0.059.

Reconcile: MF2's outcome-split early cells were small (about 360-750 transitions). What builds late in a session is the Zhejiang-vs-AI win-stay, not repeat-aversion.

**Imitation.**
- Cook 2012: +3.0 pp more draws, one-tailed p about 0.055.
- Null replications: Aczel 2012 (Hungary, -1.2 pp); Ito 2017 (Japan, +1.7 pp, n.s.). Pooled g=0.15 with a CI that includes 0.
- In the two-gesture game, the effect is tiny and appears only early (Belot 2013).

Reconcile: small samples and differing procedures. Treat imitation as having no reliable effect.

**Stakes and win-stay.**
- Wang & Xu: win-stay falls as the win/tie payoff ratio rises (rho = -0.29).
- Forder & Dyson: win-stay rises from 35.9% to 48.4% when wins are worth +2.

Reconcile: the manipulations differ (relative tie value vs win magnitude), as do the designs (between vs within subjects) and the opponents (humans vs computer). Do not predict opponents' win-stay from tournament stakes.

**Direction after a loss.** Popular media (NPR, MIT Technology Review 2014) said losers move Rock -> Paper. The data mostly show the reverse: players who lose downgrade (Rock -> Scissors) more often than they upgrade.
- Zhejiang: 0.365 vs 0.276.
- Dyson 2016: 0.405 vs 0.372.
- Australia: 0.374 vs 0.340.
- Japan: 0.399 vs 0.336.
- Near-equal in the US (0.386 vs 0.377) and Forder & Dyson (39.41% vs 39.13%).

Reconcile: the media misread 'clockwise'. Downgrading is the most common post-loss switch.

**Fixed rules vs exploitability.**
- Angle A C2 recommends outcome-specific rules, and MF1 warns that 'throw what your own last hand beats' is easily exploited (humans won 62% against such a bot over 300 rounds).
- The new time course shows humans need about 7-10 throws to read even a 90% habit (throws 1-3: +0.016, n.s.).

Reconcile by horizon: rule-based leans are low-risk inside one short bout but risky across rematches or when opponents are watching.

**Team deliberation.**
- Angle E C11: teams are more game-theoretic.
- MF5: that advantage is confined to dominance-solvable games.
- Okano: teams are closer to minimax in zero-sum games, but the advantage fades over time.

Reconcile: in RPS, team discussion helps balance and randomize play, not find edges.

**Pausing after a loss.**
- Correlations: Dyson 2021, r=0.202 (reported p=.036; about .089 two-tailed when recomputed); Dyson 2018, r about .58-.65.
- The only causal test, a forced pause, cut lose-shift by 7.7 pp but produced the lowest win rate (33.5%).

Reconcile: slowing down marks good modelling of the opponent; it does not cause winning.

**Doubled hands.** The WRPS 'Double Run' rule says that after X, X you can eliminate X. The data disagree: a third identical throw followed 28.5% (Australia), 30.5% (Dyson), 34.0% (US) and 35.8% (Japan) of the time, and 39.7% after two same-hand ties in Japan.

Reconcile: never eliminate a doubled hand; players who have already repeated are prone to repeat.

**Gender.**
- Claims: WRPS 'males lead with Rock' and the Japanese self-report (women Scissors 46.9%, men Rock 42.4%).
- Observed Australian play: no overall gender difference (Rock 35.0% for men vs 35.7% for women). Opener directions match the claims but are not significant (women Scissors 53%, men Rock 41%; p=0.18).

Reconcile: gender is at most a weak hint about openers.

errors: No wrong year, venue, author or title found for S1, S2, S4, S6-S15 or S17-S21 (metadata checked against arXiv API, PMC/Europe PMC XML, publisher PDFs and Semantic Scholar).

S4 (Xu, Zhou & Wang 2013, Physica A 392:4997-5005) is presented as an earlier, separate 12-group study. Its sessions (Zhejiang, December 2010, 72 subjects, 0.15 RMB/point) match S1's a=2 condition (experiment run December 2010-March 2014, 12 groups, r = 0.45/3), so it is very likely the same data, not an independent replication.

S24 (MIT Technology Review, 30 Apr 2014) does give a hand mapping, '(where R -> P -> S is clockwise)', which reverses the paper's definition; the sweep said 'no hand mapping given'. The canonical URL is https://www.technologyreview.com/2014/04/30/13423/how-to-win-at-rock-paper-scissors/ (the /s/527026/ link redirects there).
S23: the NPR original is at https://www.npr.org/sections/thetwo-way/2014/05/02/308953770/rock-scissors-paper-strategy-could-be-more-than-mere-childs-play; its text matches the KSUT syndicated copy.

S21 (Cook et al. 2012, Proc R Soc B 279(1729):780-786) is open in full text on PMC (PMC3248720), contrary to the sweep's 'abstract only' note; the Aczel et al. 2012 reply (PMC3385727) is also open in full.

S22 (National Geographic blog, 19 Jul 2011) misreports Cook et al.: it says sighted players moved more than 200 ms after their opponent 'on around half of the games'. The paper's separate four-pair video study found the blind player moved first in 44.7% of rounds and by more than 200 ms in 17.2%.
S23 (内田さくら 2017, 自由研究 第42集): the report spans pp. 31–36, not pp. 31–35.

S19 (WRPS 'Definitive Guide') calls Yoshizawa's data 'A 1998 Japanese study by Mitsuo Yoshizawa'. Yoshizawa's own 2019 article says only '1990年代後半' (late 1990s) and his 2006 book 'なん年か前' (some years ago), so the specific year 1998 is unsourced.

S19 (WRPS 'Definitive Guide') gives Roshambull as '36% Rock, 30% Paper and 34% Scissors'. That matches Batzilis et al. 2019's all-throws distribution (35.45/34.01/30.54) only with Paper and Scissors swapped, which points to a WRPS transposition.

S16 (Ogawa 2013) and S17 (PRESIDENT Online 2024) describe Yoshizawa's sample as '725人の学生' / '学生725人', and PRESIDENT attributes it to 桜美林大学 via a 2009 Nikkei piece. Yoshizawa's own 2019 article says 'のべ725人', recorded by 10 seminar students at 'the university where I worked then', and the 2006 book says '725人'.
S17 (PRESIDENT Online, 2024-03-06) misstates Yoshizawa's all-consecutive-pairs repeat rate (2,465/10,833 = 22.75%) as the repeat rate after a tie ('あいこになったとき、次も同じ手を出す確率は22.8％').

S02 (Eyler et al. 2009): Crossref DOI 10.4169/193113409x469578 is registered to the whole 'Classroom Capsules' section (pp. 125–130) under the authors Alfaro, Han and Schilling. It should not be cited as the DOI of the Eyler article (pp. 125–128).

S10 (Wang L et al. 2020, Sci Rep 10:13873): Table 4 is titled '52 people', but its means (106.6098, 96.29268, 97.09756) equal integer totals divided by 41 players (4,371/3,948/3,981). This inconsistency is inside the source itself.

S20 (Linux Journal, Dave Taylor, 2017-07-18) attributes 'rock is chosen 35.4%, paper 35% of the time and scissors only 29.6%' to the World RPS Society. Neither archived WRPS page examined (2009 'How to beat anyone', 2010 'Definitive Guide') contains 35.4 or 35.0.

S06 (Lanctot et al.) is listed as a preprint 'under review' at TMLR. The arXiv v2 comments say 'Accepted at TMLR October 2023'. Cite it as Transactions on Machine Learning Research (2023), OpenReview id qQnJ70DIAx, and classify it as peer-reviewed.

S14 (Gauriot, Page & Wooders 2016 SSRN working paper 'Nash at Wimbledon: Evidence from Half a Million Serves') was published as 'Expertise, gender, and equilibrium play', Quantitative Economics 14(3):981–1020 (2023), doi:10.3982/QE1563. The serial-correlation figures used in C09 (e.g. 7.0%/2.9%, which are for men's first serves) come only from the working paper.

S11 (Camerer, Ho & Chong 2004, QJE 119(3):861–898): the summary rows of Table II are labelled 'Mean 1.30 / Median 1.61'. Recomputing from the 24 τ values gives mean 1.61 and median 1.30, which matches the Sec. IV.A text. The introduction's 'median estimate is τ̂ = 1.61' is therefore actually the mean.

S23 (Guseva et al. 2023) cites the JEP:General 121(3):352–363 (1992) paper as 'Budescu & Rapoport (1992)'. Its author order is Rapoport & Budescu (1992). Budescu & Rapoport is the 1994 J. Behavioral Decision Making 7:261–278 paper.

S01 (Batzilis et al.) footnote 8 compresses the NYT quote. In Vogel (2005), the twins' reason for opening with scissors was 'Everybody knows you always start with scissors ... Rock is way too obvious, and scissors beats paper'. 'Everybody expects you to choose rock' was the reason for sticking with scissors after a tie. The NYT gives the collection as worth more than $20M and the Cézanne estimate as more than $12M. S38's '$16 million' does not appear in the NYT.

S33 (Wang et al. 2020): Table 4 is captioned as the preferences of 52 people, but its means (106.6098 / 96.29268 / 97.09756) are exact multiples of 1/41 (totals 4371 / 3948 / 3981). It therefore averages 41 players.

S20 / C14 (Dyson & Asad 2021): the sample sizes and percentages come from the PsyArXiv preprint (152 participants, 149 retained; 34.27/38.09/36.58%). The published npj Science of Learning 6:19 article reports 148 participants, 145 retained, and 34.29/38.28/36.68%.
S26 (Wei, Liu, Dollack & Perusquia-Hernandez, arXiv:2606.29423): the arXiv record says 'Accepted by ACII2025', so it is a peer-reviewed conference paper (ACII 2025), not an 'unreviewed preprint'.

S15 (Dyson, Sundvall, Forder & Douglas 2018, JEP:HPP 44(10):1483-1487): the paper reports three experiments, not two (Exp 3: N=40, 30 analysed, points converted to money at 10p per point). Its Exp 1 RTs (435/397/488 ms) are averaged over random and exploitable opponents, not random opponents only.
S16 (Dyson 2024): the post-win/post-loss RT values cited from the preprint's 'Table 2' appear in Table 1 of the published article (PMC11543769). Exp 2 N is exactly 72.

S13 (Dyson 2021, Sci Rep 11:2859): internal reporting inconsistency in the source. The Fig. 2 correlations are stated for n=72 (Exps 2-3), but their p-values (r=0.202, p=0.036; r=0.295, p=0.002; r=-0.103, p=0.287) match n of about 108. At n=72, r=0.202 gives two-tailed p of about 0.089.

C1 internal cross-reference: 'Two replications did not reproduce the effect (see C2 and C3)'. Only C2 contains the RPS replications (Aczel 2012; Ito 2017); C3 covers the Matching Pennies extension (Belot 2013) and its video-coded replication (Aczel 2015).
S30 (Kayhan et al. 2022): the article number Sci Rep 12:12967 is missing from the citation.
